title: Meyer signs maternal health bill requiring safe discharge plans

text:
New law requires hospitals to document clinical justification, transportation and backup care for pregnant patients discharged with signs of labor
DOVER — Delaware hospitals must create formal discharge plans for pregnant patients sent home before delivery after Gov. Matt Meyer signed Senate Bill 301 into law Monday.
The legislation applies when a pregnant patient experiencing signs or symptoms consistent with labor is discharged from inpatient care or observation status. It does not require hospitals to admit every patient who may be in labor, leaving the discharge decision to the documented clinical judgment of the treating health care professional.
However, when a patient is discharged, the hospital must provide a written plan intended to ensure the patient understands what to do next and has a safe way to obtain additional care.
“When a mother is in labor, ‘good luck’ is not a plan,” Meyer said. “Any pregnant woman who shows up to a hospital in Delaware should feel seen, heard and cared for until she and her baby are safe.”
The ceremonial signing was held at Josie’s Grace, a Newark-based nonprofit that provides maternal mental health support during pregnancy, after childbirth and during the transition to parenthood.
What hospitals must provide
Under the new law, a discharge plan must include:

Aftercare instructions and confirmation that they were explained to the patient, the patient’s representative or a caregiver;
An assessment of the distance and travel time between the patient’s primary residence and the hospital;
Verification that the patient has reliable transportation between the residence and hospital;
Identification of a backup hospital or facility where the patient could receive labor and delivery services; and
The clinical justification for discharging the patient.

The plan must be discussed with the patient, the patient’s representative or a caregiver and included in the patient’s medical record. If the patient or representative declines to participate, the hospital must document that refusal.
The Department of Health and Social Services may adopt regulations and enforce the discharge-planning requirements. The full bill is available through the Delaware General Assembly.
Bill received unanimous support
The legislation was sponsored by Sen. Marie Pinkney, D-Bear, and House Speaker Melissa Minor-Brown, D-New Castle. It passed the Senate 20-0 on May 20 and the House 40-0 on June 24.
“As a nurse, I know that discharge is not simply the moment a patient walks out of the hospital; it is a critical part of their care,” Minor-Brown said. “A pregnant patient who seeks help because she is in pain or experiencing labor-like symptoms deserves to leave knowing what is happening, what warning signs to watch for, what steps to take next and when to return for immediate care.”
Pinkney said the measure is intended to address gaps in maternal care, including concerns that Black women are more likely to have their symptoms or concerns dismissed by medical professionals.
The Delaware legislation was modeled after the federal Women Expansion of Learning and Labor Safety, or WELLS Act, advanced in Congress by U.S. Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and U.S. Rep. Robin Kelly of Illinois.
The federal proposal is named for Mercedes Wells, an Indiana woman who gave birth along a roadside shortly after being discharged from a hospital while experiencing labor symptoms.
“From the first trimester to the fourth trimester, we want to make sure moms and families have the support they need to be healthy,” Blunt Rochester said. “The signing of Delaware Senate Bill 301 will save lives while building on the work we’re doing in Congress to end the maternal health crisis.”
Hospitals supported goal, questioned mandate
During the legislative debate, the Delaware Healthcare Association supported the bill’s patient-safety goals but took a neutral position because of concerns about placing additional clinical requirements into state law.
The association said Delaware hospitals already operate under federal emergency-care standards and other regulatory oversight and maintain protocols for responding to pregnant patients showing signs of labor.
It recommended that the state also collect and publish annual county-level information about births that occur while a patient is traveling to a hospital or unintentionally at home. Such reporting, the association said, could help determine whether inappropriate hospital discharges are occurring in Delaware.
The law’s unanimous passage suggests lawmakers ultimately viewed the additional planning requirements as a reasonable safeguard. Implementation will now determine how hospitals document transportation, identify backup facilities and incorporate the requirements into existing discharge procedures without unnecessarily delaying care.
TO GO BOX

Law: Senate Bill 301
What it does: Requires Delaware hospitals to create a documented discharge plan when a pregnant patient experiencing signs or symptoms of labor is sent home before delivery.
Required information: Clinical justification, aftercare instructions, travel assessment, reliable transportation and a backup labor and delivery facility.
Who oversees it: Delaware Department of Health and Social Services.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Two Florida Democrats join every Republican in Congress in voting to condemn socialism and the DSA
description: Two Florida Democrats who are fighting for their political lives after seeing their congressional seats redistricted voted Tuesday for a resolution denouncing “socialism in all of its forms.” Kathy Castor and Darren Soto joined six other Democrats in supporting the resolution. The final vote was 220-192, with two Democrats voting present. The resolution “den[...]
text:
The U.S. Capitol on the evening of Sept. 30, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Two Florida Democrats who are fighting for their political lives after seeing their congressional seats redistricted voted Tuesday for a resolution denouncing “socialism in all of its forms.”
Kathy Castor via U.S. House
Rep. Darren Soto, via his Facebook page
Kathy Castor and Darren Soto joined six other Democrats in supporting the resolution. The final vote was 220-192, with two Democrats voting present.
The resolution “denounces socialism in all of its forms, including the Democratic Socialists of America.”
Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates have seen success in high-profile primary races across the country this summer, including in Florida, where Jacksonville state Rep. Angie Nixon defeated the vastly better-funded Alex Vindman in the primary for U.S. Senate last month.
Colorado Republican Rep. Jeff Crank, who sponsored the resolution, said last week that it was a “simple up or down vote” on the platform of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).
Castor has represented a district in the Tampa Bay area for 20 years, but her re-election hopes are in question after her district was redistricted to one that Donald Trump won by more than 10 points in 2024. Soto’s Central Florida district was completely wiped out, and he now is running in an area that supported Trump by more than 18 points in 2024.
Florida Republicans have seized on the momentum of the DSA nationally this summer to paint Florida Democrats as socialists, and they received a gift of sorts when Nixon defeated Vindman.
“The DSA has infiltrated the Democratic Party at all levels of government and has never been more apparent than here in the state of Florida with the election of Angie Nixon for U.S. Senate,” Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia said Tuesday during a Republican Party of Florida event in Tampa. “It has never been more apparent that the Democratic Party of Florida is the DSA.”
Most Democrats opposed the resolution because it included language urging passage of the SAVE America Act.
“House Resolution 1490 explicitly calls for enactment of the so-called SAVE America Act, which is the top legislative priority of far-right extremists. Accordingly, I will vote No on the latest MAGA effort to rig the midterm elections,” House Democratic Leader Hakeen Jeffries said.

text:
Delaware voters have multiple days to cast ballots before the Sept. 15 primary, providing greater flexibility and another opportunity to participate in decisions that often shape state and local government.
Early voting for Delaware’s 2026 primary election begins Wednesday, Sept. 2, and continues through Sunday, Sept. 13, with a two-day pause for the Labor Day holiday.
Unlike absentee voting, voters do not need to provide a reason for voting early. The process is essentially the same as voting on Election Day: Election officers verify the voter’s eligibility, the voter signs the electronic pollbook and then casts a ballot on an accessible voting machine.
A Delaware voter may use any early-voting center in the county where the voter lives. Voters do not have to use their assigned Election Day polling place during early voting. Delaware Department of Elections

The primary election will be held Tuesday, Sept. 15. Election Day polling places will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Delaware primary-election information
Who can vote in the primary?
Delaware conducts closed primary elections:

Registered Democrats may vote in the Democratic primary.
Registered Republicans may vote in the Republican primary.
Unaffiliated voters and voters registered with minor parties generally may not participate in either major party’s primary.
Not every voter will have a contested race on the ballot.

The regular deadline to change political parties for this primary was May 29.
There is a special exception for some voters automatically registered through the Division of Motor Vehicles who were not previously given an opportunity to select a party. Those voters may affiliate with the Democratic or Republican Party through Sept. 15, including at an early-voting center. Delaware voter-registration guidance
Voters should use the state’s iVote portal to confirm their registration and review their voting information before leaving home.

The Fairfield Inn location is designated for the primary only. Voters should confirm locations before traveling through the state’s official early-voting list.
What should I bring?
Poll workers will ask voters to show identification, and presenting it generally speeds up check-in. However, Delaware does not require photo identification to vote in state and federal elections.
A voter whose name appears on the poll list but who does not present identification may complete an Affirmation of Voter Identity and then vote.
Before going to the polls:

Confirm your registration and party affiliation.
Review your sample ballot.
Select any early-voting center in your county.
Bring identification if available.
Leave candidate clothing, buttons and other campaign materials outside the voting room.

Voters may bring children age 17 or younger with them. Cellphone conversations are not permitted inside the polling place. Delaware voting FAQ
Why participation matters in Delaware
Primaries can be decisive
In districts where one party has a substantial registration advantage, the winner of that party’s primary may enter the general election as the strong favorite. That gives primary voters considerable influence over who ultimately holds office.
Local decisions affect everyday life
Many primary ballots include candidates for the General Assembly, county government and other offices responsible for decisions involving state spending, taxes, schools, land use, roads, housing, public safety and business regulation.
Smaller elections magnify each vote
Delaware is a small state, and legislative and county contests involve much smaller electorates than presidential races. A relatively modest number of votes can therefore determine a nomination.
Broader participation produces a more representative result
When only the most committed political voters participate, a small portion of eligible voters may choose the nominees presented to everyone in November. Greater turnout gives candidates and elected officials a clearer picture of the priorities of the broader community.
Early voting removes Election Day uncertainty
Work demands, family responsibilities, illness, traffic and weather can interfere with Election Day plans. Voting early gives residents several opportunities to cast a ballot while allowing Election Day polling places to serve voters who need or prefer to wait.
Looking ahead to November
Delaware’s general election is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Every eligible registered voter may participate regardless of party affiliation.

The deadline to register for the general election is Oct. 10. Delaware general-election information

title: Kansas primary yields second-highest voter turnout in history
description: TOPEKA — The Aug. 4 primary election, which featured contentious races and a hot-button ballot question, had the second-highest primary voter turnout in Kansas history, according to the Secretary of State’s Office. More than 650,000 Kansans cast ballots on and leading up to the election, making it second only to turnout in the 2022 election, […]
text:
Kansas Secretary of State Scott Schwab has overseen the two highest voter turnout primary elections in state history in 2022 and 2026. He appears on May 19, 2026, at the Docking State Office Building in Topeka. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The Aug. 4 primary election, which featured contentious races and a hot-button ballot question, had the second-highest primary voter turnout in Kansas history, according to the Secretary of State’s Office.
More than 650,000 Kansans cast ballots on and leading up to the election, making it second only to turnout in the 2022 election, when more than 922,000 people voted.
Kansans in both elections were voting on pivotal ballot measures. This year, voters rejected a measure that attempted to turn Kansas Supreme Court seats into elected positions. In 2022, voters similarly rejected a measure that would have taken away abortion protections.
Kansas Secretary of State Scott Schwab announced the turnout total Tuesday after state officials certified the results.
“Today’s certification reflects the hard work and dedication of election officials across Kansas,” Schwab said in a news release. “I am grateful to the 105 counties and the thousands of election workers who administered this election and ensured the results were accurately reported.”
Nearly 224,000 people voted in advance of the primary election. Schwab announced on Aug. 14 that all Kansas counties completed post-election audits, a process that ensures hand counts match ballot tabulation machines.
He said county election officials are preparing for the midterms in November. Voter registration is open through Oct. 13.

title: Sayge is on her way to becoming a pediatric occupational therapist
description:
Sayge Bohannon is heading into her senior year in high school with confidence—juggling four college-level classes, National Honor Society, and two sports. A TikTok video sparked her interest in pediatric occupational therapy, and she's learned to trust her instincts as she applies to college.

text:
Sayge Bohannon is confident that this will be a great school year. Having done well in college-level classes last year, now she’s feeling far less nervous about taking four classes online at the Community College of Vermont (CCV) through Vermont’s Early College program, while enrolled in Richford High School.
Sayge is also president of her school’s National Honor Society chapter and stays active in soccer and track. Between the coursework and her other activities, Sayge feels ready for senior year, with just the right amount of challenge to prepare her for college.
“Of all places,” TikTok inspired Sayge’s research into her career focus
Sayge will be applying to colleges this fall as well. The oldest of six siblings (including two sets of twins), she’s been around kids her whole life and loves working with them. She knows she doesn’t want to be a teacher or in a classroom setting, although a career where she can help people appeals to her. 
She’s put those passions together and will be applying to programs to prepare her to be a pediatric occupational therapist. “Of all places, I actually found out about the career on TikTok, believe it or not,” she laughed. “At the time, I thought I wanted to be a nurse but have also always loved working with kids. I saw a ‘day in the life’ on TikTok and I was so interested in the opportunity to be able to work with kids living with disabilities.” As she researched it more, she became even more invested in the option for her future. 
To make sure it was what she wanted, Sayge shadowed an occupational therapist at the University of Vermont Medical Center. While the experience was mostly focused on older patients, she says she got a lot out of her time there, and it affirmed her interest in working with kids. 
Putting the puzzle together: preparing for college
As she’s started to put the pieces together to apply to college this year, Sayge is relying more and more on Matt Mitchell, a VSAC outreach counselor in VSAC’s GEAR UP college and career readiness program. She describes her school as a place where she feels like she always has access to the resources she needs to get help with college-related questions. Sayge started working with Matt a few years ago. 
“I meet with him every other week to work through my questions. I’ve had so many, and I want to make sure I’m on the right track,” she says. 
Her school counselor helps as well, and together, they’ve helped Sayge navigate her college-level curriculum, and now college applications. “I worked with Matt on my Common Application, and he’s always there helping to guide me and making sure that the colleges I’m looking at are aligned with my goals,” she shares. 
Matt also helped Sayge find a scholarship that will cover the cost of some of her textbooks and course materials for the CCV classes she is currently taking. She needed some financial help to make it work out, and he was able to guide her to the scholarship that would eventually cover it. 
They’re now working on the list of where Sayge will apply to college. She’s winnowing her list down to exactly what she wants, but it’s tough. She toured two colleges this summer and may be doing some more tours this fall. She had to do the FAFSA financial aid forms for her CCV program, and feels good that it’s already familiar to her, now that she’s completing it again for this fall’s college applications. 
Sayge dreams big, but trusts her instincts
“I always knew I wanted to go to college,” Sayge notes. “I’ve always enjoyed school and learning and college is something my mom always wanted for me and supported as she didn’t have that opportunity.” Sayge shares that the big goals she has for herself also make her mom proud. 
As she gets everything organized for fall applications, her essay, FAFSA, other scholarship applications, and everything else on her big list, Sayge is learning to trust her instincts, working through her questions to clarify that she’s heading in the right direction. “When I’ve done the work, I’ll know it’s the right fit,” she says. 
It’s something she learned through her CCV application process, and she’s applying that same work ethic this fall to her next steps. With hard work and a little guidance, Sayge is ready to trust the process—confident that wherever she lands, it’ll be exactly where she’s meant to be.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Collins survives Wu-backed primary challenge, Brownsberger-Lander race too close to call
description: On Beacon Hill, with a reputation for opacity and top-down leadership, swapping sitting senators for first-time progressives may have limited utility when it comes to vote count. But Tuesday sent the signal that local representatives perceived as unfriendly to the city’s goals should expect rockier roads in future primaries.
text:
SOUTH BOSTON STATE Sen. Nick Collins fended off a challenge from his left flank on Tuesday night, but Belmont state Sen. Will Brownsberger’s fate was hanging by less than 100 votes by Wednesday morning. The two senators representing Boston fought for their political lives this election season against progressive challengers backed by Mayor Michelle Wu. 
Despite Massachusetts’s notoriously uncompetitive elections, a series of progressive upstarts saw an opportunity up and down the ballot to try to boot incumbents. For the most part, they were unsuccessful. 
Collins, first elected to the Senate in 2018, is set to head into another term representing the First Suffolk district after securing about 54 percent of the vote in a tight race against first-time candidate Latoya Gayle, an early education advocate from Dorchester.  
Another first-time candidate, Daniel Lander, kept the Suffolk and Middlesex District race within an eyelash against 14-year incumbent Brownsberger. Unofficial results showed Brownsberger up by 61 votes with all precincts counted, with the possibility of a recount in the air. 
Wu took the unusual step of publicly backing primary challengers against the two sitting state senators — a level of direct involvement in Beacon Hill races that can be a risky public bet for a Boston mayor and leave questions about the presumed independence of the candidates. Wu has said it isn’t personal. The senators, she argued, were voting “against the interests of their constituents.” 
The vote that flipped the switch took place in January. The state Senate rejected Wu’s plan to temporarily shift more of Boston’s property tax burden onto commercial real estate, a move meant to soften a spike in bills for homeowners. Collins and Brownsberger led the opposition. 
In the First Suffolk District — South Boston, Dorchester, the South End — Wu endorsed Gayle over four-term senator Collins. 
“Average folks, people, don’t know what’s going on at the State House,” Gayle told WBUR while door-knocking, arguing voters were ready to ask for more than incumbency.  
“Sometimes you have to dust off the cleats,” Collins told the Boston Globe in an interview Tuesday night. “Nobody owns a seat, and I think it’s made me a better senator. It’s tested my team and brought out the best in the district.” 
Gayle conceded the race just after 10 p.m., according to the Dorchester Reporter. Of Collins’s remark that he is a better senator because of the contest, Gayle said, “I hope he means that.” 
According to the unofficial vote breakdowns, South Boston locked in the final win. While the two candidates largely split the wards throughout the district, the South Boston senator carried his home neighborhood by over 2,000 votes, with his overall margin of victory just over 2,300 votes. 
Collins dramatically outraised and outspent Gayle, with the incumbent senator and former state representative hauling in $415,000 and spending about $408,000 from January through August. Gayle, whose committee opened in December, raised about $73,000 and spent about $55,000 over a comparable eight-month span, but did not have an August filing with the Massachusetts Office of Campaign and Political Finance. 
Boston-focused political action committees were also active in the race. Citizens for an Affordable Massachusetts and A Balanced and Better Boston, which has ties to former Mayor Marty Walsh, spent at least $95,700 supporting Collins. Gayle, meanwhile, drew support from the Wu-aligned Boston Leads PAC, which spent more than $80,000 between her and the other upstart with the mayor’s backing. 
In the Suffolk and Middlesex District, spanning Belmont, Watertown, and parts of Boston and Cambridge, Wu endorsed her former City Hall aide Lander against Senate President pro tempore Brownsberger, a 14-year incumbent from Belmont. 
“My track record has been a force for good in every session,” Brownsberger told the Charles River Regional Chamber of Commerce at a candidate debate. 
Lander boasted the backing of progressives in and outside of the Bay State, including New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, US Sen. Bernie Sanders, and US Sen. Elizabeth Warren, for whom Lander served as senior political adviser to her 2020 presidential campaign. US Rep. Katherine Clark, Gov. Maura Healey, Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll, and Attorney General Andrea Campbell all endorsed Brownsberger.  
Neither candidate has August filings with the state campaign finance office. Lander’s committee raised about $187,100 from December through the end of July and spent just $44,850. Brownsberger, who started the race already sitting on roughly $180,800, pulled in another $331,900 over the same eight months and spent about $277,100. 
While the Collins seat was a test of Boston mayoral power entirely within Boston, Brownsberger represents one of the split districts where non-Boston electeds represent the capital city often chafing against Beacon Hill’s iron grip. 
Based on the Associated Press’s vote data, Lander preserved narrow margins in Cambridge and Watertown while ending with a roughly 1,700-vote lead in Boston. But Belmont came out for its sitting senator, with the Middlesex town handing Brownsberger a lead of about 2,200 votes. 
Collins and Brownsberger became the face of Wu’s frequent clashes with the state Senate, though the House has also waved away her efforts to change policy through proposals like a tax on high-value real estate sales and a swing at rent control.  
On Beacon Hill, with a reputation for opacity and top-down leadership, swapping sitting senators for first-time progressives may have limited utility when it comes to vote count. But Tuesday sent the signal that local representatives perceived as unfriendly to the city’s goals should expect rockier roads in future primaries. 
State Sen. Lydia Edwards, of East Boston, a Wu ally, told the Boston Globe earlier this year that she wondered if Wu’s endorsements constitute “normal politics” or “a division that can’t be mended.” 
The tax vote cut the other way as well, with Wu endorsing Sen. Mike Rush, a moderate West Roxbury Democrat who proposed Wu’s bill as an amendment to legislation the Senate advanced. Rush faced first own primary challenge in almost two decades from progressive attorney Persis Yu, which is also sitting at a razor thin margin with Yu up by less than a percentage point. 
No Republican has filed in either Boston district, so Collins and the ultimate victor in the Suffolk and Middlesex race will sail through the general election to fill the seats for the next term.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Ryan Fazio claims Lamont ‘destroyed’ fiscal caps. But did he?
description: While Lamont has engaged in workarounds, he says the routine has led to savings, cut pension debt and offset federal cuts to vital services.
text:
Ryan Fazio, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, hasn’t minced words when it comes to Gov. Ned Lamont’s handling of state budget caps imposed as part of a bipartisan deal in 2017, the year before he was elected to his first term.
“The governor has inherited the only good budgeting policy that the state has adopted in my lifetime,” Fazio told the Connecticut Mirror, “and has essentially destroyed [it] by the end of his second term.”
The reality is more nuanced.
Over the past two legislative sessions, Lamont and the Democratic-controlled General Assembly have used off-budget accounting to circumvent a spending cap by more $750 million, formally exceeded that restriction three times by another $1.2 billion and repeatedly underbudgeted for Medicaid and guaranteed employee benefits.
But while Lamont has engaged in alterations and workarounds, the two-term governor insists they are still keeping the state on a routine that has generated huge savings, paid down pension debt faster than any of his predecessors and offset unprecedented federal cuts to nutrition, health care and other vital services.
Meanwhile, Fazio and other Senate Republicans were the only caucus not to propose a state budget or show how they would resolve cap challenges either of the past two years.
“Ryan Fazio wants to lecture Connecticut about fiscal guardrails, as a member of a caucus that couldn’t even be bothered to put forth a budget,” Lamont campaign spokeswoman Lauren Gray said Tuesday, noting the contested spending chiefly involves affordable childcare, K-12 education and other aid to cities and towns.
“The truth is, the governor strengthened our state’s fiscal guardrails, using them to pay down billions in pension debt while still investing in what actually matters to families,” she added. “That’s what responsible budgeting looks like.”
Budget ‘guardrails’ worked because of huge federal COVID grants
Fazio and Lamont are sparring over a series of spending, borrowing and other caps adopted nine years ago with bipartisan support to stem a string of budget deficits and several major tax hikes.
Those caps have forced unprecedented savings.
In the two decades prior, the average state budget closed with a surplus equal to 1/10th of 1% of the General Fund. In the nine years under the “guardrails,” as supporters call them, the average surplus is nearly 9%.
But most of that isn’t due to bull markets on Wall Street or new operating efficiencies.
The 2017 legislature created a controversial program that captures huge chunks of income and business tax receipts before they even arrive in the state budget — without projecting how much would be removed or the ramifications for programs.
But despite generating massive surpluses averaging $1.8 billion yearly under Lamont, who inherited this system in 2019, the budget challenges were masked by COVID. Specifically, the federal Coronavirus Relief Fund and American Rescue Plan Act gave state government directly $4.2 billion officials could use — outside of cap rules — to cover almost any operating expense.
As the “guardrails” were extracting nearly $2 billion a year from core programs, Lamont and legislators could use COVID grants to blunt the pain.
Think of it as fiscal Novocain.
But state officials had assigned the bulk of those dollars by the end of the 2024 session, and nearly all have been spent by now.
Lamont initially insisted ‘guardrails’ didn’t need adjustments
Still, when the CT Mirror outlined the impending problems as these grants wound down, Lamont, a fiscal moderate, said there was no need to “fuss” about the numbers. “I think we’re OK,” he said.
We weren’t.
Connecticut would overspend its Medicaid account by almost $160 million in 2024. Rather than tightening program eligibility to cut costs or budgeting more funds, Lamont and legislators did neither, relying on the guardrails-generated surplus to clean up the mess.
Lamont and the legislature legally exceeded the spending cap to close a $284 million Medicaid shortfall in 2025 and by $80 million to plug a gap last spring.
Republicans cried foul, noting surplus dollars were supposed to pay down Connecticut’s hefty pension debt — not to cover hidden Medicaid costs intentionally left out of the budget.
Similarly, Democrats underbudgeted by nearly $130 million over the past two years for healthcare benefits guaranteed by contract for retired state workers, ignoring cost projections from state Comptroller Sean Scanlon. The retiree healthcare account had a special reserve with roughly a matching amount of funds, but that’s now largely been exhausted.
“The governor has taken magic and deception to the levels of Harry Houdini,” said House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford.
And while Candelora declined to engage in semantics about whether they were destroyed, he said Lamont clearly has departed significantly from the budget caps he followed earlier in his administration.
The governor and Democratic legislators also have worked around the cap in a more open fashion.
They created a $40 million account outside of the budget in 2025 to mitigate a financial crisis in local schools’ special education programs.
Their biggest end-run around the cap, an off-budget endowment to dramatically expand affordable childcare, has received $712 million in surplus over the past two years.
And while this year’s budget legally exceeded the cap to cover Medicaid costs, it also did so to send an extra $280 million in aid to cities and towns, which Lamont says will help many communities stave off property tax hikes.
But government will be expected to maintain those investments in future years, and there is no additional federal pandemic aid on the horizon.
“We’re going to have to pay the piper, and it’s going to be on the taxpayers’ back,” Fazio said.
Ritter: Governor compromised on caps for the right reasons
House Speaker Matt Ritter, D-Hartford, said the Democratic track record speaks for itself.
The single-largest move around the cap was aimed at a childcare shortage that threatens all communities and the state’s economy.
Reducing municipalities’ reliance on local property taxes to fund schools and other services is equally essential, he said.
And the last large chunk of funds set outside the cap, about $550 million, was provided so Connecticut could mitigate the most painful human service cuts ordered last year by President Donald Trump and the GOP-led Congress.
When roughly 143,000 residents lost a collective $295 million in federal tax subsidies that had helped them purchase health insurance on the state exchange, Lamont used $115 million from the state response fund to mitigate the loss.
Another $8.5 million was used to provide $300 grocery store gift cards to 25,000 residents who lost federal nutrition assistance, while more than $20 million went to bolster food banks and pantries.
But Fazio and other Republicans say Lamont’s maneuvers around the cap have served his political agenda.
Working around the cap allowed Lamont to provide most unionized state employees with annual raises around 4.5% since 2022, compensation that tops most private-sector pay hikes, Republicans argue.
Many in the GOP balked last month when the governor used $5 million to support residents affected by federal changes to immigration rules and particularly to Temporary Protected Status provisions.
But Ritter added, “There will be some people on both sides” of the budget caps debate. Many progressives argue Lamont should have compromised more on budget caps and remains too focused on shrinking debt.
The governor committed more than $1.4 billion in surplus to reduce pension debt following each of the past two fiscal years. Between 2020 and 2024, the average pay-down was $1.5 billion. Before Lamont, Connecticut never had used budget surplus to reduce its unfunded pension obligations.
When the budget caps were created in 2017, legislators hoped to end deficits, build reserves and possibly shrink pension debt, Ritter said. But now, even while continuing to attack unfunded pension obligations that still top $30 billion, officials want to assess services in need and temper problems created by massive federal spending cuts.
“Government is not static. There are changes,” Ritter added. ““Am I confident we will strike the right balance? Yes.”
Mark Pazniokas contributed to this report.

The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.

Catching Our Eye


Issue 3. Signal Ohio’s Andrew Tobias is reporting, “What is Issue 3? Ohio’s voter ID amendment, explained.”
Ohio Republicans held a call to action over the weekend – urging voters to show their support for President Donald Trump by approving Issue 3.
At an event in suburban Columbus, Republicans compared Issue 3, the only statewide question on Ohio’s ballot this November, to the SAVE America Act, a federal bill that would require all Americans to prove their citizenship in order to register to vote. The federal bill, which also has a voter ID component, is Trump’s top legislative priority and is being blocked by Democrats in the U.S. Senate.
“They can’t pass the Save America Act. OK, fine,” Ohio Republican Party Chairman Alex Triantafilou said at a pro-Issue 3 Saturday event that also featured Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and U.S. Sen. Jon Husted. “But you know what we can do in Ohio? We can pass Issue 3.”

Data Centers. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Karen Kasler is reporting, “Data center ban in southwest Ohio city must go before voters, says Ohio Supreme Court.”
The Ohio Supreme Court is ordering a southwest Ohio city to let voters decide on a ban on data centers. The unanimous decision to put the ban before voters in Trenton near Cincinnati comes in the second case the court considered on data centers in the last month.
There are two proposed data centers planned for Trenton, and there’s the possibility of a third coming. Five Trenton residents wanted to amend the city’s charter to include a ban on construction of new data centers, so they circulated a petition and submitted a ban on data centers to Trenton City Council in July. The city charter requires the petition be signed by 10% of the electors of the municipality. The Butler County Board of Elections said there were 1,277 residents who voted in the general election on Nov. 4, 2025, and that the residents had 336 valid signatures. Residents said that was more than twice the 128 signatures they needed.


Measles. The Atlantic’s Tom Bartlett is reporting, “The Measles-stricken mother who lost her newborn son.”
When the Amish man emerged from his barn to greet me, he had no idea that his newborn son’s death had become national news. The man wore a straw hat, black trousers, and suspenders over a long-sleeved blue shirt; one of his similarly dressed sons was guiding a horse-drawn plow in a nearby field.
The man told me that, like most Amish people, he and his family don’t watch TV or use the internet. They don’t read the newspaper either. So they didn’t know until I told them that last Tuesday, Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, held a press conference to announce the first two “measles-associated” deaths in the state in 35 years. Both of the people who died were from Lancaster County, which is home to the largest Amish community in the country and has been hardest hit by the state’s months-long measles outbreak.

title: Calls for a ban on Flock grow in Nevada as critics say new guardrails won’t be enough
description: While some Nevada officials want to implement guardrails to limit the use of automated license plate readers like Flock, others have warned regulations won’t go far enough and want Nevada to ban surveillance technology outright.  Democratic Assemblymember Selena La Rue Hatch of Reno confirmed with Nevada Current she plans to introduce legislation to prohibit[...]
text:
"Thinking there's some sort of happy medium in a surveillance state is just a misnomer,” said the ACLU of Nevada's Athar Haseebullah. (Photo: Flock Safety)While some Nevada officials want to implement guardrails to limit the use of automated license plate readers like Flock, others have warned regulations won’t go far enough and want Nevada to ban surveillance technology outright. 
Democratic Assemblymember Selena La Rue Hatch of Reno confirmed with Nevada Current she plans to introduce legislation to prohibit the use of APLRs in Nevada.
In a statement to the Current, she said people have a “fundamental right to privacy and protections against unreasonable searches.”
“I’m not sure that there are any safeguards you can put on a surveillance state that would make people feel comfortable with being spied on,” she said. “Wagging our fingers and saying, ‘Government and tech oligarchs can spy on us, but only a little!’ is not going to fix the underlying issues or put our constituents at ease.”
Nevada, like most states across the country, is experiencing a broad public backlash to the use of automated readers, with people calling on local and state officials to rein in surveillance tools like Flock. 
The state legislative interim Judiciary Committee voted in late August to request a bill be drafted for the 2027 Legislative Session, which begins Feb. 1, to regulate ALPRs. 
Potential measures the committee identified include:

mandating ALPR staff be trained on lawful use and data-protection requirements; 
require independent audits for compliance with adopted policies; 
and submit annual reports on ALPR activity, audit findings, and policies to the Attorney General, the Governor, and the Legislature.

That’s not enough, said Athar Haseebullah, the executive director of the ACLU of Nevada.
“Thinking there’s some sort of happy medium in a surveillance state is just a misnomer,” Haseebullah said. “It’s not realistic to assume that there’s any layers of transparency there. If there was, then we wouldn’t have to be suing all these government agencies, and they could simply put the ACLU out of business.” 
The civil rights organization has repeatedly sued local law enforcement,  the Clark County School District, and other government agencies, for public records, including access to body-worn camera footage. 
“The government is incapable of regulating surveillance technology, and the Nevada legislature, which convenes for four months every two years, will not be the one to litigate any of these issues when people are impacted by this,” he said. 
Haseebullah argued it is more prudent for state lawmakers to ban the technology rather than relying on civil rights groups to have to sue to ensure transparency and spend the legislative  interim “cleaning up their mess.”
DeFlock, which tracks license plate readers throughout the country, has found more than 50 communities or law enforcement agencies nationwide have canceled contracts, deactivated cameras, or rejected contract proposals so far this year.
The backlash spans the political spectrum, and includes red states; Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who is seeking reelection this year, last week ordered state agencies to pause spending money on ALPRs.
“The backlash is bipartisan and it’s easy to see why — people don’t like their government spying on their every move, end of story,” La Rue Hatch said. “It is our job as legislators to listen to our constituents, put their wishes into action, and protect their fundamental rights. Banning ALPRs is in line with all of those imperatives.”



Quotation







“Wagging our fingers and saying, ‘Government and tech oligarchs can spy on us, but only a little!’ is not going to fix the underlying issues or put our constituents at ease.”


– Nevada Assemblymember Selena La Rue Hatch



Organizers, attorneys, and the public in Nevada have pleaded with state and local officials to take action. 
In Northern Nevada people have swarmed city council meetings and held a protest in August against the use of ALPRs. 
During a legislative interim Judiciary Committee meeting in June, Paloma Guerrero, with the Clark County Public Defender’s office, called for the state to reel in the technology.  
She pointed to reporting across the country that has shown ALRPs like Flock being used for immigration enforcement.
Investigations from Mother Jones and The Washington Post have shown countless cases of law enforcement using technology to track the whereabouts of significant others, exes, and even random strangers.  
Nevada lawmakers didn’t need to reinvent the wheel and could look at other states that have implemented laws that prohibit the use of ALRP to track or monitor specific individuals without a warrant, Guerrero said. 
The City of Sparks opted not to renew its contract with Flock but instead switched to Axon, which handles body worn cameras for law enforcement. 
“Flock just happens to have the most expansive network that allows and most expansive database systems that have led them to be the face of this issue,” Haseebullah said. “All these companies are dangerous. Saying you’re ending a contract with Flock and then awarding it to another ALPR company is not a win. That’s actually a loss for the people in that community.”
But the focus has been mostly on Flock. 
Last week, Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, who is running against Republican incumbent Gov. Joe Lombardo, called for “stringent rules to protect against the abuse of Flock cameras,” and said if elected governor he would work with legislators to enact “essential guardrails. Until Nevadans have these protections, I do not support the use of Flock cameras.”
In a statement to the Current, Drew Galang, a spokesman for Lombardo, said the governor supports “responsible use of advanced technology, including cameras and automated license plate readers, to fight crime and protect Nevadans.” 
“These tools can strengthen public safety, but they must be accompanied by strong safeguards to protect the privacy and constitutional rights of citizens,” Galang said. Lombardo declined to answer what kind of guardrails he would support or if he would support a complete ban.
Prerna Jagadeesh, spokesperson for Ford for Nevada, said in a statement Tuesday that Ford is open to banning Flock cameras, adding that “his first priority is bringing together legislators and communities to hear from everyone and then make an informed decision.” 
The Nevada Latino Legislative Caucus last week also condemned the use of Flock automated license plate reader network by law enforcement agencies across Nevada and called on them to suspend their use of the technology until “binding safeguards, meaningful public oversight, and clear accountability measures are established.” 
La Rue Hatch said she believes ALPRs are already unconstitutional under Nevada law, “but apparently we need to spell that out in state law, which I am more than happy to do.”
Haseebullah also questioned whether the current use of automated license plate readers in any existing form is constitutional, saying the legislature never gave local agencies the authorization to utilize them. The organization is exploring lawsuits against ALPRs, he said.
“We have people who are afraid to go to the hospital,” he said. “We have people who are afraid to go to their religious worship center. We have people who are afraid to go to protests. We have people who are afraid of being retaliated against by law enforcement if they’re to file a complaint. We’re seeing people afraid consistently. Giving the government more tools to track people’s movement every single hour of the day is incredibly dangerous.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC uses orphaned children’s benefits to pay for their care. Governor vows that will stop.
description: South Carolina is the 36th state to say it will stop pulling the benefits, though the change can't start until next year.
text:
A change in South Carolina policy would allow foster children whose parents died to receive all the money their parents earned in Social Security benefits. (Photo by Getty Images)COLUMBIA — South Carolina will stop pulling money from orphaned foster children’s benefits if the Department of Social Services can get enough funding to cover their care, Gov. Henry McMaster announced Tuesday.
The Palmetto State is the 36th to end or announce an end to the practice, which is often called the “orphan tax,” according to the federal Department of Health and Human Services. But the change depends on whether the state Department of Social Service can get enough money to cover the difference, according to the agency.
When a child’s parents both die, that child can receive any Social Security benefits their parents earned during their lifetime. However, states can use that money to pay for that child’s care until they turn 18.
“It seems too cynical to be real,” Alex Adams, assistant secretary of the Administration for Children and Families, told the SC Daily Gazette.
As of December, 39 states, including South Carolina, did just that, Adams said.
The amount each child might receive depends on how much their parents earned in Social Security through their paychecks while they were alive. On average, the monthly benefits are about $1,100, Adams said.
That could amount to tens of thousands of dollars by the time a child turns 18 and leaves the foster care system, Adams said.
Children leaving foster care face more financial difficulties than their peers because they don’t have parents to help support them, he said. Former foster children are more likely to be homeless after turning 18 and less likely to get a college degree.
Getting Social Security benefits could mean an 18-year-old is able to pay rent, buy a car to get to and from work, or pay college expenses, Adams said.
“This is significant money for youth exiting foster care,” he said.
The cost for states to cover the difference is relatively small. In South Carolina, DSS would need an additional $1.6 million to cover the cost of care for the 301 children who qualify now, according to the agency.
That’s a relatively small number of students compared to the nearly 3,500 total children in foster care. The benefits kick in only if a child is orphaned, meaning the change won’t apply to most foster children.
“This change will give children in foster care greater stability and more resources as they build toward a brighter future,” DSS Director Tony Catone said in a statement.
Adams learned about the practice while working for the child services agency in Idaho, he said. He was shocked to learn the agency pulled from children’s benefits and how little it would cost to cover the care with taxpayer dollars, he said.
“It meant everything to the children but was pocket change to the agency,” Adams said.
In December, Adams sent letters to governors of the 39 states that still used federal benefits to pay for foster children’s care, asking them to reconsider. South Carolina’s leaders were very receptive to the idea, he said.
During the late 1980s and early 1990s, states started using the money as an additional source of revenue for underfunded child welfare programs. It’s unclear when South Carolina began pulling from children’s payments.
“When a child enters foster care, our responsibility is to protect that child and give them every opportunity to build a better future,” McMaster said in a statement. “By ensuring these benefits stay with the children they were intended for, we can give them resources to help build that future.”

But the practice won’t end before McMaster leaves office in January.
The policy change itself doesn’t need legislative approval. But because of the need for funding, the earliest it could start is July 1, 2027, said agency lobbyist Connelly-Anne Ragley.
Sen. Tom Young, who chairs the Family and Veterans’ Services Committee, said he would work to ensure the money gets into the budget next year.
Young, also a member of the Senate Finance Committee, heard about the issue a few weeks ago and told DSS leaders the state needed to fix it as quickly as possible. He was glad to hear a change was already in the works, he said.
“The money’s intended for the child,” the Aiken Republican said. “At the end of the day, this is the right thing to do.”
How the money will get to the children is yet to be determined. The funds could go into interest-bearing bank accounts for youth to access once they turn 18.
Or, the money could go toward Fostering the Future Accounts, which are like Individual Retirement Accounts, often referred to as IRAs, but with different rules about withdrawing funds for major life events, such as to pay for education or buy a first home.
First lady Melania Trump launched the initiative in June as a way for foster children to benefit from Trump Accounts, tax-advantaged investment accounts for children created by last year’s massive federal tax law.
Regardless of the specifics, what matters is that the child is getting the money and not the state, Adams said.
“The important thing is that it’s there for the child and the child’s benefit instead of the state’s coffers,” Adams said.

name: Nevada Current
title: Prosecutor challenging incumbent in Clark County District Court Dept. 8
description: Clark County Judge Jessica K. Peterson is hoping to retain her seat in District Court Dept. 8 after a bumpy first term. Earlier this year, the Nevada Supreme Court found Peterson violated the First Amendment when she ordered the removal of reporters from her courtroom and altered a court transcript, a move her opponent calls […]
text:
Austin Beaumont and Jessica Peterson (Campaign photos)Clark County Judge Jessica K. Peterson is hoping to retain her seat in District Court Dept. 8 after a bumpy first term. Earlier this year, the Nevada Supreme Court found Peterson violated the First Amendment when she ordered the removal of reporters from her courtroom and altered a court transcript, a move her opponent calls “a tornado warning siren” of an activist judge. 
“Everyone makes mistakes,” Peterson acknowledged during a recent interview with the Current.
In January, Peterson had three Las Vegas Review-Journal reporters removed from the courtroom when they refused to agree not to publish the name of a victim in a high-profile sexual assault trial. The defendant, Nathan Chasing Horse, a former actor who appeared in the movie Dances with Wolves, was found guilty.
Peterson says she was “attempting to balance the rights of the state, the rights of the defendant to confront his accuser, with the rights of the press and the public to be present in the courtroom, and the rights of the victim to protect her anonymity and her safety.” 
The victim, who was a minor when the crime occurred, was a young mother at the time of trial. 
The newspaper later noted it had no intention of publishing the name of the victim, which had already been disclosed in public documents and in open court. However, the decision whether to use the woman’s name, the R-J asserted in its writ to the Supreme Court, was the publication’s to make, not Peterson’s.
Supreme Court Chief Justice Doug Herndon wrote that the court “manifestly abused its discretion in imposing an unconstitutional prior restraint” and in violating the reporters’ First Amendment right to observe and report the trial. 
Herndon wrote that “disturbingly,” Peterson used the victim’s real name in court, but had the transcript altered to appear as though she referred to the woman by a pseudonym. 
Peterson did not respond when asked via email about Herndon’s assertion. 
Peterson’s opponent, Austin Beaumont, calls the judge’s attempt to change the official record “evidence of a judge who is using the power of the bench to enact a personal agenda.” 
Beaumont, a chief deputy district attorney who appears in Peterson’s department, says he declared his candidacy against the judge before the incident in which she violated the First Amendment. 
He has since asked Peterson to recuse from his cases, pending the election, but says she declined. 
In the RJ’s 2025 Judicial Performance Evaluation, 54% of the attorneys who responded recommended Peterson be retained. 
Of the 101 judges evaluated, only five received scores under 50%, while 14 received scores of 90% and above. 
Peterson “could be doing things much, much better, and simply isn’t,” says Beaumont, adding that “temperament and ability to accurately apply the law were her lowest scores. I think that’s consistent with what I’ve seen.” 
Peterson earned her law degree at Thomas M. Cooley School of Law in Michigan and has been in practice for close to two decades. She says “taking off the advocacy hat” and not second- guessing attorney strategies has been the toughest adaptation since taking the bench. 
She cites the Nevada Policy Research Institute’s legal effort to disqualify public employees from serving in the Legislature as her initial case of first impression, meaning there are no precedents in Nevada law. 
The issue – whether the legislative service of teachers, prosecutors, and other public employees violated the separation of powers doctrine – “had been floating around for years and years,” Peterson says. Her decision in favor of allowing public employees to serve was appealed to the Nevada Supreme Court. 
“It was a four-three decision, and we still have a citizen legislature,” Peterson observed.  
Law is a second career for Beaumont, who was in hotel management for 15 years before coming to Nevada. He earned his law degree from the University of Idaho and was admitted to the Nevada Bar in 2016.He says his business knowledge is an asset in his current role prosecuting white collar crime.  
While he has only tried criminal cases, he previously served four years as a law clerk for Judge Kerry Earley and Judge Michael Cherry, where he assisted with civil litigation. 
Beaumont counts the prosecution of a man who claimed he could facilitate legal immigration into the U.S. from Mexico among his most impactful cases.  
“Everyone involved in trying to come into the country legally wants to speed it up,” Beaumont says of the victims, who collectively paid “roughly half a million dollars” before being ghosted. 
“He told them, ‘What are you going to do? Go to the cops? I’ll get you deported if you don’t stop bothering me about your money,’” Beaumont recalls.
“I faced some blowback, not from my office, but from folks who were reaching out saying that these aren’t real victims, because they’re trying to cheat the system in some way,” Beaumont says. “But these are all true victims.”
About a dozen victims appeared by Zoom to speak at sentencing. 
“They were afraid that if they came to court to speak that they’d be deported,” Beaumont said. “I know there were a number of people and organizations that were not pleased, but I stake my reputation on doing what I believe is right – to have their day in court and see justice be done.”
The defendant was sentenced last month to a minimum of seven years in prison.
Beaumont has endorsements from more than a dozen law enforcement unions, the Southern Nevada Building Trades, and Laborers Union 872 in the nonpartisan contest. As of the end of June, he had raised $40,000 and had $3,600 in the bank. 
Peterson, who is endorsed by the Ironworkers union, IATSE, AFL-CIO, as well as PLAN Action and the National Organization for Women, raised $287,000 and had just under $225,000 on hand.  
Early voting begins Oct. 17. Election Day is Nov. 3.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ students head back to school with new mandate: no phones from first bell to last
description: New Jersey school districts can disagree on how to keep students away from phones, but a new law requires them to ban their use during school hours.
text:
Students walk along Park Avenue on their way to school in Glen Ridge on Sept. 1, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Students are returning to classes this week with new backpacks, new outfits, and a new rule: no phones out during the school day.
New Jersey children are starting their first school year under a statewide law aimed at banning students from using their cellphones during the school day — from the first to the last bell — a sweeping policy change that education officials are confident will have a positive impact on kids, though they say it’ll take months to know the full effect.
“The idea of the bell-to-bell ban is that phones are just separate from the school day. It’s not even coming out in the hallways or between classes. I think the spirit of the ban is to make a pretty global culture change around the relationship to the phone,” said Jeffrey Lane, a Rutgers University researcher and associate professor at the School of Communication and Information.
The law, signed by former Gov. Phil Murphy in January on his way out of office, requires every K-12 public school in New Jersey to bar students from using smartphones, tablets, smartwatches, and other internet-connected devices from the start of the school day until dismissal.
How the new ban plays out looks different from district to district. In some schools, students each morning will drop their phones into magnetic locking pouches that don’t open again until dismissal. Other schools will require their students to turn their phones off and keep them in their lockers or backpacks for the entire school day.
With Labor Day late this year, some New Jersey schools started the new year Tuesday, some start Wednesday, and some don’t go back until next week. Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat who took office in January, said the response to the cellphone ban so far has been largely positive, noting her team met with students and parents in the spring and summer.
Gov. Mikie Sherrill has made online safety for young people a top priority for her first term in office. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
She said students have mentioned “feeling a little freer when they’re not connected” to their phones, and they are realizing that rampant cellphone use is “impairing their ability to just socialize and relax a little bit.”
Sherrill, who has four kids, said it’s an ongoing issue in her household trying to find activities for her kids to keep them off the couch locked in on their phones. As a parent, she welcomes phone-free school days.
“The best way I can describe it is almost a sense of relief. Everybody needs a break,” she said.

The ban goes into effect weeks after Sherrill signed a three-bill package aimed at boosting online safety for minors. One of those bills was the New Jersey Kids Code Act, which restricts platform features designed to keep young users constantly engaged and requires companies to default to their highest privacy settings for young people. Some of those restrictions are mirrored in a new legal settlement between Facebook owner Meta and states including New Jersey that will impose similar restrictions on Facebook, Instagram, and Threads next year, including daily time limits and notification pauses.
The cellphone ban bill won near-unanimous approval from the Legislature last year, with just three no votes among the 120 members. One of the critics was Assemblyman Brian Bergen (R-Morris), who has mocked his colleagues as Luddites for supporting it.
“Fun fact: NJ ALSO still has a 1989 law making it a criminal offense for a student to carry a BEEPER. We never repealed it. We just banned the next device. In 30 years, kids will laugh at this law the way we laugh at the beeper ban,” he said on social media last week.
Nearly two dozen states across the country have adopted cellphone bans during the school day, including California, Florida, Ohio, South Carolina, and Virginia.
Under New Jersey’s law, students will be able to use their phones in case of an emergency, for translation services, and when a cellphone is part of a student’s educational curriculum.
The law leaves details of enforcement up to individual districts, and does not mandate a single statewide method. The Department of Education released an FAQ and guidance for school officials over the summer.
Betsy Ginsburg, executive director of the Garden State Coalition of Schools, said she’s hopeful the ban will cut down on classroom distractions and improve students’ mental health, particularly by reducing online bullying.
“Students will start relating to each other one-to-one instead of via their cellphones,” she said.
She noted that the culture around cellphones in schools shifted around the time COVID-19 restrictions led to school closures. When students were at home taking classes over Zoom in their pajamas, they had more freedom to use their phones and that carried over into schools when they reopened the following year, she said.
Not all parents are on board. Ginsburg said the most common complaint she’s heard is from parents worrying how they will reach their kids during emergencies, whether during extreme weather or school shootings. She stressed that districts are required to notify parents by phone or text about emergencies, and that school security experts advise against students being on their phones during lockdowns.
“The distraction of a cellphone sometimes interferes with a school official’s ability to make sure that the students are as safe as possible in an emergency,” she said.
Lane conducted a survey for the state Department of Education to help inform the law. He noted the research didn’t take a position on the ban itself; it studied how New Jersey minors are using their phones and social media.
Nearly 40% of teens use social media four hours a day, with sleep, attention span, and lack of physical activity emerging as top concerns for parents and teens, he said. Only a small fraction of parents thought cellphone use should be unrestricted in schools, while the majority “understands something has to be done to limit cellphone use,” he said.
“Some parents are accustomed to communicating with their kids during the school day, and it’s a pretty big culture shift to all of a sudden take cellphones out of the school day,” Lane said. “I think it’s an opportunity to redesign the whole day — not just the school day — and it’s kind of like an opportunity for households to change the relationship to the phone and social media.”

Nikita Biryukov contributed.
