name: Michigan Advance
title: As James pushes local control on data centers, past congressional votes sought to limit just that
description: U.S. Rep. John James of Shelby Township, the Republican nominee for governor, has staked his campaign’s data center platform on local control. But in Congress, he voted for legislation that would expressly prohibit state and local governments from regulating artificial intelligence systems — including data centers. “My priority is frankly local control, prot[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. John James speaks to reporters after submitting his nominating petitions to the Michigan Bureau of Elections in Lansing in his bid for Republican nominee for governor. April 20, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. U.S. Rep. John James of Shelby Township, the Republican nominee for governor, has staked his campaign’s data center platform on local control. But in Congress, he voted for legislation that would expressly prohibit state and local governments from regulating artificial intelligence systems — including data centers.
“My priority is frankly local control, protecting our water, protecting and preventing pollution, making sure that electricity bills do not go up, and also making sure that we prioritize blighted and brown fields over productive green farmland,” James said of data centers at a gubernatorial debate in early July. “That would be my moratorium, that would be our standard. We absolutely cannot have an additional data center until we protect the people and communities. That’s no NDAs, that’s making sure we don’t have the ground, air, and water, also the noise pollution, and making sure that, again, we protect local control.”
However, James voted in May 2025 for the U.S. House’s version of H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which included an explicit 10-year moratorium stating that “no State or political subdivision thereof may enforce any law or regulation regulating artificial intelligence models, artificial intelligence systems, or automated decision systems.”
GOP Gubernatorial candidates (L-R) Mike Cox, John James and Perry Johnson on stage at a debate hosted by Fox 2 Detroit. July 8, 2026. | Screenshot
That moratorium, part of a $500 million investment in an “artificial intelligence and information technology modernization initiative,” did not make it into the final version of H.R. 1 that became law. However, as a member of the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, James voted in favor of the specific moratorium three times: twice voting to advance it out of committee, and once voting against an amendment that would have removed it from the bill.
“John James voted for H.R. 1 to deliver historic tax relief to working families across the country. His approach to data centers has been clear: no new data centers until we protect our people,” Alyvia Bailey, a spokesperson for the James campaign, wrote in a statement to the Michigan Advance. “He will re-establish local control, ensure no utility rate increases for residents or secret deals, protect our water and air, prioritize brownfields, and preserve farmland.”
Bailey did not directly address questions about James’ votes for the moratorium within the House version of H.R. 1.
The National Conference of State Legislatures, a bipartisan organization representing the interests of state legislatures, cautioned against a vote in favor of that provision, writing that it would “circumvent their authority to regulate the permitting, construction and operation of data centers within their borders” for states. 
“This will severely limit the ability of states and localities to make decisions regarding the siting and operation of these large-scale projects, raising costs for ratepayers, jeopardizing zoning decisions that protect our mutual constituents and impacting existing infrastructure such as power grids and generating facilities,” Tim Storey, the group’s CEO, wrote in a letter. 
Meanwhile, James, who has aligned himself closely with President Donald Trump and received his endorsement in the primary election, must now navigate Trump’s enthusiastic support for data centers. 
In a post Monday on Truth Social, Trump said that the United States should “let Data Reign” and that if communities push back against data centers, they “want to end up being backwards and poor.” 
President Donald Trump speaks at a roundtable event at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency on Thursday, July 23, 2026. The event promoted the administration’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge that seeks to cap utility prices in communities that have new data centers. (Screenshot from White House livestream)
But data centers remain unpopular in Michigan. A survey conducted Aug. 22 through Aug. 28 by EPIC-MRA found 73% of respondents were opposed to “current federal tax breaks and other federal policies that were put in place to encourage and speed up the development of data centers.” Meanwhile, a Detroit Regional Chamber poll conducted in May 2026 found that while an overwhelming majority opposed data centers in their regions, with regulations in place, “a plurality of Michigan voters would shift to consider a data center within 25 miles of their homes.”
James has continued emphasizing his messaging in favor of local control in the lead-up to the primary and in the weeks since, even as the head of his party has publicly disagreed.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“My position is we need to have a plan to protect our communities. Until we do, then we have to make sure that we have local control,” James said on CBS Face the Nation on Saturday. “Our electricity bills can’t go up. We must protect our water. We have to prevent pollution, that includes land, air, and noise pollution, and then we need to make sure that we prioritize blighted brownfields over productive green farmland.”
The push for local control in data center development crosses party lines — James’ Democratic opponent, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, said at the Michigan Democratic Party nominating convention on Saturday that “there needs to be a moratorium on data centers unless we know that we have those guardrails in place.”
“If any corporation, be it a data center or anyone else, wants to come to Michigan, they have to play by our rules,” she said. “They cannot use or abuse our natural resources. They cannot drive up energy costs, and they have to have the will of the people and the welcoming of their community on their side if they want to set up shop in any community in the state.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: A hemp farmer has some questions for Rhode Island’s next attorney general
description: Last October, Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha joined 38 other state attorneys general in signing a letter urging Congress to change the federal definition of hemp. On Aug. 4, Neronha signed another multistate letter, this time urging Congress to reject any effort to “delay, repeal, suspend, or weaken” hemp restrictions enacted in November 2025. [[...]
text:
CBD products grown in compliance with Rhode Island state law in Hopkinton may naturally exceed  more than 0.4 milligrams of THC per package, which violates a new federal definition of hemp enacted late last year.
(Photo courtesy of Lovewell Farms)Last October, Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha joined 38 other state attorneys general in signing a letter urging Congress to change the federal definition of hemp. On Aug. 4, Neronha signed another multistate letter, this time urging Congress to reject any effort to “delay, repeal, suspend, or weaken” hemp restrictions enacted in November 2025.
I have now written twice in the last year about the problems with this federal policy and its consequences for Rhode Island farmers and small businesses. I write as the co-founder of Lovewell Farms, Rhode Island’s only USDA-certified organic hemp farm, founded in 2018. I write this with nearly 20 years experience in cannabis and drug policy. Lovewell Farms supports strong regulation of hemp products, including testing, reasonable potency limits, child-resistant packaging, accurate labeling and restrictions on sales to minors. 
What we do not support is describing Rhode Island’s regulated hemp industry as something that is harmful.
That was one of the central problems with the October 2025 attorneys general letter. It described a national hemp market in which products are sold “without consistent age restrictions, labeling standards, or safety requirements,” while discussing gummies and beverages marketed to children and synthetic cannabinoids produced through chemical conversion. Those concerns may be legitimate in states that have failed to regulate hemp products. They do not accurately describe Rhode Island. Neronha signing this letter made it appear he agreed with these claims, and that they were reflective of our state’s program.
But Rhode Island has a state-regulated hemp program. Businesses like mine operate under state licenses and are subject to the exact same requirements governing testing, potency, labeling, packaging and age restrictions as the state’s medicinal cannabis program. The state has also placed specific limits on THC in consumable hemp products. There is certainly room to debate whether those regulations should change, but it is simply inaccurate to describe Rhode Island’s hemp market as unregulated and unsafe. 
This distinction became particularly important after Congress enacted a new federal definition of hemp last November. Rhode Island Sens. Jack Reed and Sheldon Whitehouse both opposed an amendment that would have removed the hemp provision, and their offices subsequently told Rhode Island Current that they did so “at the urging of the vast majority of the state attorneys general.” Neronha’s participation in the October letter therefore had consequences beyond Rhode Island. It provided the justification for a congressional vote that now threatens farmers nationwide.



Quotation







What we do not support is describing Rhode Island’s regulated hemp industry as something that is harmful.


This August letter is more troubling after the U.S. House of Representatives on Tuesday passed legislation that would give farmers another month before the new definition takes effect. The provision is part of a short-term government funding bill to avoid a federal shutdown this fall. It keeps the federal government funded through Dec. 11 and was already approved by the Senate in early August. If signed into law by President Donald Trump, the effective date of the hemp product ban would also be moved to Dec. 11. Rather than support that effort, Neronha joined other attorneys general in asking Congress to reject any delay or modification. 
The problem remains that the federal definition is much broader than the synthetic and highly intoxicating products discussed throughout both letters. The August letter itself acknowledges that the new law excludes final hemp-derived cannabinoid products containing more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container. That threshold does not merely eliminate synthetic delta-8 products or high-potency THC gummies. It threatens ordinary, naturally extracted, full-spectrum CBD products containing trace amounts of THC like those manufactured on our farm.
This is important for farmers like me. CBD-rich hemp flower plants naturally produce small amounts of THC. Full-spectrum extracts preserve most of the natural cannabinoids in the plant. Our products can therefore be non-intoxicating, produced without chemical conversion, and compliant with state law, all while containing more than 0.4 milligrams of THC per package.
The August letter nevertheless states that the new definition will preserve “safe, nonintoxicating hemp products” and “will not inhibit the cultivation of hemp.” For cannabinoid hemp farmers, those assertions deserve considerably more scrutiny. Congress should be able to prohibit synthetic intoxicants or establish reasonable national standards without defining naturally occurring, non-intoxicating full-spectrum CBD products out of existence.
AG candidates: Please answer the following
This issue now has particular relevance in Rhode Island because Neronha is term-limited. The state will elect a new attorney general this year, and that person will inherit the authority to sign letters like these on Rhode Island’s behalf. The candidates for attorney general should therefore explain their positions on hemp before the primary election.

Do you support Rhode Island’s existing regulated hemp industry? 
Do you believe naturally occurring full-spectrum CBD products should remain legal? 
Do you support the federal 0.4-milligram-per-container standard, even when it prohibits non-intoxicating products that are legal under state law? 
Do you support distinguishing those products from chemically converted intoxicating cannabinoids? 
Will you consult Rhode Island regulators, farmers, and licensed businesses before signing national policy letters that make factual claims about our state?

When an attorney general signs such a letter, the signature carries the authority of the state. As the congressional response to the October letter demonstrated, those signatures can influence federal policy. The August letter suggests that there is still a substantial disconnect between the national hemp debate and the businesses operating under Rhode Island law.
The next attorney general has an opportunity to approach this differently. Rhode Island does not need someone who automatically agrees with the hemp industry, nor should the industry be exempt from scrutiny. We need an attorney general who understands the laws already in place and distinguishes between regulated and unregulated markets, intoxicating and non-intoxicating products, and synthetic cannabinoids and the naturally occurring compounds found in a legal agricultural crop.
Rhode Island has already chosen to regulate hemp rather than prohibit it. Our next attorney general should explain whether they intend to defend that decision, or abandon it.

name: National
title: Immigration activity is taking a toll on children’s health, doctors say
description: In Minnesota, an elementary schooler has gone without surgery to treat a rare, life-threatening neck infection that isn’t responding to antibiotics. Another young child can’t use their hearing aids because the family ran out of batteries and hasn’t come to get replacements. Yet another child’s cochlear implant surgery was delayed by several months.  These pa[...]
text:
A child looks up at a masked federal agent as his parents are spoken to before being let go after a court hearing in immigration court in New York City in September 2025. The Trump administration’s immigration arrest program is creating a chilling effect, causing fear and isolation among families who are avoiding interacting with systems —  including by missing critical pediatric health appointments. (Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)In Minnesota, an elementary schooler has gone without surgery to treat a rare, life-threatening neck infection that isn’t responding to antibiotics.
Another young child can’t use their hearing aids because the family ran out of batteries and hasn’t come to get replacements.
Yet another child’s cochlear implant surgery was delayed by several months. 
These patients’ families, all immigrants, have been afraid of showing up to the hospital after immigration officers flooded their communities in recent months, said their doctor, pediatric otolaryngologist Asitha Jayawardena, a head and neck surgeon at Children’s Minnesota. 
Clinicians like Jayawardena say immigration arrests and detentions are taking a particularly acute toll on children’s health as families isolate at home. He’s seen some cases — such as the child with the neck infection — worsen because fearful parents aren’t coming in. 
ICE is using Medicaid data to find out where immigrants live

“Without a doubt, it oscillates between being infuriating and absolutely disheartening,” Jayawardena said about the chilling effect. 
As the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement leads to sweeping arrests, healthcare workers say those actions have hit children hard — including children who are U.S. citizens and those in families without arrests.
Many healthcare providers report that since January 2025, they’ve seen a surge in missed pediatric appointments, delayed preventive care, and sick or injured kids going without treatment. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests have continued to climb — with a record 51,000 arrests in July — and experts predict continued unhealthy outcomes among children, causing collateral damage that could extend for years. 
Healthcare workers told Stateline that in addition to the physical healthcare fallout, they’ve also seen a significant increase in depression, anxiety and post-trauma symptoms among their pediatric patients. 
Delayed healthcare has critical consequences for young kids. For example, hearing loss, such as that experienced by Jayawardena’s patients, can hinder crucial development including speech, language and social skills. Along with missing health milestones and getting needed healthcare, kids are grappling with the long-term trauma of losing a parent.
“Community-wide trauma that is being inflicted is having a really important impact on families and children in particular. There are children that are losing their guardians. There are families that are losing their breadwinners,” said Amy Liebman, chief program officer of the Migrant Clinicians Network, a nationwide organization of healthcare workers serving migrant families.
“That certainly is going to ultimately impact their health and then their ability to access care,” she said.
The Trump administration also has introduced rules that allow federal agencies to take into account a family’s use of public benefits when reviewing applications for lawful immigration status. Dr. Gabriela Maradiaga Panayotti, a pediatrician in Durham, North Carolina, pointed to studies showing that such policies lead to a decrease in healthcare use, including among U.S. citizen children.
One of her patients, a U.S. citizen on Medicaid, had stopped a medication for ADHD that had helped him achieve better grades at school. His parents feared being targeted through Medicaid paperwork, so they didn’t refill his prescription. The child’s grades began to drop again.
“They didn’t want to be labeled as utilizing resources,” Maradiaga Panayotti said. “I hurt for him, especially because he’s at this tender preteen age where self-confidence and performance at school can really either build on and set a good foundation for success in high school, or can drop.”
Millions of children
Researchers at the Brookings Institution, a public policy research nonprofit, estimate that since Jan. 20 of last year, the day President Donald Trump was sworn in, and through early April of this year, over 146,000 U.S. citizen children have had a parent detained.
But many more are living with that fear. 
The Pew Research Center estimates 4.6 million U.S.-born children lived with an unauthorized immigrant parent in 2023, and roughly 2.5 million children could face the detention of both household parents, according to a Brookings analysis. 
But the trend cuts across immigration status — including those born to refugees, DACA recipients, asylees and people with temporary protected status. Across the nation, about a fourth of children are born to immigrant families, according to the Migrant Policy Institute.  
State, local officials plan for potential immigration enforcement at schools

Increased ICE activity has included arrests at hospitals, and the agency has also made unprecedented efforts to obtain private health data, including Medicaid patient records, to extract addresses and immigration statuses — another major source of fear for families.
Jayawardena and his colleagues published a study in the American Academy of Pediatrics medical journal in August measuring whether pediatric outpatient care visits were disrupted during and after the large-scale immigration raids of Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis, when the Trump administration deployed 3,000 agents, heavily targeting Somali and South Asian communities. 
The research team found that the rate of missed appointments among Hispanic or Latino children increased by over 50% during Metro Surge compared to the same time period — the first week of December to second week of February — in the prior two years.
Missed appointments increased by 80% among Spanish-speaking families and 53% among families needing language interpretation services. 
“The barrier is not necessarily lack of access, but more the fear and the isolation, and so the enforcement is having this chilling effect on immigrant families who, even though they may need these critical services, may be avoiding the hospital, the counseling, the victim services, and other essential care,” said Jasiel Fernandez, vice president of psychosocial supports at the global pro bono nonprofit KIND, or Kids in Need of Legal Assistance. “We see that happening over and over.”



Quotation







It's just very disheartening knowing that there's something I can do, but I am prohibited from doing it because families don't feel safe.


– pediatric otolaryngologist Dr. Asitha Jayawardena, a head and neck surgeon at Children’s Minnesota


The Migrant Clinicians Network, along with Physicians For Human Rights, surveyed nearly 700 healthcare workers across 30 states between March and August of last year, amid spikes in immigration activity. Most of the surveyed professionals — 84% — reported significant or moderate drops in pediatric patient visits since Trump’s January 2025 executive orders on immigration.
Kids also were spending less time outdoors, which affects overall health, and saw delayed diagnoses of their conditions.. About 27% of clinicians said patients feared enrolling in benefits for their children, and couldn’t afford doctor visits. Preventive care, such as vaccinations, as well as chronic disease management and mental health care were the most affected, healthcare workers reported. 
And in both the survey and through interviews with Stateline, clinicians have reported seeing kids show up to emergency departments alone.
In Missouri, one pediatric emergency medicine physician, who spoke with Stateline on the condition of anonymity because he feared retaliation against his hospital, recalled an 11-year-old child who had been attacked by a dog, his legs riddled in bites. He came to the hospital with only his teenage sister.  
“He told us that (his parents) were scared to come in because ICE might be at the hospital,” the physician recalled. 
Others aren’t showing up to care at all. “Kids like these are so vulnerable that they kind of could fall through the cracks,” he added. “We see the downstream effects of policy changes, and we try to address all these needs. But when kids are coming in, they’re super sick.” 
Missed care, advanced illness
Some clinicians told Stateline that by the time some children reach their clinics, their health conditions have advanced to a more difficult stage. 
One North Carolina pediatrician has seen kids with asthma miss inhaler prescriptions, leading to more asthma attacks. In another case, a large family of refugee children came in covered in splotchy, itchy rashes — scabies. The family had been sharing two bedrooms. Afraid, they had postponed care for four weeks. 
“All of these children, totally ridden throughout their bodies, and it’s so uncomfortable. You can’t sleep because it’s horribly itchy,” said the pediatrician, who spoke to Stateline on the condition of anonymity, fearing retaliation since her clinic receives federal funding. 
“We’re creating tremendous problems for our community that will probably come back to bite us, because now these kids are going around with untreated medical conditions that are only going to get worse,” she said. “It’s a time when they need even more support than before, and our administration just isn’t really allowing that.”
Changes to immigration program for domestic violence victims impede safety, advocates say

She and others said they’re also noticing worsening depression among their patients.
“They’re spiraling out, and they’re not getting any support because they can’t come in and get care,” said the North Carolina pediatrician. She recalled one teenager telling her that they couldn’t sleep at night. “ ‘I’m sobbing and crying, terrified that my parents will be taken away,’ ” she recalled the teen telling her.
Elsewhere, one of KIND’s clients in California, a preteen sexual assault victim, has gone weeks without mental health care.
“The child’s sponsor, who is undocumented, is very afraid to take the young person to mental health appointments or any other kind of follow-up service,” Fernandez said. “Choosing basically to forgo that for the time being.”
In Texas, which has the most immigrant detainees of any state, a 14-year-old’s primary caregiver was detained. The teen has been suffering suicidal ideation.
“That young person is unable to access services,” Fernandez said. “Even if we think that a teenager has a certain level of agency to do certain things, when the caregiver is removed abruptly … the sponsor is not able to support, is not able to meet significant needs and monitoring for that young person.”
Fernandez said KIND has been offering Uber and Lyft rides to field offices because clients are afraid to drive to appointments to receive healthcare.
In southeast Florida’s Indian River County, Heather Miranda is CEO of Treasure Coast Community Health, which runs multiple clinics serving nearby communities of agricultural workers. Clinic staff in the northern area of the county, where Miranda said most immigration enforcement activity has been concentrated, told her they’ve seen a significant decrease of kids coming in — nearly 500 pediatric no-shows since February, 16% of all appointments. 
“They’ve seen kids not coming in for sick visits,” Miranda said. “Not coming in for their well-child or their vaccines. … It’s just been, overall, a decrease in preventative care, which is really, really important.”
Back in Minneapolis, Jayawardena said that even months after Operation Metro Surge, fear among his patient families remains “a persistent problem.”
“I want to help take care of these children, and the families want to get taken care of, as does my entire hospital system — and we cannot get them just physically into the hospital for things that are necessary,” he said.
“It’s just very disheartening knowing that there’s something I can do, but I am prohibited from doing it because families don’t feel safe.”
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Thousands of Hoosiers removed from food assistance
description: Eighty-two thousand fewer Hoosiers are receiving benefits through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program since President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act took effect last October. The law brought major changes to the nation’s most prominent food assistance program, commonly known as food stamps. The results were swift: Nearly 13,000 Hoosiers[...]
text:
A sign advertises that SNAP benefits are accepted at a Hornbacher’s in north Fargo, North Dakota, on July 7, 2026. (Photo by Ceilidh Kern/For the North Dakota Monitor)Eighty-two thousand fewer Hoosiers are receiving benefits through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program since President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act took effect last October.
The law brought major changes to the nation’s most prominent food assistance program, commonly known as food stamps.
The results were swift: Nearly 13,000 Hoosiers lost their SNAP benefits between October and November — more than 10 times the number removed the previous month.
Another 12,500 Hoosiers were disenrolled the following month, rising to 14,000 in January and peaking at 16,000 in May. That’s a 14.5% drop since October 2025.
FSSA data shows 30,000 Hoosiers were removed from SNAP prior to the implementation of the One Big Beautiful Bill last year — totaling 112,500 from January 2025 through June of this year.
The Indiana Family and Social Services Administration, which administers SNAP benefits, could not answer how many of those Hoosiers were removed due to ineligibility versus procedural reasons like missing or incomplete paperwork.
“There (are) a number of reasons an individual may have been removed for noncompliance, one prominent reason is failing to provide requested verification information,” said FSSA Spokesman Tyson Runkle.
Indiana’s Medicaid expansion program is also seeing thousands of Hoosiers removed from the program.
What’s changed
House Resolution 1, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, imposed new restrictions on which refugees and asylum seekers are eligible for assistance through SNAP.
Able-bodied adult veterans, homeless people and young adults who have aged out of foster care, once exempt from work requirements, must now prove they are working at least 80 hours a week or lose their benefits.
The same work requirements now apply to able-bodied seniors until they turn 64.
Caretakers of dependent children are exempt until their youngest child is 14 years old — lowered from age 18.
Failure to meet work, school or volunteer hours for more than three months in a three-year period will result in benefits termination, said Emily Weikert Bryant, executive director of Feeding Indiana’s Hungry.
New applicants must now report the names and citizenship status of all household members and prove their Indiana residency.
Seniors who once qualified for simplified applications due to age or disability are now subject to more frequent check-ins and eligibility redeterminations until they turn 64.
Indiana’s Senate Enrolled Act 1 lowered the asset limit back to the federal $3,000 limit too, though households with at least one disabled person or adult over 60 can keep assets of up to $4,500.
Cost-sharing puts pressure on state
Indiana will pay a greater share to administer SNAP benefits come October, at which time the state will be on the hook for 75% of administrative costs.
But the most significant change won’t take effect until next October. If Indiana does not bring its SNAP error rate below 6%, the state will start paying for a portion of those benefits for the first time.
The minimum fiscal impact if the state does not comply: $64 million, according to Sunshine Beam, director of the Division of Family Resources within FSSA.
SNAP resources will likely be a key discussion point as lawmakers craft a new two-year state budget starting in January.
The error rate is calculated by looking at a random sample of 100 SNAP households to determine what percentage received too much or too little in benefits — not in determining eligibility.
Indiana’s error rate hit 9.77% in 2025, up slightly from the previous year, but Beam said the rate is trending down since FSSA started hiring additional workers to focus on compliance.
“I’m cautiously optimistic,” she said. “Everybody is working really hard. We have so many people working on this, and the staff are taking extra thoughtful consideration and making sure we’re reviewing their cases.”
Indiana SNAP payment error rate rises, increasing likelihood state will be on the hook for benefits

The errors are a combination of agency mistakes — missing a key number or reading a paystub incorrectly — and recipients not reporting accurate household income or other information the agency needs to calculate benefits, Beam said.
“We are held responsible for those errors as well,” she said.
FSSA reviews employment income and bank accounts to verify applicants meet income and asset limits.
At least 30 days of recent pay history are needed to determine eligibility, which may be verified through paystubs or employer statements, according to Runkle.
Quality control then reviews cases and conducts interviews with applicants before benefits are issued to minimize errors.
Are rapid changes contributing to errors?
Bryant, of Feeding Indiana’s Hungry, wonders whether federal and state changes to SNAP policy are contributing to the state’s error rate.
Indiana’s 9.77% error rate for federal fiscal year 2025, which ended September 30, was calculated before the One Big Beautiful Bill took effect.
“I can’t see how that number gets any lower,” Bryant said. The policy, procedural and eligibility changes “create an atmosphere rife for making mistakes,” she said, “because you’re having to retrain everyone to different standards.”
If Indiana’s error rate rises to 10%, Bryant said, the state would owe $127 million a year just for benefits.
“That’s not what we’re seeing,” Beam said, adding, “These changes, both at the federal and at the state level, do not appear to have made the error rate worse.”
Still, Bryant said she worries what would happen should the state decide it can’t or won’t pay for benefits.
“There’s nowhere (in the law) that the state has to sign on the dotted line to say, ‘We’re going to do this,'” she said, “and it’s pretty unclear if states say we’re not going to pay the benefits cost share — what happens? Do the households in the state still get benefits? Do they get benefits minus the 10% that the state was supposed to be paying?”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Is Indy news biased? Here’s my advice for finding reliable sources
description: What’s the No. 1 complaint I hear from Indy residents about our local news? It’s biased. At every single public event I host, at least one participant tells me they can detect bias in our news, and, as a result, they consume less news.  Hoosiers aren’t alone in these sentiments. In fact, Pew Research Center, […]
text:
Pew Research Center, a not-for-profit research organization, found in 2025 that 58% of Americans say most journalists are biased, creating a lack of confidence in today’s news. (Getty Images)What’s the No. 1 complaint I hear from Indy residents about our local news? It’s biased. At every single public event I host, at least one participant tells me they can detect bias in our news, and, as a result, they consume less news. 
Hoosiers aren’t alone in these sentiments. In fact, Pew Research Center, a not-for-profit research organization, found in 2025 that 58% of Americans say most journalists are biased, creating a lack of confidence in today’s news.
Here’s a few comments I’ve gathered during my outreach events around town:
“What frustrates me about the news is when it is biased.” 
“How does one know when the reporter is telling the truth, opinion or slanting the facts to control the reader’s perception and choices?” 

I’d love to hear from you! Please write to me at indypubliceditor@poynter.org with your questions, concern and feedback about the local press.

“Not knowing if I’m getting factual information or if there is political slant, I am more cautious about what I believe and feel like I usually need to do more follow-up research. And, sensationalizing things/events is frustrating.” 
Most people who share this insight with me do not want to be named. They don’t want to pick a fight or be labeled for turning away from current events. They want their concerns heard and taken seriously.
This widespread belief that our news is biased presents a challenge. Here’s why: When people can’t agree on a set of facts or a source of truth, we can’t collectively address problems.  
After talking to experts, I learned that perceptions of bias are rooted in consumers’ media habits. And, as news consumers, we can take action to weed out the sources we don’t trust and focus on those that provide the facts we’re looking for.
Three types of bias permeate our perceptions 
There are typically three ways bias is perceived by news consumers.

Some people will call a news outlet biased because of the stories they tell or the topics they cover. If this is you, you might get irritated when stories seem to embrace political views that are different from your beliefs. And, you might yearn for coverage of issues that you deeply care about. Below, I’ll share how you can still find value in news that doesn’t seem like a perfect fit for you. 

Other people detect bias in the tone of certain stories, or the preference for sources with a particular point of view. This might leave you feeling skeptical of particular stories because they don’t seem balanced or neutral. 

And other people find it difficult to distinguish between journalists who deliver straight facts and the “talking heads” that offer their opinions or are trying to persuade you. If you watch 24-hour cable news, this might sound familiar.  

“Journalists do a poor job often explaining which type of content is which, and that leaves news consumers not sure what the goal is,” said Joy Mayer, founder of Trusting News, a nonprofit resource that helps journalists build their credibility with audiences.
The news is not going to change, but here are some better approaches for your news consumption habits
There is bias in journalism, but it’s not often a flagrant disregard for one particular viewpoint. Newsrooms have a preference for controversy and recent developments. Journalists tend to focus on what’s broken, rather than what’s working. And many times, when a reporter selects a story, it’s because that reporter believes the story is the most important issue to cover that day. Those are all forms of bias. 

While you may not share those same biases, don’t let that stop you from getting the news you need. 

Even when the biases in a news story differ from your own, the information may still be reliable. Vanessa Otero, CEO and founder of Ad Fontes Media, created a media bias chart at an inflection point in political polarization in the U.S., to help family members who were unfollowing each other on social media during the Trump/Clinton election of 2016. What started as a personal project quickly became a guide for news consumers.

“I wanted to honestly just talk to my friends and family about how some news sources are better and worse and some are left and right and there’s nothing wrong with that, but some are really extreme and it’s important to tell the difference between those things,” she said.

Her staff ranks stories on both reliability and political bias. She recommends that consumers look for reliable news outlets that skew slightly rather than significantly.

Since there’s no such thing as a perfectly neutral news source, it’s better if consumers can analyze the news that comes across their feed. 

“It’s sort of a fool’s errand to try to tell people, ‘Hey, here are the outlets to look for that are not biased,’” said Alex Mahadevan, a faculty member at the Poynter Institute and director of MediaWise, the institute’s AI and media literacy division. “I mean, everyone brings their own perspective to the reporting and writing that they do. It is literally impossible to find an unbiased person, let alone an unbiased news outlet.”
Nine recommendations for a healthy news diet
If you adopt a handful of these suggestions, you’ll save yourself time, energy and frustration. Ultimately, you will become a savvy news consumer. 

1. Make deliberate choices about what form of news you consume.

Do you enjoy listening to local and national news as you head to work? Do you tune into a local news broadcast as you get ready each day? Or, do you begin your day scrolling through headlines on social media from sources you trust? Narrow down which form of news best suits your lifestyle and be consistent with your routine. Eliminate sources that feel like noise. 

“Keep in mind that the news landscape, it’s literally tens of thousands of information sources you could go to, so you want to be able to consciously choose the news sources that you’re consuming,” Otero said. “You only have so many hours in a day to follow the news.” 

2. Go to the original news outlet that first reported a story—all the rest is just a rehash.

A lot of the noise you encounter on social media and elsewhere can be avoided by checking out who first reported a story and going to that outlet for firsthand information. For instance, for news about a natural disaster, look for reporters who are close to the scene. 

“Even though there are so many, tens of thousands of news sources, most of the new, original, important information still stems from the people who are working as journalists,” Otero said. 

3. Install news apps from the outlets you trust and go to them for local, national and international news consistently.

Have you already decided which journalists you trust most and which are a turnoff because of their tone and the sources they use? If so, you can comfortably select the apps of local, national and international news outlets.

Otero recommends downloading a local news app, which is usually free, in addition to respected national and international outlets like AP, Reuters, BBC, The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and The Washington Post. (Hack: Having a public library card can get you free access to some of these national outlets with paywalls.) Local Indy TV news apps are free. WFYI has a free app and so does NPR, which you can set to WFYI. Same goes for Axios Indianapolis. And, the IndyStar’s app will let you see headlines for free.

4. Go local and consume less national news.

When you think of the news, do you lump local with national news and call it all bad? National news outlets tend to reflect the values of the large cities where they are headquartered. They also are more likely to blur the lines between straight reporting and news with an opinion, which they sometimes call “analysis.” Distinguishing between local and national news can help narrow your focus.

Mahadevan advises people to simplify their lives by consuming more local news and avoiding opinionated content. 

“I always say ‘go local,’ because I think when people think the news is biased, what’s in their head is talking heads that are on the major broadcast channels,” he said. “Many of whom are opinion journalists or columnists or people, who look like journalists because they’re wearing a suit and they’re a talking head on TV, but they actually work for a think tank in D.C. or something.”

5. Judge the experience of the reporter on the beat, not the outlet overall.

Read the bylines. Learn the names of expert reporters. Then follow their work. This will save you from wasting time sorting through random bits of misinformation your friends might post on social media. 

Ask questions: Is the reporter an expert? Do they routinely cover whatever they’re reporting on? Is there charged or loaded language or unnecessary adjectives in the content? Are they quoting legitimate sources? Asking these questions will help you form healthy news judgment, Mahadevan said. 

6. Do your research on the news outlets you frequent, checking Wikipedia for basic information.

Wikipedia can offer some clues if you’re still not knowledgeable about your news sources. If you don’t know a news outlet’s reputation, a quick search will help you glean information you need to judge whether it should be part of your news diet. Look for an “about” page on a website. For local Indy newsrooms, check out our database. 

“While there are some people who try to politicize Wikipedia, it’s still a very, very solid source for finding out more information about an outlet,” said Mahadevan. You can learn who owns the outlet, if there have been controversies with deep bias and what the outlet typically covers.

7. Get news from a variety of sources.

Mayer also advises news consumers to seek out a variety of news sources. If you have a good understanding of how your news providers line up on a political spectrum, make it a point to tap into different ones on the same issue.

“Every journalist is coming from somewhere, and it’s always a good idea to see how different journalists are covering the same thing,” she said. 

8. Seek out news outlets and sources that have representation across the political spectrum as their value proposition. 

Some news providers make it a point to show their audience exactly how issues are reported from different political perspectives. 

Mayer recommends two sources that are helpful. Ground Newslabels the political bias and shortcomings present in various news stories on a daily basis. Tangle News is a daily newsletter that covers the top issues of the day with a deliberately neutral approach. It then shows consumers how liberal and conservative newsrooms are framing the stories. Starting with these sources will eliminate any guessing games and doubts around political slant. 

“It involves a lot of opinion journalism, but it does a really wonderful job of engaging with the best version of arguments from different sides,” Mayer said of Tangle News. 

9. When you are frustrated, give news outlets feedback.

Giving feedback will help both you and the journalists. “Whenever you feel like you can be specific about what they’re missing, what they’re mischaracterizing, what they’re getting wrong, that’s actually very useful,” said Mayer. CNN and other big companies might not listen to your criticism, but local outlets and local journalists are more likely to take feedback, she said. 

Let local journalists know if they missed something. Most people think journalists have ulterior motives for the way they report a news story, but usually that isn’t the case. Helping reporters see alternative sides to a story can help them improve their reporting.

I also want your feedback. If you are among the many people frustrated by bias in the news, try some of these techniques. And let me know how they work. You may discover a new approach that could help others. Together we can help make media literacy second nature and keep your news diet healthy.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A dam owner drained this secluded pond. DEEP wants it restored
description: Wright Investors Service Holdings conducted a drawdown of the pond after it found the dam it owns was leaking. CT wants the company to fix it.
text:
Throughout most of her 40 years living on Old Killingly Pond, Susan Rosenstone Larrow had easy access to its placid waters, which she and her neighbors also touted as some of the clearest in the state.
From her upstairs studio, the former art teacher spent afternoons painting scenes of life on the pond: her husband, Gene, fishing with his two grandchildren from a dock in summer; amber leaves scattered along the shore in autumn; a bald eagle perched on a branch in search of fish.
Then one morning last October, Rosenstone Larrow and her neighbors awoke to find water gushing out of the old stone dam that had held the pond in place for over a century. Spurred by concerns over the dam’s safety, state officials had authorized its owner, Wright Investors’ Service Holdings, to conduct an emergency drawdown of the pond.
In a matter of months, the pond shrank to a quarter of its former size, leaving behind acres of rocks and mud. Docks where generations of children had once learned to swim were left suspended over bare ground.
“I like painting rocks, I never thought I’d have this many to chose from,” Rosenstone Larrow said.
The decision to drain Old Killingly Pond — a man-made body of water on the border between Connecticut and Rhode Island — kicked off a campaign by local residents and town officials to restore the water levels in the pond and have the state take ownership of the dam, providing for its long-term maintenance.
On Tuesday, the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection announced it had taken the first step in an enforcement action against WISH, the dam’s owner, by sending the company a draft consent order to fix the dam and restore water in the pond to its pre-drawdown levels. Officials said the decision was made based on the agency’s determination that the continued drawdown of the pond would have an adverse impact on habitats for protected plants and animals, including several species of damselflies.
The agency didn’t comment on whether it was considering taking over the dam.
Water from Old Killingly Pond trickles through Killingly Pond Dam’s low-level outlet gate on Dam Road on Tuesday, August 18, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Graham Stevens, the head of DEEP’s Bureau of Water Protection and Land Reuse, said Tuesday’s letter essentially invites WISH to enter into an agreement to make the necessary repairs to the dam. Should the company decline, he said, the agency has other enforcement tools at its disposal to get the dam repaired.
“Regardless of the negotiation outcome, this will be a long process, and this is just the first step,” Stevens said.
Stevens said WISH didn’t immediately reply to the letter Tuesday. He added that work to restore the dam and raise water levels would likely take several years and could cost “multiple millions of dollars.”
Old Killingly Pond is the first in a series of reservoirs created in the first half of the 19th Century by the construction of dams used to power local mills. Over time, the mills declined and they, along with the dams, passed through a series of owners before ending up in the hands of WISH, a holding company based in Mount Kisco, N.Y.
In an email on Tuesday, WISH’s acting chief financial officer, Harold Kahn, said the company has no business operations and no revenue. He declined to comment further on issues involving the dam.
Today, the pond is home to around a dozen year-round residents, along with several seasonal cottages that are occupied in the summer months. Before the drawdown, the pond was about 138 acres in size, split between Connecticut and Rhode Island.
Most of the land surrounding the pond is held in public trust by the two states, including portions of Killingly Pond State Park. The dam owned by WISH, along with most of the residences, are located within Connecticut.
In addition to the loss of waterfront property, residents and town officials said the drawdown has caused several wells feeding seasonal cottages to dry up and resulted in excess sediment flowing downstream to other reservoirs. Fire officials in East Killingly, a section of town that lacks access to hydrants, warned that the drawdown left them without a place to fill up tanker trucks needed to respond to fires.
Lower water levels also exposed a suspected Native American burial ground that had been flooded by the construction of the dam in the early 19th Century.
Residents along the pond say it’s unclear what work, if any, WISH performed to maintain the dam at Old Killingly Pond. Several said they were unaware the company owned the dam until it began draining the pond last year.
Seasonal resident Jamie Chaparro walks through exposed lake bottom at Old Killingly Pond on Tuesday, August 18, 2026.  Before the dam drawdown, the area was covered in water. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Stevens, who oversees dam safety at DEEP, said the agency was notified by the owners last year that an inspection had found the dam was leaking water, raising concerns about its structural integrity. In response, he said, DEEP authorized an emergency drawdown.
“There was a fear that this dam might fail, and if it were to fail, it put at risk life and property — not to mention the environmental consequences of such a catastrophic event,” Stevens said.
Once the drawdown was complete and the risk of failure had abated for the time being, Stevens said, the owner was directed to come up with a long-term plan for safely operating the dam. In response, WISH proposed a plan to keep the pond drained in order to reduce pressure on the dam, Stevens said.
That proposal drew stong objections from local residents and elected officials in Killingly. Stevens said Tuesday’s letter effectively served as a rejection of WISH’s plan to keep the pond drained.
State Sen. Mae Flexer, D-Windham, announced the news of DEEP’s decision following a meeting Tuesday with the agency and town officials. Asked whether the idea of a state takeover was broached at the meeting, Flexer said the effort the get WISH to pay for repairs to the dam represented the “beginning of the process.”
“I think any takeover or ownership [change] is months away,” she said. 
“Today’s action shows that DEEP has been methodically trying to find a solution to this issue,” Flexer added. “I’m grateful for them for taking action and holding these dam owners accountable.”
Residents, meanwhile, reacted to the news with a mixture of relief and trepidation over whether WISH would be responsive to the state’s efforts to broker a solution. 

An acrylic painting of Old Killingly Pond by Susan Rosenstone Larrow Credit: COURTESY/ SUSAN ROSENSTONE LARROW

“Now we have to hope” that WISH agrees to fix the dam, Rosenstone Larrow said. “I’m not too convinced that WISH will do it.”
Justen Fisher, who lives with his wife and two daughters in a house the family had built on the pond, praised DEEP for being responsive to the pleas from the small community of residents on the pond. 
“To feel the support and actually to feel being heard… it’s super relieving,” Fisher said. “Now we’ve got the state on our side, let’s take it to the finish line.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michiganders speak out on Consumers Energy’s proposed sale of 13 dams to private equity
description: With state energy regulators expected to decide in the coming weeks whether to allow the sale of 13 hydroelectric dams, residents, business owners and conservation advocates made their way to the Michigan Public Service Commission to make their voices heard.  Consumers Energy announced in 2025 that it had secured a buyer for 13 dams built […]
text:
Foote Dam in Iosco County, one of 13 hydroelectric dams proposed for sale by Consumers Energy. (Photo from Consumers Energy)With state energy regulators expected to decide in the coming weeks whether to allow the sale of 13 hydroelectric dams, residents, business owners and conservation advocates made their way to the Michigan Public Service Commission to make their voices heard. 
Consumers Energy announced in 2025 that it had secured a buyer for 13 dams built across five rivers between 1906 and 1935. However, the sale cannot move forward without the approval of the Michigan Public Service Commission.
Opponents of the sale have raised concerns about Consumers’ plan to sell the dams to Confluence Hydro, a subsidiary of Hull Street Energy, a Maryland-based private equity firm. They argue that the deal lacks the protections to ensure the dams are operated safely. Supporters argue that if the dams are not sold, they will be decommissioned, bringing changes to local landscapes that could result in lost recreational opportunities and harm to property values.
“If you do not move forward and get this contract signed, Consumers may decide to remove the dams and the economic ramifications and natural devastation would be huge,” said Karen Reese, who lives near Croton Pond, which was created by one of the hydroelectric dams along the Muskegon River. 
Map of the 13 hydroelectric dams proposed for sale by Consumers Energy. (Graphic by Consumers Energy)
“The sobering effects on the thousands of people living on and around these dams would be horrific,” Reese told the commission at their Aug. 27 meeting. “Many families have built their lives on these backwaters for over a hundred years. They would lose huge values on their homes and businesses would lose revenue and may have to close their doors.”
Alec Chesley, who lives near the Croton Dam, warned that if the dams are removed, and reservoirs drained, businesses such as campgrounds and marinas could be forced to close. 
George Heartwell, the former mayor of Grand Rapids who lives downstream from the Croton Dam, raised concerns about the potential buyer.
“Will my Muskegon River be safe under an unregulated, profit-driven company with no ties to Michigan?” Heartwell said, claiming that Hull Street Energy had created shell corporations as owners of each dam. “Why would you do that? Unless you knew you would be safe bankrupting one or more of those shells and letting Michigan taxpayers pick up the responsibility.” 
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer previously raised concerns about the risks of selling the dams, writing in a letter to the commission that the deal “lacks firm, enforceable protections to ensure the dams will be properly maintained and safely retired when they are no longer economical to operate.”
The deal also does not require Hull Street Energy to cover all future repair, accident, environmental and decommissioning costs or to maintain reserves to cover those expenses, Whitmer said. 
While Consumers Energy says it will set aside $270 million to protect Michigan communities in the event of unforeseen safety concerns, Whitmer said the fund is “too little, too late, and too difficult to access – leaving the Fund unable to prevent nearterm safety failures or reliably cover the dams’ enormous long-term costs”
The Michigan Public Service Commission is expected to make a decision on the sale at its Sept. 10 meeting.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Milwaukee residents object to proposed We Energy rate increase
description: Dozens of southeastern Wisconsin residents, community organizers, local leaders and environmental activists voiced their opposition to a proposal from the electric utility We Energies to raise rates during a series of meetings in Milwaukee Tuesday.  At a rally outside the We Energies offices Tuesday morning and at a public hearing on the rate increase held [[...]
text:
Yusuf Adama of Walnut Way speaks against We Energies' proposed rate increase at a rally in Milwaukee Sept. 1, 2026. (Henry Redman | Wisconsin Examiner)Dozens of southeastern Wisconsin residents, community organizers, local leaders and environmental activists voiced their opposition to a proposal from the electric utility We Energies to raise rates during a series of meetings in Milwaukee Tuesday. 
At a rally outside the We Energies offices Tuesday morning and at a public hearing on the rate increase held by the Wisconsin Public Service Commission on the Marquette University campus in the afternoon, opponents of the planned increase by as much as $22 per month by 2028 complained that the company was raising money that would go to building data center infrastructure and executive salaries on the backs of Milwaukee residents struggling to get by. Opponents also demanded that Wisconsin change direction as the state continues to fall behind its neighbors in renewable energy development. 
The proposed rate increase comes as public attention has focused on the structure of Wisconsin’s energy system and the sources of its power due to widespread opposition to the construction of hyperscale data centers — particularly in the communities of Port Washington and Mount Pleasant. The issue has become a major topic in the ongoing race for governor as both Democrat David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, and Republican Tom Tiffany, a member of the U.S. House of Representatives, argue for their vision for the future of data centers and energy in the state. 
Crowley has said he wants to require that data center developers pay the cost of their own energy use while pushing them to construct renewable sources of energy such as utility-scale solar and wind. Tiffany, whose campaign  ads attack “data center David,” has argued that data centers, wind and solar farms are all taking too much of the state’s farmland. 
Voters across Wisconsin have expressed frustration recently with the lack of oversight or regulation of polluting industry. A group of activists in western Wisconsin recently successfully challenged the state Department of Natural Resources’ decision to grant a controversial Pierce County factory farm a permit to expand on the grounds that there weren’t enough protections for local groundwater. 
We Energies’ request to raise rates would increase monthly bills by $13.35 per month in 2027 and another $8.69 per month in 2028, adding up to about $22 more per month after two years, for a household that uses 660 kilowatt-hours per month. 
At the rally in Zeidler Union Square Park, directly in front of the We Energies headquarters, attendees complained that the PSC hearing was being held on the first day of school, when many of the working families who will be most affected by the rate increase are too busy to attend; that the utility has increased rates several times in recent years as the company’s profits have continued to go up; that, on a hot and muggy late summer day in Wisconsin, poor residents in the city would have to choose between cooling their homes and other necessities and that the state’s utility companies have continued to extend the lives of coal and natural gas power plants. 
“I didn’t come here to complain. Y’all know we do not complain. That’s not what we do. We have a reason to be angry, though,” Antonio Butts, executive director of the local non-profit Walnut Way Conservation Corps, said. “They’re asking for $480 million —  $480 million on top of hundreds of millions that they’ve asked for in previous years. We have a right to be angry. We literally have a right to be angry. But being angry has never reduced our energy bill. Not one time.” 
Most of the speakers complained that the utility has continued to reap massive profits and returns to shareholders — and paid its CEO $12 million in 2025 — while many Milwaukee families are struggling to make ends meet. 
“We have a runaway monopoly that are supposed to be stewards of a necessity, a necessity that we all need,” Rev. Steve Tipton, pastor of El Bethel Church of God in Christ on the city’s northwest side, said. “We need to be warm in the winter, and you know how Milwaukee is. Y’all know how Milwaukee is. And we need to be comfortable in the summer. You see how we are sweating right now. So imagine how homes and families and people that are working, people that are working with two and three jobs that are trying to take care of their children and still keep their household together, and still have to deal with a bill where they got to make a choice whether it’s going to be groceries, their medication, or the necessity of energy.” 
Throughout the rally, speakers explicitly tied the fight against the rate increase to the broader fight against climate change and pushing Wisconsin’s energy system to use more renewable energy. 
“Climate change is no longer some distant environmental problem, it is an issue of public health, infrastructure affordability, and ultimately human safety,” Yusuf Adama, a Beloit common council member and environmental justice advocate with Walnut Way, said. “And we continue to see another reason why we need to move from our dependence on volatile fossil fuels like methane gas when our energy systems depend on fuels whose prices can fluctuate because of markets and events far outside the control of other Wisconsinites.”
State Sen. Chris Larson (D-Milwaukee) was at the rally and hearing Tuesday, arguing that government officials should listen to the demands of the activists in Milwaukee on Tuesday and Wisconsinites who are fighting against data centers across the state. With Democrats confident they’ll win control of state government in November, he said he wanted to push for protections against data center-caused increases in energy and water use, cap utility rate increases at 2%, bar utility companies from lobbying and forcing more renewable energy development. 
Larson made that argument as Tiffany’s campaign for governor argues explicitly against renewable energy and for the increasing Wisconsin’s use of fossil fuels. 
“Tom Tiffany is lying through his teeth, or maybe he’s too dumb to realize,” that he’s been deceived by fossil fuel “propaganda,” Larson told the Examiner. “The cheapest form of energy is solar.” 
Adama, of the Beloit common council and Walnut Way, told the Examiner that while Tuesday’s hearing was about the rate increase, it’s important to keep the focus on the “cohesive set of circumstances” that form the state’s energy policies and push for broader policies to fight climate change.

title: A diehard Wichita friendship tested through seven decades of life and, now, death
description: Gwendolyn Nevada Toney, 96, died peacefully in her sleep the Sunday morning of Aug. 24. Gwennie long had been the caterer of choice for Wichita’s elite. A mother of five who lost four before her death. A faith-filled Christian. A neighbor who offered children M&Ms from the candy dish in her immaculate living room. According […]
text:
Gwendolyn Nevada Toney, 96, died last month. She enjoyed a lifelong friendship with Cindy Carnahan. (Photo provided by Cindy Carnahan)Gwendolyn Nevada Toney, 96, died peacefully in her sleep the Sunday morning of Aug. 24.
Gwennie long had been the caterer of choice for Wichita’s elite. A mother of five who lost four before her death. A faith-filled Christian. A neighbor who offered children M&Ms from the candy dish in her immaculate living room.
According to Cindy Carnahan, the honorific “friend” offered the truest measure of Toney’s steady magnificence. Their friendship spanned more than 70 years of love and heartbreak and laughter, and perhaps most important, interdependence.
“I’ve loved Gwennie before I knew what love was,” Cindy said. “I considered her more than a friend. She’d been my closest confidante. I could tell her anything and blindly trust she’d never tell.”
I’ve juggled two book projects since 2025: A collection of my Kansas Reflector columns and a book built on the 70-plus year friendship between Cindy (who is white) and Gwennie (who is Black), where age and racial differences mattered not. The project became a friendship covenant, where precious memories would endure.
Cindy Carnahan (left) was 3 years old when she met Gwendolyn Nevada Toney. (Photo provided by Cindy Carnahan)
As Gwennie’s lifetime of memories dissolved like sand through an hourglass, Cindy worked to save all the memories she could.
Their story began with a mistake.
Gwennie worked at The Forum near downtown Wichita. Her supervisor loved her energy, and when Gwennie requested more work, this supervisor advised her on where to look. She told Gwennie to board the city bus headed east on Douglas, get off at Belmont Place, turn left, and knock on doors asking if anyone needed help.
She did everything correctly until she turned right instead of left. She landed at the Clarke home, where Cindy’s mother hired her. Cindy was 3.
Gwennie was born March 4, 1930, in the Dust Bowl’s murk and in the depths of the Great Depression, in historic Boley, Oklahoma. Black advocate and educator Booker T. Washington once visited Boley, calling it “the most industrious of all the Black towns.”
This might explain her astonishing John Henry work ethic. For virtually all of her adult life, she poured herself into at least two jobs.
She represented Black entrepreneurial grit, uplift suasion, but also proximity to high society. She prepared tasty desserts and delectable food, along with staging her work in colorful displays. She loved bright colors. She met the iconic Julia Child in Wichita, who entrusted her with a recipe sent with a signed card of good wishes.
She continued this work as her connection to Cindy bloomed.
What a pair. A little Lucy and Ethel, a little Thelma and Louise. As the saying goes, a good friend will help you move. A best friend will help you move a body.
Cindy remembered asking Gwennie to buy her a bra before she had much use for it. She playfully obliged, and facetiously said, looking at the loose straps on the sagging garment, “I sure am glad we got you that bra. We really needed it.”
They would listen to the Isley Brothers’ 1969 hit, “It’s Your Thing.” Cindy would ask Gwennie to dance with her, and Gwennie suggested, smiling, that Cindy practice with the door. Cindy did, hips swiveling, one hand holding the knob, the other hand waving over her head.
Gwennie also protected Cindy. She once rushed to East High to pick up Cindy when she heard a radio report about possible violence. She loved Cindy and wanted the best for her.
But those roles flipped.
It began when Gwennie opened a painful portal into her life of relentless tragedy as Cindy grew into a successful businesswoman. She asked Cindy to help arrange an emergency divorce. It was Cindy’s first inkling of what her lifetime friend endured privately. Later, she asked Cindy to serve as her power of attorney. Gwennie realized her memory had begun to fray.
Gwennie lost four of her five children, which entombed her in grief and guilt. She worried that years of multiple jobs might have harmed her children. Cindy asked during one discussion: “Aren’t you proud of me? You helped raise me.”
Gwennie smiled because for years, when shopping at Carl Bell’s Wholesale Meat, she’d been telling people Cindy was her daughter. She giggled at the confused expressions.
As Gwennie’s memory deteriorated, Cindy moved deeper into her life, eventually selling Gwennie’s car and home and admitting her into a memory-care facility. Gwennie had worked so hard for so long. Cindy wanted to ensure Gwennie’s last days were safe and comfortable.
Earlier this year, an employee at the care home punched Gwennie. At 95, she could no longer talk. Cindy arrived and cupped Gwennie’s face. Gwennie’s bruised eye was swollen shut. It broke Cindy’s heart.
The memory care home fired the aide, but there wasn’t enough evidence for prosecution. Cindy also routed a “relative” who demanded Gwennie’s power of attorney.
“Not gonna happen,” Cindy said.
Walter Winchell once said: “A real friend is one who walks in when the rest of the world walks out.” Henry Drummond once said: “Wherever we are, it is our friends that make our world.” George Herbert once said: “The best mirror is an old friend.”
Gwennie and Cindy meant all these things to each other. Gwennie’s deterioration proved painful. Cindy sometimes tried to reach her friend, through Gwennie’s fog, with a song.
She’d sing softly in Gwennie’s ear, “It’s your thang, do what you wanna do…”
Sometimes, Gwennie smiled.
Cindy felt prepared for Gwennie’s death. Though it would hurt, she wasn’t afraid. They would revisit everything saved in their covenant of memories.
“I know where she’s going, and where I’m going. I know I’ll see her again.”
Mark McCormick is the former executive director of the Kansas African American Museum, a member of the Kansas African American Affairs Commission and former deputy executive director at the ACLU of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate.
