name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Milwaukee further restricts Flock as controversy continues to grow
description: Milwaukee is tightening the leash around Flock automatic license plate reader cameras, with elected leaders calling for more oversight and restrictions as investigations into misuse by officers continue.  Flock cameras utilize AI-powered technology to identify vehicles and license plates that pass within their view on roadways. The data is stored for several[...]
text:
A Flock camera outside of Washington Park in Milwaukee, WI. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)Milwaukee is tightening the leash around Flock automatic license plate reader cameras, with elected leaders calling for more oversight and restrictions as investigations into misuse by officers continue. 
Flock cameras utilize AI-powered technology to identify vehicles and license plates that pass within their view on roadways. The data is stored for several weeks or longer, allowing law enforcement officers from anywhere across the country to search for specific vehicles as long as their agency has a contract with Flock. 
An analysis by the Wisconsin Examiner found that at least 221 Wisconsin law enforcement agencies searched the Flock network during the first half of 2025, and that officers often used vague search terms to query the system. That same year, the multi-billion dollar Flock Safety company spent $102,000 lobbying the state government for grants to allow law enforcement agencies to acquire license plate reader cameras, though the Republican-backed bills were unsuccessful. 
The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
On Tuesday, a directive went out from the office of Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley to county departments and the Milwaukee County Sheriff’s Office to limit Flock-related operations on county property, and to work towards adopting new transparency and accountability standards. 
“Public safety partners should have the right tools to keep Milwaukee County safe, but unchecked surveillance isn’t the answer,” said Crowley, who is running against Republican Tom Tiffany to become Wisconsin’s next governor, in a statement. “We have seen what can happen when this technology operates without clear rules, transparency and accountability. Protecting our residents’ privacy and maintaining the public’s trust is a responsibility I take seriously. That is why I am directing all County departments to limit the usage of all Flock camera systems and establish safeguards proactively, before a breach of public trust can occur.”
Crowley is calling on the Office of Corporation Counsel and the Information Management Services Division to evaluate current policies governing the use of any surveillance tech and to develop binding standards for its use. The standards will determine how surveillance technology can be used, how long data is kept, who can access that data and why, and limit when data is shared with an emphasis on prohibiting use for federal immigration enforcement without a judicial warrant, a county press release stated. These standards would also establish independent audits and enforceable consequences when surveillance technology is misused. 
Crowley is also calling on other local elected leaders to look closely at their own use of Flock cameras and adopt similar policies. Ultimately, these efforts could result in the adoption of a consistent standard across the county for Flock. 
In April Tiffany said he had never heard of Flock cameras, when he was asked about controversy around their use. “I’m going to sound ignorant on this, what are Flock cameras?” Tiffany said during a virtual question-and-answer session. 
More recently, Tiffany said that “government should not be building an AI surveillance network that tracks law-abiding Wisconsinites everywhere they drive.” Tiffany said that he would pause state funding for Flock and create a task force to establish stronger protections, penalties for misuse, limits on data sharing, and safeguards against foreign adversaries. Tiffany criticized Crowley for “repeatedly” seeking to install “more red-light cameras, speed cameras, and massive funding increases for automated license plate readers.” 
Tom Tiffany (right) and David Crowley (left). (Photos by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
Police departments often acquire Flock cameras through non-competitive sole source contracts which bypass a public bidding process, keeping local councils and residents from even knowing that the technology has been acquired.
The changes in Milwaukee County come after the Milwaukee Police Department announced on Monday that it will be further restricting its Flock network. In a Monday press release the department said that it “supports the use of technology to assist in solving crimes that cause harm to our community,” and that new technology can help solve cases more quickly than traditional methods for investigations. 
“With that, we recognize that the use of such technology, like Flock technology, comes with great responsibility,” the department said in the press release. “These tools must always be used to prevent and reduce harm, not create more.” The department acknowledged the growing discontent and angst over Flock technology in the community, saying that “we do not dismiss these opinions.” The department went on to say that it “acknowledges the harm that former department members have caused that has damaged the trust we work so hard to build” and that it “acknowledges the human error that comes with the use of technology” and that the department is “working tirelessly to reduce error as much as we can.”
The Milwaukee police  announced that access to Flock has been restricted to supervisors only, and that the department will no longer share its Flock data with neighboring jurisdictions. Furthermore, the cameras may only be used for “Part I crimes” such as homicide, rape, robbery, aggravated assault including non-fatal shootings, burglary, larceny, motor vehicle theft, arson, human trafficking, as well as for critically missing people and investigating drug trafficking organizations. 
Earlier this year, the department began revamping its auditing procedures and limited the number of officers with access to Flock cameras to an “as needed basis,” risk manager James Lewis told the Examiner in June.
“MPD will continue to robustly audit its Flock systems,” the department’s Monday press release reads. “We are better together!”

A Milwaukee police squad in front of the Municipal Court downtown. (Photo | Isiah Holmes)
The changes were followed on Tuesday by a statement from Mayor Cavalier Johnson that while technology can help law enforcement, “it is essential that we recognize the limitations and dangers associated with these tools.” Johnson added that “I recognize the benefits of the Flock cameras system.” He said that “on multiple occasions this tool has located critical missing persons and helped apprehend violent criminals in Milwaukee. The technology has also been misused in several notable instances, both locally and nationally, compromising the rights of individuals.” 
Several of those cases played out in Milwaukee and elsewhere in Wisconsin. Josue Ayala of Milwaukee, Cristian Morales of Menasha, and Frank McGrath of Kenosha County were all charged with either misdemeanor or felony misconduct in public office after using Flock to surveil their current or former romantic partners. Ayala was given a year of probation and avoided incarceration, whereas Morales was sentenced to six months in jail and three years of probation while avoiding prison time. McGrath’s case is still ongoing. 
In July, Tehrangi Chapman, a Milwaukee police internal affairs detective who was involved in investigating Ayala’s misuse of Flock, was also charged with using the cameras and car-mounted GPS devices to keep tabs on someone who he’d surveilled since 2019, before Flock even arrived in Milwaukee. Chapman has been charged with felonies, and his case is still ongoing. On Aug. 26, Chapman pled not guilty, and is expected back in court for a scheduling conference on Oct. 7, according to online court records. 
Each of the officers who’ve been found to have abused their access to Flock used terms like “suspicious” or “investigation” to search the Flock network, which were common terms found in the Examiner’s 2025 analysis. Other cases have also emerged, such as that of a man who is now suing the Waukesha County Sheriff’s Department after a deputy searched him in Flock following a traffic stop, for which the man sought to file a complaint against the deputy. 
A Flock camera outside of Washington Park in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
As misconduct cases have emerged, communities across the state have opted to drop their Flock cameras including Kaukauna, Sturgeon Bay, Verona, Appleton, Oshkosh, Dane County and Stoughton. 
In Oshkosh, the request to cancel the Flock contract actually came from the police chief, who told local elected officials that representatives of the multi-billion dollar Flock Safety company had misled him on whether the cameras were able to develop heatmaps depicting a vehicle’s movement patterns. 
Elsewhere, community members have packed public meetings to tell local officials that they don’t want to be placed under perpetual surveillance, expressing fears about how the cameras could be misused by both local and federal law enforcement. Police leaders have had mixed responses to the concerns from residents. The police chief in Green Bay has opted to keep the cameras, citing their usefulness in solving violent crime while also acknowledging that steps need to be taken to protect people’s privacy, while a chief in the small city of Chetek threatened to do background checks on residents who spoke against the cameras in a public meeting.
Exactly how to handle the cameras is still a question local and national leaders are trying to answer. In August,  President Donald Trump said that the cameras have “pros and cons” and that “it’s being studied right now, we’ll have an answer soon as to our views on it.” When asked whether he’d consider banning Flock cameras statewide, Democratic Gov. Tony Evers said, “I don’t know what the solution is, but I think there’s people all across our country that’s talking about it.” Evers said he recently talked with Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz about Flock cameras. “Whether that [banning the cameras] is the answer, all’s I know is that we need to have an answer.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Mainers tell advisory council they’re concerned about data centers — and the risk of missing out
description: At two listening sessions with the Maine Data Center Advisory Council, residents from across the state voiced concerns about data center development — but also the risks of opting out of the industry boom.  The council is tasked with evaluating issues related to large-scale data centers and providing strategic input on policies to address the […]
text:
An Amazon Web Services data center is shown situated near single-family homes. (Photo by Nathan Howard/Getty Images)At two listening sessions with the Maine Data Center Advisory Council, residents from across the state voiced concerns about data center development — but also the risks of opting out of the industry boom. 
The council is tasked with evaluating issues related to large-scale data centers and providing strategic input on policies to address the potential benefits and drawbacks.
As part of that process, the council held two virtual listening sessions to hear from the public about their concerns as well as possible recommendations. The council is tasked with presenting a final report to lawmakers in January.
The vast majority of speakers said they had many concerns about data centers, but there were some speakers who also pointed out the potential benefits of the development. Much of the discussion mirrored earlier debates on the issue in the state Legislature, including concerns about the impacts on Maine’s water and environment, as well as energy use and noise pollution. 
At the first session last week, Jackie Elliott said those complex factors led her to support a moratorium on data centers, until the issue can be better understood. 
“We’ve got to know what we’re doing here, and I don’t think we really do,” she said. 
Elliott said most of the information on artificial intelligence and data centers is still speculative, and that she feels the industry is a bubble that is going to burst. 
“And that, in this old lady’s mind, raises a question about who’s going to be paying the cost of what gets broken along the way,” she said. “And I am of the strong opinion that whoever breaks the stuff needs to pay for it, and we need solid agreements on the front end of all of this — costs cannot be shifted onto the public pocketbook.” 
Jay data center on hold indefinitely as company backs out, despite veto of statewide ban

Other speakers, including Maura McDermott, echoed concerns about the state being left responsible if the industry collapses. 
“I am afraid they’re going to come in, sweep in, overtake us, and do whatever they want, and then we’re left holding the bag, like all these PFAS chemicals,” she said, referring to the widespread contamination of so-called forever chemicals. 
She said that Maine is a recreation-focused state, and the outdoor environment is a key part of that identity.
“Everything that the data centers bring and talk about is in opposition to what we know and love in Maine,” McDermott said. “That’s who we are. We are outdoors people. We’re strong. We’re resilient. So I want us to think about this, and let’s make some demands.”
At the second session Tuesday, Karen Raye, an Eastport city councilor, asked the advisory council to consider the costs that a small municipality can accrue just to assess a data center project. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission is considering an application for an underwater data center in Passamaquoddy Bay. 
“In our case, before equipment ever enters the water, the community begins paying a price,” Raye said. “In fact, before the developer’s FERC application was even accepted, we’ve been forced to spend very scarce taxpayer dollars.”
She said the town has already had to review ordinances, attend hearings, consult attorneys and navigate the overlapping jurisdictions of state and federal government. 
“Eastport has a very small tax base,” Raye said. “We do not have scientists, engineers or attorneys on staff. Yet we must evaluate this project’s impacts on fisheries, navigation, water quality, the electrical grid, emergency response and our working waterfront.”

Sen. Stacy Brenner (D-Cumberland) echoed the need to support local officials. 
“Many of Maine’s small towns simply don’t have the planning capacity or technical expertise to evaluate developments of this scale and the impacts may extend well beyond municipal boundaries,” Brenner said. 
Brenner, who is also the president of Maine Farmland Trust, urged the council to protect the state’s farmland. She compared the data center boom to the development push for large solar developments in recent years. Brenner said the council should consider farmland protections like those the Legislature passed in 2023 that protected farmland from solar developments. 
“Data centers are different from renewable energy projects, and they bring their own questions around land, water, infrastructure, energy and community impacts,” she said. “But Maine does not need to start from scratch.”
Rep. Melanie Sachs (D-Freeport), who sponsored a bill vetoed by Gov. Janet Mills that would have created a moratorium on large scale data centers, said she has been closely following the council’s work. 
Like other speakers, Sachs said that Maine can’t rely on federal regulations to protect the state from data centers. And that any environmental review needs to be thorough and required of developers. 
“I would urge not providing any exemptions to the environmental review of any data center, regardless of megawatt size or square footage,” Sachs said. 
There were a range of opinions on how much of the regulations should be handled at the state or local level. 
Brett Brockway, who said he works in housing construction in central Maine, urged the council to ensure that local municipalities get the final say — and said that it shouldn’t be impossible for the towns that want the development to get it.
“So, my recommendation is actually very simple: don’t create another layer of bureaucracy,” he said. “Set clear statewide guardrails for the things that genuinely require statewide oversight, and do it quickly. Protect the ratepayers, protect the grid, enforce our environmental laws and then let the towns decide.”
Brockway is also a founder of Maine Vision 2040, an initiative that encourages responsible artificial intelligence infrastructure to prepare the state for economic opportunity. He said that banning data centers could have a serious economic impact on areas already struggling after losing a major employer, such as a paper mill. 
“There are communities in Maine that have the luxury of asking whether they want more growth,” he said. “There are other communities that have spent 40 years wondering where the growth went.”
But at the earlier session, Amy Davidoff said that a data center is never going to impact only one community, and there should be a mechanism for the surrounding area to play some sort of role in local considerations. 
“This isn’t a one-town deal,” she said. “It’s many of us, and I don’t know how to create such a mechanism, and maybe that’s why it needs to be at the state level.” 
Kat Taylor said she is concerned that the state’s unorganized territories will be targeted for data centers, because they don’t have the same home rule rights as other towns and cities.
Taylor said she is “agnostic” about data centers but added, “I don’t think that data centers are a bad idea if handled correctly.” 
Remick French, a retired technology executive and a founder of Maine Vision 2040, also emphasized the economic opportunity data centers could bring to Maine. 
“The goal should not be to approve every data center or reject them as a category,” French said. “It should be to create a framework that allows Maine to say yes to the right projects and no to the wrong ones, based on clear standards, public interest and evidence.”
He said the state should prioritize creating a predictable pathway for projects. 
“Maine should not wait for individual proposals and then improvise,” he said. “The state should identify where these facilities make the most sense, especially locations with suitable infrastructure, community support and opportunities to reuse formal industrial sites.”
The council will review all written and verbal comments at its next meeting, scheduled for Wednesday, Sept. 9.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Utility executives and cybersecurity experts warn Pa. lawmakers of growing threats
description: Utility executives and cybersecurity experts warned lawmakers cybersecurity measures come at a cost to ratepayers, and asked for any new requirements to take that into account.
text:
Power lines cross a field in Snyder County, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)In the past year, FirstEnergy Pennsylvania has seen a growing number of attempted malware and cyberattacks around their critical infrastructure. 
“Our defensive systems block tens of thousands of automated malicious connection attempts against public facing services each month,” said Brian Harrell, the chief security officer at the company that serves 2.1 million electric customers across 56 counties in Pennsylvania. “These statistics underscore why cybersecurity requires constant attention and continual enhancement.”
He was speaking to a panel of Pennsylvania House members about the increased cybersecurity threats utilities across the state are facing.
In the last few years, criminal and state-sponsored actors have increasingly targeted critical infrastructure across America and Europe. And as utilities and grid infrastructure increasingly rely on internet connections to function, bad actors’ tools have become more sophisticated.
“They’re seeking to manipulate, disrupt or disable the very control systems that provide light, heat and clean water for our communities,” said Rep. Pat Gallagher (D-Philadelphia), chair of the House Consumer Protection, Technology and Utilities Committee’s subcommittee on utilities. “Protecting our public utilities requires a unified front, one that bridges private operators, public regulators, state agencies and both political parties.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Utility executives and cybersecurity experts agreed that, at this point, investments in cybersecurity have become nearly as necessary as spending on infrastructures. But they warned lawmakers they come at a cost to ratepayers, and asked for any new regulations or requirements to take that into account.
“These investments are necessary, but cybersecurity now competes for the same limited resources needed for pipes, pumps and capital improvements,” said Craig Fahnestock, the director of government relations for the Pennsylvania Municipal Authorities Association. “We’re asking for requirements that are achievable.”
Fahnestock’s group represents nearly 700 municipal water authorities. Many are on the smaller side, serving rural communities, and don’t have the money of their counterparts in larger cities.
“All of them are working to address it, but their resources vary considerably,” he said. 
While lawmakers were not discussing any particular legislation, Fahnestock asked that any new law implementing cybersecurity requirements include funding, or that the state otherwise help connect smaller authorities with technical experts.
Transmission lines along a highway in Lancaster County on October 14, 2025. (Photo by Jessica Kourkounis for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Samit Nair, the Chief Information Officer for Essential Utilities, the parent company of Aqua Pennsylvania and People’s Natural Gas, said his company has managed to ward off any significant cyberattack, in part through funding cybersecurity initiatives.
“We treat cybersecurity spending as a normal, prudent part of running safe and reliable utility operations, the same way we treat the investment in pipes, treatment plants and distribution infrastructure,” he said.
While Nair said the company has not experienced any incidents that have disrupted operations, interrupted service to customers or caused a “material financial impact,” that doesn’t mean increased cybersecurity threats haven’t cost them. 
The company requires cybersecurity insurance. And the costs can vary depending on a firm’s  track record.
“The premium rates, a lot of it depends on how solid your practice is,” he told lawmakers. “So there’s a whole bunch of questions that insurers ask us, and validate us, before they even provide us insurance.”
Jeremy Young, president and CEO of Federal Resources Corporation, an organization that provides cybersecurity expertise to government and public sector organizations, warned lawmakers that artificial intelligence has only increased the cybersecurity needs of utilities. 
“Attackers now have access to automation and artificial intelligence that can accelerate reconnaissance, phishing, vulnerability, discovery and exploitation,” he said. “A utility may have thousands of employees, devices, applications, identities, suppliers, systems and vulnerabilities to protect. An attacker only needs one successful path.”
While he stressed defense against cyberattacks required action, he also warned against legislation that’s too prescriptive in a quickly changing environment.

“A security control that worked when it was audited six months ago may not be working today,” he said. “That’s why I believe cybersecurity needs to become a continuous risk management discipline rather than a periodic compliance exercise.”
He encouraged lawmakers and state regulators to focus on regulations that require risk monitoring and taking proactive cybersecurity measures, but that allow utilities to decide what works best for them and their ratepayers, who often foot the bill for new spending requirements.
“I believe we should give utilities flexibility in how they achieve cybersecurity outcomes while requiring evidence that those outcomes are being achieved,” he said. “Because ultimately the question for this committee and PA ratepayers should not simply be, ‘How much did we spend on cybersecurity?’ It should be, ‘Are Pennsylvanians safer because of it?’”
Young also noted that better cybersecurity doesn’t always require big spending. He said a large majority of cybersecurity incidents can be avoided by educating staff on how to detect and avoid threats, like phishing. 
Steve McElwee, the chief security officer at PJM, which operates a massive electric grid across Pennsylvania and 12 other states, also warned lawmakers that changes in power usage from things like data centers have opened electric companies up to greater threats of cyberattacks. 
“As electricity demand grows and supply becomes more scarce, the power grid has less flexibility to absorb the impacts of disruptive events,” he said. “In addition, the growth of large computational loads has changed the grid operating conditions, creating challenges like over-voltage, over-frequency and oscillating conditions.”
Harrell, the Chief Security Officer at FirstEnergy also asked lawmakers to consider a particular weak point when crafting bills or regulations.
Electric utilities, he said, are subject to federal cybersecurity regulations and increased scrutiny as cyberattacks on critical infrastructure have become more common. But the companies they do business with, who may have data on their systems and customers, are just as vulnerable to attack.
“While we have done a really good job at defending ourselves, it’s the third party supply chain, it’s our vendors, that may have your data, our data, and customer data,” he said. “We need to be just as sharp with them in ensuring that they are doing what they say they have done.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: New invasive insect poses ‘serious threat’ to Georgia farmers
description: A grass-eating invasive pest has been spotted in Georgia, and it could mean further headaches for cattle ranchers and farmers. The pasture mealybug has been spreading across the Southeast since it was first confirmed in Texas last October, and Georgia Agriculture Commissioner Tyler Harper announced recently the insect had been spotted at a turf business […]
text:
Pasture mealybug. Isaac L. Esquivel/University of FloridaA grass-eating invasive pest has been spotted in Georgia, and it could mean further headaches for cattle ranchers and farmers.
The pasture mealybug has been spreading across the Southeast since it was first confirmed in Texas last October, and Georgia Agriculture Commissioner Tyler Harper announced recently the insect had been spotted at a turf business in Decatur County in the southwest corner of the state in August.
“Pasture mealybug is a serious threat to Georgia agriculture, and we’re asking Georgia farmers and producers to stay vigilant in order to protect their operations,” Harper said. “This pest can spread quickly and kill grass, potentially causing significant losses for our farmers and making biosecurity more important than ever.”
Pasture mealybug infestation on grass. Isaac L. Esquivel/University of Florida
Female pasture mealybugs are wingless and appear white and fluffy. Males are gnat-like and have wings but no mouthparts, do not feed in their adult stage and only live a few days as adults.
They can produce up to 100 offspring at a time and can have three generations in a year. They feed on grass by sucking out sap, which damages the plants and makes them more susceptible to disease. They also inject toxic saliva into the plants and produce a thick honeydew that promotes mold growth.
Researchers say the bugs could pose a major economic threat to livestock because they can decimate grazing grasses that cattle rely on, and they also pose a threat to crops like rice and sugarcane, both of which are types of grass.
“We still know very little about it overall, since it is relatively new to the United States,” said Lisa Baxter, a professor at the University of Georgia’s College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences who studies crop and soil sciences. “But our understanding from literature is that any warm season grass could be affected, so that means pastures, hay fields, lawns, sod farms, seed farms, crop fields that are grasses. People forget that things like corn and wheat and things like that are grasses.”
According to UGA, which is tracking sightings of the bug throughout the state, beef was the second most valuable farm commodity in 2024, generating $1.2 billion to the economy.
But cattle ranchers have reported struggles in recent years from droughts and higher costs for inputs like fuel and fertilizer, and the U.S. cattle herd is at its lowest point since the 1950s.
The pasture mealybug’s newness on the scene in the U.S. also means farmers and scientists don’t know what kinds of pesticides might be effective against them. Baxter said researchers are testing existing products, and if one is found effective against mealybugs, it could receive temporary approval, but so far nothing has been found.
Baxter said that means it’s important for farmworkers to take precautions to slow the spread of the bugs as much as possible. Young mealybugs can be blown from place to place by the wind, and they can also hitch a ride on animals, including humans, attaching to their clothes, tools and vehicles.
“It’s keeping people and animals and equipment clean as you are moving from farm to farm, limiting traffic through your farm and monitoring, like, always looking down, keeping an eye as to what’s happening,” she said. “And if you have an infected area, kind of self-quarantine it off, and make sure that we’re cleaning equipment from the infected area to the non-infected area or cleaning your boots from one area to the next.”
Signs of infestation can appear within a week and may include yellowing leaves that progress to purple or red discoloration and death of the plant.
University of Georgia entomology professor Shimat Joseph stressed that much is still unknown about how this bug could affect crops in the United States, but he said the creatures are likely to cause problems for pasture growers, and they could also create challenges for commercial sod and turf farms and for those who grow ornamental grasses.
Turfgrass was a $284 million business in 2024, according to UGA.
But he said he is hopeful that, based on infestations in other countries, the mealybugs will not be a major threat to residential lawns or places like parks or golf courses with regularly maintained grass.
“It was introduced for a long time in Australia, it’s been there. And wherever they reported problems in turfgrass, it was when the grass is not mowed or the grass is growing very tall, so if we keep the grass mowed and keep it low, most probably we may not see this as a major problem in turfgrass. But again, this is all based on what we know from Australia and in Florida, but as time goes, we might know more about this.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Where have the workers gone? 2 million foreign-born men have left the country, analysis says
description: Economists, policymakers and journalists have been puzzling over why so many workers between 25 and 54 have been leaving the labor force over the past two years. An Ohio data analyst has identified one cause that could be a warning sign for the overall economy. About 720,000 Americans seemingly stopped looking for work between May […]
text:
An employee walks behind cattle on an Idaho dairy farm in an undated photo. Dairy farms in Idaho say they depend on immigrant workers without legal work authorization and oppose mandates to check legal status with the federal E-Verify system. (Photo courtesy of Idaho Dairymen’s Association)Economists, policymakers and journalists have been puzzling over why so many workers between 25 and 54 have been leaving the labor force over the past two years.
An Ohio data analyst has identified one cause that could be a warning sign for the overall economy.
About 720,000 Americans seemingly stopped looking for work between May and June alone, CNBC reported. And Policy Matters Ohio reports that 74,000 fewer people are seeking jobs in the Buckeye State than were this time last year.
One reason for the losses: millions of foreign-born men are no longer in the country, according to an analysis that was published on Sunday. Happening amid President Donald Trump’s mass deportations, many were probably forced to leave.
Eric Pachman used government data to determine that 2.1 million foreign-born, working-age men have left the country since the start of Trump’s second term. Eighty-eight percent of them were working when they left the country, according to the analysis.
“Over the past two years foreign-born men’s labor force shrank by 1.4 million,” the report on Pachman’s website, Data 4 the People, says. “But in a normal pair of summers it would have grown by about 360,000 — so measured against trend, the swing is 1.8 million.”
The losses of foreign-born men last year and this year were by far the biggest in the datasets with which Pachman worked.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.In 2025, the United States lost 1.2 million foreign-born men, followed by 919,ooo so far this year. The next closest year — at the height of the pandemic in 2020 — saw only 336,000 foreign-born men left the country.
Analysts who study the government’s data regarding Trump’s mass deportations say there are reasons to question their reliability. But with the government reporting as many as 10,000 deportations in a month, it’s reasonable to assume that many of the male, foreign-born workers who have left the country did so via deportation.
Pachman’s analysis didn’t find similar steep declines in the number of foreign-born women. That raises the possibility that many more men than women are being deported, thereby breaking up families, the researcher said.
Other analyses indicate that historically, the great majority of deportations involved men.
Pachman said the fact that native-born workers haven’t rushed to fill jobs vacated by foreign-born men undermines a basic tenant of Trump’s deportation project: the claim that foreign workers took jobs that the native-born want.
“There’s a narrative that a lot of people believe despite their political party. Call it the labor-displacement effect,” Pachman said in an interview. “It says that if an immigrant takes a job, that is a job that’s being taken from another individual, say a native-born, white American. 
“If that is true, what we should be finding when we look at the public data is that as jobs go away that immigrants were holding, those jobs should be getting filled by native-born men. But we’re not finding that. We’re finding that the participation rate of native-born men is continuing to decline.”
Pachman looked at the kinds of jobs in which foreign-born men were most prevalent. 
First was farming, fishing and forestry, where they made up 42% of the workforce. That was followed by construction and extraction at 34%, 30% in building and grounds maintenance, healthcare support at 27%, 25% for food preparation and serving, and another 25% in transportation and material moving.
Those are fields that the native-born apparently find less attractive than their foreign-born counterparts.
In addition to Trump’s tariffs, healthcare cuts and his war with Iran, his mass deportations may be yet another drag on the economy.
“If this displacement theory does not hold, then we’re playing with fire with the economy,” Pachman said. “All that is going to do is lead to certain vacancies in the economy for certain types of jobs that were more likely to be done by the foreign-born. If they go unfilled, then all this does is lead to more inflation.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: The girls who survived
description: This article was first published by The Marshall Project, a nonprofit news organization covering the U.S. criminal justice system. Sign up for their newsletters, and follow them on Instagram, TikTok, Reddit and Facebook. It was hard not to feel hopeless. Locked away from everyone and everything they knew, they spent their teenage years inside youth […]
text:
Clockwise from top left, Samantha Primeau, Isabella Ramirez, Paitin Pahoundis and Jaycee Seele spent some of their teenage years inside youth residential treatment centers in Ohio.
(Photo by Bethany Mollenkof for The Marshall Project)This article was first published by The Marshall Project, a nonprofit news organization covering the U.S. criminal justice system. Sign up for their newsletters, and follow them on Instagram, TikTok, Reddit and Facebook.
It was hard not to feel hopeless. Locked away from everyone and everything they knew, they spent their teenage years inside youth residential treatment centers, face to face with violence.
In the chaos, the children found strength in the bonds they formed as they cared for one another. When they left the treatment centers, those bonds helped them survive and, at times, thrive, even while they struggled with nightmares of waking up inside a facility.
They live on their own now across Ohio, their relationships grounded in a pursuit of accountability for what happened to them inside — and support for what happens next.
They exchange text messages to pass along details of how to get records from the treatment centers, pry loose bodycam footage from police, and connect with other survivor groups and nonprofits. And they root for each other, as they earn college degrees, attend night school, raise their newborns, try out new hair colors, navigate breakups, apply for jobs and rent apartments.
“We brought each other back to life,” Paitin Pahoundis said of herself and the other now-young women survivors, “just by simply being there, knowing we aren’t alone. Even if we hated each other. I didn’t fully realize how much I needed that understanding until I got out … We yearn for each other.”
As Paitin, Jaycee Seele, Isabella Ramirez and Samantha Primeau told their stories of survival over the last two years — stories that were part of The Marshall Project’s investigation into residential treatment facilities — it became clear their lives were intertwined.
 Keeping each other alive

For Jaycee, Isabella was a lifeline. Isabella was the one who stopped her from banging her head against the wall on the inside. Jaycee said she had wanted to stop the thoughts of wanting to die. Isabella would place a cold wash rag on Jaycee’s forehead to calm her down.
After residential treatment, Jaycee showed up for Isabella. When Isabella was close to term, Jaycee, who had already given birth to her own baby, drove across Ohio with clothes and items to help welcome her friend’s new baby girl into the world.
Nowadays, Jaycee’s lifeline is her daughter.
“She has changed my life,” Jaycee said. “I feel like I have a purpose since I got out. I want to protect her so she doesn’t go through what I went through.”
Jaycee now works with the Ohio Youth Advisory Board, helping to shape foster care and residential treatment policy. She has a TikTok account where she posts bodycam footage and other public records obtained by disability rights groups or advocacy organizations to raise awareness about what’s become known as the “troubled teen industry.”
 Learn to heal

Isabella never thought she’d graduate from high school. Now, she’s in college.
She graduated high school shortly after her daughter was born. Building her education and working toward a career are among her proudest accomplishments, besides being a good mother. She hopes to become a nurse.
“I just want to spread the word about everything that happened. I was at school telling everyone,” Isabella said. “I feel like my story and what I have been through is not going to waste.”
 Searching for truth

Samantha spends as much time as she can under the open sky.
She loves the freedom she has to listen to music and get lost in lyrics — she remembers a time when she was starved of art and sound. She experiments with photography with her friends, finding outdoor backdrops for portraits.
Even in those peaceful moments, she worries about the kids inside the locked facilities across Ohio.
So she continues trying to learn more about her experience. Along with Paitin, they file records requests for bodycam footage of her time on the inside and scour social media, in part, to find former staff members who are willing to talk.
“People don’t know these places exist unless you know people who have been there or you’ve been in the system,” she said.
 Learning to be free

Paitin still dreams of running.
Sometimes she wakes up and forgets she’s no longer locked inside a treatment center. Other days, she dreams of what life is like outside of Ohio and its expanse of cornfields. She remembers a time when she’d have to remind herself that she didn’t need permission to go outside.
Over the past two years, she’s worked on her anxiety. She used to be too scared to have a public-facing job. Now, she works in a restaurant and pays rent. She’s proud of her own apartment.
Paitin and Isabella had run away together while in treatment. They wept as they shared their stories and recalled protecting one another, kicking down doors, trying to intervene in restraints. They also laughed at police trying to catch them as they hid in bushes or crossed highways.
Isabella taught Paitin how to hitchhike and run toward the horizon.
For now, Paitin leans on her fellow survivors. They Snapchat, call and text each other. They gather evidence. They hope for change.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: New Ohio Senate bill would legislate higher ed viewpoints, further power of S.B. 1
description: In the 1957 case of Sweezy vs. New Hampshire, the U.S. Supreme Court warned states that “liberties in the areas of academic freedom and political expression” were “areas in which government should be extremely reticent to tread.” Since then, courts have generally followed a rule of thumb that states can specify what college instructors can […]
text:
(Stock photo from Getty Images)In the 1957 case of Sweezy vs. New Hampshire, the U.S. Supreme Court warned states that “liberties in the areas of academic freedom and political expression” were “areas in which government should be extremely reticent to tread.” 
Since then, courts have generally followed a rule of thumb that states can specify what college instructors can teach, but not what they conclude about it. In other words, as long as professors stick to talking about things relevant to the course topic and their own area of expertise, the First Amendment strongly protects their liberty to present whatever viewpoints they feel are relevant to discuss. 
This distinction – that the state gets to choose the topic and faculty decide how to pursue it – has largely held for the past seventy-five years or so. In Ohio, the state legislature broke with this precedent when it passed its claimed omnibus higher education reform bill, Senate Bill 1. A small, unremarkable provision of that law tip-toed past the larger controversies raging over the bill and quietly stepped over that line. 
Buried deep in the 42 page law is the requirement that newly state-mandated civics courses include reading at least “five essays in their entirety from the Federalist Papers.” Fine. This would pass the test affirmed this summer in Pernell v. Florida, by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit, that held that the government can dictate programs but not viewpoints. But the next short sentence opened the door to blowing up this distinction. 
“The essays shall be selected by the department chair.”
By itself, having a department chair determine which of the 85 Federalist Papers are most worthy of teaching is probably not a clear violation of academic freedom principles (though given the range of the Federalist essays, which ones a professor chooses to highlight can be very ideological). 
But for the first time, it specifically establishes in Ohio law the power of a state bureaucrat (yes, Virginia, chairs and deans are government functionaries, ultimately beholden to their bosses rather than their own principles) to pick and choose how a particular subject is to be taught. 
S.B. 1 was passed in the spring of 2025, and in the year since, its sponsor has been unsettled by how one aspect of it has been rolled out. State Sen. Jerry Cirino, R-Kirtland, discovered that some professors were not going to teach a celebratory and patriotic version of American history and he introduced a follow-on bill, S.B. 461, to, as he put it, “close the loophole.” 
Senator Cirino has been remarkably candid about his determination to legislate the viewpoints that he wishes to see taught. He recently spoke on Ohio Senate Majority Communications Director John Fortney’s podcast:
Fortney: There’s even a new textbook called Unpatriotic Civics, explicitly designed to fulfill the requirements of Senate Bill 1, but “without endorsing the patriotic narrative.” That’s how far some of these leftists will go to try and get around the law. 
Cirino: Well, we’re not going to have any of that in the state of Ohio … So what we’ve done in Senate Bill 461 is we set it up that the directors of the five centers as a group need to be the ones in the future who will be approving the courses that qualify … That way we are not going to have any of this funny business which the academicians will definitely attempt to do, putting courses in there that don’t meet the intent of the legislation that we passed.
For full disclosure, I am the author of Unpatriotic Civics and its companion book, The Civics of Pluralism, that will be made available at no cost to all Ohio students through the Ohio Open Ed Collaborative, a project of the Ohio Department of Higher Education. 
Cirino didn’t fully explain his own bill, because S.B. 461 does much more than merely approve courses. The law gives his Ohio Civics Board “sole and exclusive authority over all aspects of American civic literacy courses…including course modality, syllabi, class size, faculty teachers, and course content.” 
This is a level of control reminiscent of the way the Soviet Union would station political overseers at desks next to government officials to ensure they toed the line and to report on their loyalty. 
I suspect that such a Civics Board will look unfavorably upon a textbook that highlights facts including that slavery was a major issue in the American Revolution, the idea that many patriotic Americans viewed the Constitution of 1787 as an aristocratic coup, that Dr. Martin Luther King’s Letter from a Birmingham Jail was in violation of the prohibited concepts in S.B. 1, and that Adam Smith was not a consistent believer in the free market but wanted state controls over major portions of the economy. 
Cirino has also explained that he established the structure of the Ohio Civics Board to insulate it from any popular attempts to check its power. As envisioned in S.B. 461, the board is composed of five GOP loyalists who are not elected and cannot be removed or appointed by the governor. They will enjoy a budget that would be the envy of every college dean in the state. 
Not only will they directly receive the tuition dollars of students taking their classes, but were the Ohio legislature to decide to cut its share of funding to these civics centers, the university must make up all the shortfall in their budgets from its own general funds. 
All of these barriers to democratic controls were explained by Cirino this way: 
“The current chancellor is doing a really good job of ferreting out, you know, some of the courses that have been proposed to qualify, but what (S.B.) 461 is attempting to do is to solidify this a little bit more and protect it because there will be future governors, future chancellors, future legislators, who may want to, you know, water things down.”
Ohioans who care about the quality and independence of their universities and colleges might want to pay attention to S.B. 461 this fall.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Nepal’s calamity is a call for action here
description: Is it not a matter of conscience to prevent the warming that will be visited upon our descendants regardless of race, wealth, nation, religion, ethnic identity, or politics?
text:
The heartbreaking Nepal calamity, caused in part by a collapsing glacier, was the predicted outcome of climate-warming disruption caused by the burning of oil, coal, and natural gas.  
Sadly, Nepal’s per capita carbon footprint is a fraction of that of Western nations.
The melting of permafrost and glaciers, warming oceans, severe storms and droughts, extreme heat and worsening wildfires –- all caused by climate change — are costing lives and livelihoods in the United States as well.  This will worsen if we do not act to halt the warming of the climate.  
Is it not a matter of conscience to prevent the warming that will be visited upon our descendants regardless of race, wealth, nation, religion, ethnic identity, or politics?  Is it not a matter of national security to ensure we are building the industries that are already advanced in other nations rather than continuing to cede expertise and renewable energy primacy to other nations?
There are several steps that we can immediately take that will most certainly build industries and jobs, while reducing pollution -– all of which should attract bipartisan support if done correctly.
On the national level, Senate Majority Leader John Thune should bring permitting reform to the floor, which will help move energy projects to the approval or rejection stage more quickly and shore up or rebuild decaying electric grid infrastructure. To save jobs and lower electricity costs, the bill should ensure that renewable projects, once approved, cannot then be rescinded on presidential whim.
On the Connecticut state level, we must remove the unnecessary and business-killing cap on the size of solar projects so that solar businesses can compete to build large solar arrays.  
We should also research with solar companies what sensible steps can be implemented that will reduce the cost of Connecticut’s residential solar to (at least) the cost of that of Texas (residential solar in Texas costs about half that of Connecticut).  We should also offer a contest with a sizeable prize to renewable business incubators that solve problems while increasing businesses in Connecticut: for example, reducing the cost of solar canopies.  
We have numerous resources in Connecticut that could solve problems.  Surely technical schools and universities could team up to solve problems, win financial backing, and create new businesses and jobs for people residing right here in Connecticut.
Conscience calls us to immediate action.
Susan Chapin lives in Mystic.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Connecticut’s climate costs are coming home to Glastonbury
description: Connecticut needs a Climate Superfund modeled on the "polluter pays" principle to fund climate adaptation and resilience.
text:
One of my favorite things about growing up in Glastonbury has always been our farms. I grew up picking blueberries at Dondero Orchards and strawberries at Belltown Hill Orchards with my dad. I worked at a local farm stand. For me, these places are more than just businesses; they are part of my town’s identity.
That is why the flooding that hit Connecticut farms in 2023 felt so personal. Farms along the Connecticut River experienced heavy and devastating crop losses. Somebody has to pay for these damages. And the question Glastonbury residents have been asking is: who pays?
Five other residents and I recently spoke during public comment before the Glastonbury Town Council about a proposed municipal resolution supporting a Connecticut Climate Superfund.  The proposed resolution would express municipal support for state-level legislation intended to create another source of funding for climate adaptation and resilience.
Being a young person leading this effort seemed daunting at first, but I quickly realized this issue needed a voice, and that I could be that voice. Engaging with other Glastonbury residents and the Town Council members on this issue taught me the importance of community engagement and being an active resident.
The Climate Superfund is modeled on the “polluter pays” principle behind traditional environmental cleanup programs. Under the proposed Connecticut approach, certain major fossil fuel companies responsible for substantial historical greenhouse gas emissions would make payments into a state-administered fund. The Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection would oversee funding for eligible climate adaptation and infrastructure projects.
So why should that matter to a town like Glastonbury?

Allison Desmarais

Without additional sources of funding, many climate-related damages become public expenses. Connecticut residents already face high housing, energy, food, and tax bills. Municipalities and taxpayers are often left paying for infrastructure damages and resilience projects, instead of the major companies driving these expenses.
That is why I believe the Climate Superfund proposal deserves public conversation.
I had hoped the Glastonbury Town Council would have listened to the youth in town and added the municipal resolution on an upcoming agenda. Although that has not happened, I appreciate The Glastonbury Citizen for covering the issue, the council members who have expressed interest in the proposal, and the residents who have participated in the conversation. 
Glastonbury cannot establish a statewide Climate Superfund on its own. It is crucial that more towns express their perspectives and stories and contribute to debates at the Capitol. Municipalities understand firsthand what it costs to maintain roads, protect water systems, respond to floods, and preserve local resources. Municipalities and towns are going to continue footing the bill when extreme weather strikes if the State does not step up. 
As Connecticut considers how to prepare for a changing climate, we should at least be willing to have a serious conversation about whether taxpayers should continue bearing these costs on their own, and what responsibility the companies that contributed to greenhouse gas emissions should have in helping communities prepare for what comes next.
Allison Desmarais is a senior at the University of South Carolina and a Glastonbury resident .

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: What Bridgeport and Fairfield reveal about who shows up for school
description: We are very good at counting whether families show up for institutions. We should become just as serious about whether institutions show up for families.
text:
Bridgeport and Fairfield share a border. When it comes to school attendance, they can look like two different Connecticuts.
During the 2024–25 school year, 33.1% of Bridgeport Public Schools students were chronically absent, compared with 8.8% in Fairfield. Connecticut’s statewide rate was 17.2%. Chronic absenteeism means missing at least 10% of the school year, or roughly 18 days in a typical 180-day year.
We can look at that difference and ask why Bridgeport families aren’t getting their children to school. I think that’s the wrong question. I don’t believe parents become less invested in their children’s education when they cross a town line. A mother in Bridgeport doesn’t want less for her child than a mother in Fairfield. What changes are the circumstances around them and the demands placed on the institutions serving them.
I’ve seen that tension in my own work. In New York City Public Schools, I led community engagement efforts that brought families and educators face to face with system leadership. I learned quickly that what looks accessible from inside an institution can feel anything but accessible to the people trying to navigate it.
Bridgeport serves far more students experiencing economic hardship and far more multilingual learners than Fairfield. Those realities matter because attendance does not happen in a vacuum. But demographics cannot become our stopping point. A school system serving families facing greater barriers needs more time to solve problems, more staff who know families by name and more ways for parents to reach an actual person.
Think about something as ordinary as a 6 p.m. school meeting. One parent leaves work, drives ten minutes and takes a seat. Another loses an hour of pay by leaving early, catches a bus and still has to figure out who can watch the other children. Both may care just as much, however our systems are simply better at seeing one of them.
Children need to be in school. Missing weeks of instruction has consequences. But responsibility cannot belong only to families.
And this isn’t only a Bridgeport story. Waterbury’s chronic absenteeism rate was 25.8% in 2024–25. Regional School District 15, serving Middlebury and Southbury, reported 8.6%. Different communities but yet a familiar divide.
Connecticut’s Learner Engagement and Attendance Program, or LEAP, offers a useful lesson. LEAP sends trained school staff or community partners to meet directly with families, not to enforce attendance rules, but to build relationships and understand what is keeping a student from school.
A 2022 evaluation of students served during the 2021–22 school year found that attendance improved after LEAP visits. It also found that visits at a student’s home or school had significantly greater effects than visits conducted by Zoom or phone.
New Haven offers an even sharper lesson. The district did not initially conduct one-on-one visits as the LEAP model intended. Instead, a nonprofit partner canvassed neighborhoods with high concentrations of chronically absent students. The evaluation found no measurable impact on attendance there. New Haven later changed its approach to more closely match the model used in other districts. Same program name but yet a very different result.
Counting an outreach attempt is not the same thing as making a connection.
Bridgeport’s more recent numbers make this worth watching. The district reported chronic absenteeism at 22.6% in October 2025, down from 32% in October 2024. Those are preliminary, point-in-time numbers, not final school-year results, and no single program can claim credit for them. Still, the direction matters. Relationships aren’t the soft side of attendance work. They are part of the infrastructure.
Connecticut should start measuring them that way.
The Connecticut State Department of Education should pilot a family-responsiveness measure in districts with persistently high chronic absenteeism, including districts already doing relationship-based attendance work. And it shouldn’t be another satisfaction survey.
The families who find institutions hardest to navigate may also be the least likely to complete one. So measure what institutions actually do. How long does it take to respond when a family asks for help? When a school reaches out about attendance, did someone actually connect with the parent or guardian? When a problem is raised, was there follow-through? Those aren’t sentimental questions. They are questions about institutional performance.
Connecticut already includes chronic absenteeism in its 12-indicator Next Generation Accountability System. A family-responsiveness pilot could tell us whether measures of actual connection and follow-through reveal something our current indicators miss. If they do, CSDE should consider incorporating that information into the state’s broader accountability framework.
We are very good at counting whether families show up for institutions. We should become just as serious about whether institutions show up for families. Bridgeport and Fairfield share a border. Their attendance numbers tell us that proximity does not mean families experience public education in the same way. Before we decide that some families simply need to show up more, our institutions should answer the harder question of what have we done to make showing up possible?
Mychael Williams lives in Waterbury.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Koh comes out on top in crowded primary race to replace Moulton
description: Koh will face Republican Micah Jones in November. If Koh wins, as he is heavily favored to do, he would be Massachusetts’s first Asian American congressperson.
text:
IN HIS SECOND bid for a congressional seat, former Biden White House aide Dan Koh won the Democratic nomination to succeed US Rep. Seth Moulton on Tuesday, with the presumed front-runner taking top spot in a crowded five-way field. 
The Associated Press called the race for Koh at 10:27 p.m., with 43 percent of the vote and a 12-point lead over state Rep. Tram Nguyen. 
Elsewhere on the congressional map, incumbent US Reps. Stephen Lynch and Richard Neal held off challengers from their lefts, laying out a path to a mostly unchanged Massachusetts delegation. 
Moulton’s unsuccessful Senate bid opened the first competitive race in the Sixth Congressional District — which runs from Lynn up the North Shore to the New Hampshire border — in more than a decade. Five Democrats were openly in contention after Mariah Lancaster dropped out in the campaign’s final days and endorsed Nguyen. 
Koh, 41, grew up in Andover and worked for Boston Mayor Marty Walsh and later the Biden administration. He entered primary day as the best-funded candidate, with about $4.7 million raised.  
In a year when many Democrats sought to distance themselves from the Biden presidency, Koh leaned in. He touted endorsements from former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris, as well as the Massachusetts AFL-CIO, and branded himself as someone whose top issues were fighting Donald Trump and “protecting democracy.” 
He’d nearly made it to Congress once before. In 2018, he lost the Third Congressional District Democratic primary to now-Rep. Lori Trahan in a packed primary by less than half a percent of votes cast, after a district-wide recount. Trahan picked up the seat with 21.6 percent of the vote. 
Some Massachusetts Democrats had begun coalescing around Nguyen, 40, as the race waned. She arrived in the US as a refugee at 5 years old after her family fled Vietnam. In 2018, she unseated Republican Rep. Jim Lyons, who went on to chair the state GOP, by 10 points, becoming the first Vietnamese American woman elected to office in Massachusetts.  
Congresswomen Ayanna Pressley and Koh’s former rival Trahan both endorsed Nguyen for the seat, as did House Speaker Ron Mariano. The representative leaned into an affordability platform, centering housing and economic justice. 
A late-July internal poll for Koh’s campaign, conducted by Global Strategy Group, had him at 34 percent — roughly double the level of support for attorney John Beccia and Nguyen. That poll predated Nguyen’s endorsements from Pressley and Trahan. 
Nguyen was sitting at almost 30 percent of the vote when the Associated Press called the race. 
The race had a few echoes of the last time a Markey challenge opened up a US congressional seat. In 2020, when Joe Kennedy III unsuccessfully sought to unseat Markey, the Fourth Congressional District primary ballot featured seven Democrats. 
Current US Rep. Jake Auchincloss came out on top by a mere 1.4 percent margin over Jesse Mermell, capturing about 22 percent of the vote. 
In both the 2018 and 2020 congressional races, progressives decried the number of candidates that split the vote. Koh came out with a more decisive lead, though he didn’t crack a majority of the votes. 
Former state Rep. Jamie Belsito and software engineer Beth Andres-Beck rounded out the field. Beccia was showing about 12 percent of the vote at 10:30 p.m., Belsito almost 9 percent, and Andres-Beck and the late exit Lancaster each with almost 4 percent. 
Koh will face Republican Micah Jones in November. If Koh wins, as he is heavily favored to do, he would be Massachusetts’s first Asian American congressperson. 
To the west, US Rep. Richard Neal turned back a primary challenge from Northampton teacher Jeromie Whalen on Tuesday, likely extending his almost four-decade hold on the district. 
Ways and Means ranking Democrat Neal, 77, is seeking a 20th term for the Massachusetts First Congressional District. He was facing Whalen, who built his campaign around taxing the wealthy, single-payer health care, and lost school aid. “I’m a public servant, not a politician,” Whalen told WWLP in launching his bid. 
The Associated Press called the race for Neal at 11:07 p.m., with the congressman at 55 percent of the vote and holding a roughly 10-point lead over Whalen. 
Neal’s last real primary fight, a 2020 race against then-Holyoke Mayor Alex Morse, ended in an 18-point win. 
The contest came amid a wave of incumbent losses nationally — including Neal’s own Ways and Means colleague, Rep. John Larson of Connecticut, who lost his primary the month before, according to NOTUS. Neal waved off the comparison, telling NOTUS that challengers tend to act like political history started the day they were born.  
Previous challengers have “really been unable to fracture, nevermind break” his longstanding relationships in the district, he told the publication. 
Neal’s victory means a rematch: independent Nadia Milleron, who took 37 percent of the vote against Neal in 2024, is running again, alongside a second independent, Anthony Celata. 
Along the coast of Boston, US Rep. Stephen Lynch fended off the most serious challenge of his decades-long career on Tuesday, defeating 39-year-old Patrick Roath in the night’s third rebuke to generational change messages. 
Lynch, 71, was looking to secure a 13th full term in the Massachusetts Eighth Congressional District against Roath, a voting rights attorney and former aide to Gov. Deval Patrick.  
The Associated Press named Lynch the projected winner just 20 minutes before midnight on Tuesday, with about 57 percent of the vote and a secure 13-point lead over Roath. 
Roath was banking on a surge of enthusiasm for candidates that would take on the Trump administration. He rolled out a slew of local backers, like former Gov. Deval Patrick; state Reps. Jay Livingstone, Sam Montaño, and John Moran; Boston City Councilors Enrique Pepén and Ben Weber; the four Quincy city councilors who just ousted incumbents in an uprising against mayor Thomas Koch, a long-time Lynch ally; an array of school committee members across the district;  and teachers unions like the Massachusetts Teachers Association and Boston Teachers Union. 
Lynch, running a mailer campaign pitching himself as the sensible middle, asked voters, “When the political extremes drown everyone out, who is listening to you?” 
Lynch leaned on labor support from groups like the Professional Firefighters of Massachusetts and the Iron Workers Local 7, as well as seniority on the House Financial Services Committee, meeting the challenge with little sense of public concern. The few times he faced primary challengers, in 2018 and 2020, he stomped them by around 30 percentage points.  
The race drew some attention from a national PAC looking to support progressive challengers to Democratic incumbents. By June, Roath had out-raised Lynch $1.1 million to $817,000 since the head-to-head began. 
The sitting congressman will match up against Republican Robert Burke in November, in a district Lynch has held since a 2001 special election.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Same-day events underscore strategic differences in Maine’s pivotal US Senate race
description: Troy Jackson fielded questions Tuesday night during his first U.S. Senate campaign town hall from voters who have grown skeptical of the Democratic Party and who feel he is not critical enough of his opponent, U.S. Sen. Susan Collins.  “This is what representative government is supposed to be,” Jackson said, standing next to an empty […]
text:
Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Troy Jackson speaks to voters at his first town hall in Lewiston on Sept. 1, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)Troy Jackson fielded questions Tuesday night during his first U.S. Senate campaign town hall from voters who have grown skeptical of the Democratic Party and who feel he is not critical enough of his opponent, U.S. Sen. Susan Collins. 
“This is what representative government is supposed to be,” Jackson said, standing next to an empty chair he said he saved for Collins at the Franco Center in Lewiston. 
Hours earlier, the incumbent Republican greeted workers during the morning shift change at Bath Iron Works, the Navy shipbuilder she has supported with billions of dollars of defense funding during her tenure. 
“We’ve seen promises made during election season that are forgotten by the time the next contract fight rolls around. That’s not you,” a group of 100 BIW workers wrote in a letter that shipbuilders Glenn Chateauvert and Ray Gauthier gave to Collins Tuesday morning. “You’ve been showing up for us since before most of these young guys on the line were even hired on.”
The rivals’ contrasting campaign events on Tuesday underscored their differing approaches to winning over voters, as well as the tensions at play 63 days out from the Nov. 3 election. 
Troy Jackson secured third-most donations of Senate candidates through ActBlue in July

Jackson, former state Senate president and logger from Allagash, has been meeting with voters at union halls and on picket lines. The Lewiston town hall is the start of a series of open forums he is packing into his condensed campaign timeline. 
Town halls had similarly been a staple of former Democratic nominee Graham Platner, who held more than 80 before dropping out in July after an accusation of sexual assault, and were also used by some of Collins’ earlier challengers. They all criticized the five-term senator for not hosting a town hall in over two decades, a common critique among Democrats in recent campaign cycles. 
Collins’ staff told Maine Morning Star that she meets with thousands of Mainers every year and prefers individual and small group gatherings. This election cycle, the senator, who is known for her constituent services, is sticking to the tactic she’s used for all of her campaigns: a bus tour throughout the state, stopping at community events and highlighting projects she helped fund. 
That approach feeds into her overall pitch to voters that she delivers for Maine as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. It continues to resonate with some BIW workers, but it did not with Jackson supporters Tuesday night. Several said they want to see the Democrat focus more on chipping away at that aspect of Collins’ persona, which has led her to defy polls and get reelected in the past. 
“Why have you been so soft on Susan Collins?” an attendee named Fred asked. 
After Collins proposed a TV debate series to start the week of Sept. 6, Jackson invited the senator to join his town halls, the first of which she did not attend. Jackson said he wants at least two debates to be town hall-style with questions from attendees. 
There are also six declared write-in candidates in the race, though they will not likely be included in debates, which typically require candidates to poll at a certain level.
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins greets Bath Iron Works employees on Sept. 1, 2026. (Courtesy of Collins’ campaign)
Parallels to Platner 
In many ways, Jackson’s town hall was similar to Platner’s, starting with music, a series of speakers and a stump speech from Jackson before opening up to questions. While questions were often yelled out from the crowd during Platner events, Jackson’s campaign collected questions from attendees as they entered and picked them during the event using raffle tickets. 
When asked what he’d do first if elected, Jackson responded that he’d push for Medicare for All. 
In response to a question about who he’d work with, Jackson said, “anyone that’s going to be willing to do whatever I think is good, whatever we think is good, for the people in the state of Maine and the people in this country.” 
For example, he said he’d work with Republicans on property tax cuts. 
“I think Democrats have a lot of work to bring working class people back into the fold,” he said when asked how he’d convert swing or Republican voters.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Jackson’s stump speech drew several direct parallels to Platner’s. He said he is not afraid to stand up to Trump and Republicans, but that he is also not afraid to stand up to people in his own party. 
Some in the audience came skeptical of Jackson, including Tori Leigh of Auburn, an independent, who said she is horrified by MAGA but also “disillusioned by the patronizing and ineffectual lip service of the establishment left.” 
“I’ve seen your ads, and I notice that you keep referring to ‘our ‘movement that ‘we built.’ Honestly, it feels disingenuous,” Leigh told Jackson when her raffle was picked. “Because the movement that was building was built by someone else. You weren’t nominated by votes. Why should frustrated Mainers like me trust you as a person to take over leadership of that movement?” 
Jackson responded with something Platner had often repeated, that the campaign is not about him or any one candidate. 
“This isn’t about Troy Jackson, but I don’t even think it’s about Graham,” Jackson said. “I think it’s about people across this state that know there’s something fundamentally wrong with the way things are going.” 
Leigh told Maine Morning Star she was satisfied with his response. “It seemed authentic and it seemed humble,” she said. 
As other attendees came up to her after the town hall and thanked her for asking that question, Leigh explained that she’d attended the event to see whether Jackson actually listened to what voters had to say, which was a key reason she’d previously liked Platner. She said she felt he did, but added, “You should never stan a politician. Your vote should be strategic.” 
Dueling records
Pointing to Jackon’s decades in Augusta, including six years as president of the Maine Senate, Collins’ spokesperson Blake Kernen said, “He’s running around the state telling Mainers that the status quo isn’t working. Well, he was the status quo.”
When Platner was still in the running, many liked the fact that he was an outsider, a political newcomer. Though Jackson shares many of the same progressive policy stances, he is well known as an experienced insider. Some who attended his first town hall see that as a plus. 
“He has been in the trenches and had to work with different kinds of people,” said Chris Bean, a lifelong Democrat who had not supported Platner and will be voting for Jackson.
With focus on fraud and ‘socialism,’ Vance returns to Maine to rally for Republican candidates

Jackson and his supporters spoke to some of his legislative work Tuesday night, such as the bill he sponsored that created universal free school meals. But Jackson also acknowledged shortcomings. 
“I am upset, frustrated, mad a lot, and that’s why I got into state government,” Jackson said. “And a lot of what I tried to do, we weren’t able to change.” 
A card carrying union member, Jackson has earned endorsements from more than 20 labor unions, including the national union representing most of the people employed by BIW, the International Association of Machinists. The local chapter has not weighed in, but previously endorsed him during his recent unsuccessful bid for governor. 
The disconnect between the national union’s endorsement of Jackson and some of the workers’ support for Collins highlights the tension between populist union labor and the establishment appropriations industries rely on. 
“The rank and file workers know that I have worked with them over the years and I have delivered for Bath Iron Works, and many of them told me as they went through that I had their vote,” Collins told NEWS CENTER Maine during her visit Tuesday morning. “They are independent people and they make their own decision.”
Jackson argued during his speech Tuesday night that Collins’ appropriations wins mask a broader record that hurts Mainers. He and other speakers also emphasized his first-hand experience with the challenges of t working-class Mainers — “ He knows what it looks like from the bottom,” as Western Maine Labor Council President Linda Dean put it. 
“You are part of a new union tonight,” Portland Mayor Mark Dion said before Jackson took the stage. “The union of Troy Jackson.”
