text:
Lara Korte graduated from the University of Kansas' William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communications. She reported for Stars and Stripes and was fired on Aug. 21, 2026. (Photo submitted by Lara Korte)LAWRENCE — A University of Kansas journalism graduate is suing the Pentagon after being fired from the Stars and Stripes for comments about the military publication’s editorial freedom.
Lara Korte received a notice of separation from the Pentagon on Aug. 21, along with editor-in-chief Erik Slavin and publisher Max Lederer.
“I was stunned. I couldn’t believe it at first,” Korte said. “We quickly realized that this is something that we should fight.”
Korte has worked for the publication since 2024, covering the U.S. military in the Middle East. The Pentagon cited the reason for the firing as “insubordination,” which Slavin and Korte said is related to interviews they gave on “CBS Sunday Morning” in July.
Korte said the following in her CBS interview: “I’m working for Stars and Stripes. Not for the Pentagon, not for any administration, not for any policymaker. I’m here to cover the military community.”
Korte joined Slavin and Lederer as a plaintiff in a lawsuit against the Pentagon, with lawyers going to court Friday to seek a temporary restraining order and get plaintiffs on administrative leave during litigation. The Pentagon agreed to pause the firings while the case is litigated.
The federal lawsuit, which was filed Thursday, argues plaintiffs were terminated after an article about conditions aboard the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln was published, and that the reason for the firings was for comments made on CBS five weeks before.
Plaintiffs are suing the Department of Defense; Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth; Sean Parnell, a senior adviser to Hegseth; and Andrew Brey, a deputy assistant to Hegseth for public affairs.
Plaintiffs are seeking their jobs back, legal fees and a ruling that the January repeal of the publication’s editorial rights was unlawful.
Stars and Stripes is part of the Department of Defense, making its reporters Pentagon employees — but they maintain editorial independence, and have since its creation. The news outlet publishes stories online and still puts out a print version for service members in remote areas overseas.
Parnell, who acts as the chief Pentagon spokesman, said on X in January that the Pentagon is “modernizing” the Stars and Stripes and wants to get rid of “woke distractions that syphon morale.”
“The fact that they took issue with me reasserting our editorial independence, that makes me a little bit queasy,” Korte said. “When I applied for the job, I was reassured about editorial independence. People aren’t going to read something if they just feel like it’s another press release from the Pentagon.”
The Pentagon declined to comment for this story.
Korte said her time at KU gave her valuable news experience and that she wouldn’t be where she is without the journalism school.
“I don’t know what my GPA was, but it probably wasn’t that great because I was skipping class a lot to go write for the University Daily Kansan,” Korte said. “I was surrounded by really supportive professors and really ambitious peers who encouraged me to do better and do more.”
In her time at KU, Korte wrote more than 200 articles for the University Daily Kansan as a reporter, news editor and editor-in-chief of the student newspaper.
“During her time at KU, Korte was a juggernaut,” KU journalism professor Eric Thomas wrote in a Kansas Reflector column. “Her investigative work for the student newspaper showed fellow students how to do watchdog reporting: articles about sexual assault, budgetary gambles, fraternity hazing and white nationalism on campus.”
Although her work as a military reporter differs from U.S.-based political reporting, Korte said working for Stars and Stripes has embedded her in the military community.
“I go out to the bases in the Middle East and really get to live and work alongside the military community,” Korte said. “As much as we cover the big picture stuff, we’re still a hometown newspaper for these military families. This is very much a paper for the military community about the military community. I think it provides morale to them and also provides perspective for Washington.”
Korte said, according to her lawyers, the firings were unconventional because the Pentagon “waited a long time,” or roughly six weeks, to deliver disciplinary action.
“I don’t know what comes next for me,” Korte said. “But at the end of the day, I still want to keep doing journalism, defense journalism specifically. We just don’t know yet. I don’t know what the future holds.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Keeping cool saves lives yearly, including in Mississippi. But experts say it’s at a cost of worsening global warming
description: FILE - A man repairs air conditioners on the street in Lagos, Nigeria, July 15, 2024. (AP Photo/Sunday Alamba, File)
text:
Cooling from air conditioning saves lives — more than 5,000 a year in the United States alone — but it also heats up the planet and taxes our electrical grid, scientists say.
As the world warms, air conditioning is needed and being used more than ever. Heat waves are striking nearly every continent and United Nations officials estimate that about half a million people die a year from heat. A study in Nature Health reported Monday that air conditioning saved nearly 58,000 lives between 2010 and 2020 in the U.S. Air conditioning use is skyrocketing around the world, with electricity demand from cooling expected to triple, according to the International Energy Agency and the United Nations Environment Programme.
It’s also more of a problem than ever. Because most of the electricity for cooling comes from the burning of fossil fuels, the U.N. projects the amount of heat-trapping gas spewed into the atmosphere from air conditioning will rise from 4.5 billion to 7.2 billion tons in the next 25 years or so. That 7.2 billion tons is almost as much as the carbon pollution from the United States and Europe now.
FILE – An worker installs a new air conditioning unit during a hot summer day in Belgrade, Serbia, June 30, 2026. (AP Photo/Darko Vojinovic, File) Credit: AP Photo/Darko Vojinovic
“Everyone knows air conditioning works, but air conditioning from a climate change perspective is not an ideal,” said Kai Chen, an epidemiology professor at the Yale School of Public Health who was the senior author on the new study. “It leads to more carbon emissions … then it accelerates the climate warming problem.”
Because of a global energy crunch triggered by the war in Iran, eight countries — Bangladesh, Cambodia, Jordan, Malaysia, the Philippines, the Seychelles, Singapore and Sri Lanka — have limited how cool air conditioning can be in offices or even mandated one day a week for public offices to switch it off, according to the IEA. In 2025 the Indian government proposed limits on how cool air conditioners can go.
Experts from 75 countries and 250 cities are trying to walk the tightrope of creating more cooling to reduce deaths from the rising heat, but without worsening climate change. The Global Cooling Pledge will meet in September in Singapore.
One measurement experts use to tally accumulated heat as related to potential air conditioning use is something called “cooling degree days,” a calculation of how much energy is needed to cool buildings when it’s hot outside. The number of cooling degree days in the United States has increased by 28% since 1990, with 2024 setting a record, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Through May, 2026 has been on pace to beat 2024 for the most cooling degree days, EIA data shows.
In Europe, the number of cooling degree days has more than doubled since 1990, and air conditioning use there has jumped by 44%. Meanwhile, usage has tripled in India and more than doubled in Southeast Asia, the IEA reported.
Air conditioning is saving lives, including in Mississippi
In the new study, Chen and his team went through 30 million U.S. death records over an 11-year time span, used county-by-county calculations for levels when heat becomes dangerous and calculated how many lives air conditioning saved during extreme heat. The most lives saved were in Arizona, Florida, Texas, Louisiana and southern parts of Nevada, Alabama and Mississippi. More than a dozen northern states, from Washington to Maine, had fewer than 10 lives a year saved, according to the study.
Chen said the study concluded that “the essential role” of air conditioning saved on average 5,267 lives a year. But it also found that has to be balanced with “overuse.” He pointed to offices — like his — which are cooled so much that many workers wear sweaters even in the summer. More than half the cases researchers looked at could be considered overuse, he said.
Many places use 75 degrees (24 degrees Celsius) as a reasonable limit for air conditioning, Chen said.
He also said the study found that using more air conditioning than needed doesn’t save more lives, but it does worsen climate change.
Air conditioning in cities adds extra warmth to the urban heat island effect, as anyone who walks by air conditioning units knows because that’s where waste heat is expelled outdoors, Chen said. And the added power use increases traditional soot and smog air pollution.
Fairness, smog and urban waste heat
It’s also an issue of fairness since many of the world’s most vulnerable populations don’t have access to or can’t afford air conditioning, according to both Chen and U.N. officials.
FILE – Jenny Sakellariou uses a hand fan while men play backgammon in an air-conditioned cooling center operated by the Athens municipality throughout a heat wave in Athens, Greece, Aug. 24, 2026. (AP Photo/Thanassis Stavrakis, File) Credit: AP Photo/Thanassis Stavrakis
Lily Riahi, head of the cooling buildings and energy unit at UNEP, said that in this year’s heat waves, “many families had to choose between paying for medicines or running their air conditioner.”
“In a warming world, thermal comfort should not be a luxury,” UNEP chief heat officer Eleni Myrivili said. “It’s becoming a prerequisite for health, dignity and increasingly survival.”
Riahi said the goal is not less cooling but rather “smarter and more equitable cooling,” and she pointed to Singapore as an example for effective solutions.
“Singapore is a country I think has really tackled cooling from a very comprehensive perspective, looking at individual adaptation measures, early warning systems, passive measures in the city in terms of urban greenery, which saves them, I think, $35 million in energy costs per year,” Riahi said. Officials there also require new and old buildings to have more efficient cooling and ventilation systems.
Singapore has lowered temperatures in some places by 14 degrees (8 degrees Celsius), Riahi said.
But sometimes it can get so hot and humid in places that even green solutions aren’t enough and air conditioning will be needed, Riahi said.
Until it’s too hot and humid, fans and a low level of air conditioning work, Chen said.

(Stock photo from Getty Images.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Catching Our Eye



Beef. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Karen Kasler is reporting, “Ohio farmers push back on Trump’s 90-day tariff free imported beef plan.”
Ohio’s farmers could be hit hard by President Trump’s new round of 50% tariffs on most goods from Canada that started Aug 22, and Canada’s retaliatory tariffs starting Sept. 8. But they’re also very concerned about another big tariff action that starts on Tuesday.
Farmers support the goal of leveling the playing field with other countries, which tariffs seek to do, said Jack Irvin with the Ohio Farm Bureau. But they’ve been mostly critical of tariffs, including the 90-day expansion of lower-tariff imports for up to 300,000 metric tons of beef, which Trump said will lower record prices consumers have been paying.

Vaccines. The Ohio Newsroom’s Erin Gottsacker is reporting, “More Ohio kindergartners are getting vaccine exemptions, amid measles outbreak.”
A growing share of Ohio parents are opting not to vaccinate their kids for diseases like measles and polio.
Data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows nearly 6% of the state’s kindergartners got vaccine exemptions last school year. That’s more than double the percentage of Ohio kids who got vaccine exemptions prior to the COVID pandemic — and it’s higher than the national exemption rate of about 4%.
“Unfortunately, when parents do not vaccinate their children, diseases that aren’t normally seen can pop back up,” said Valerie Wallace, a communicable disease nurse with the Tuscarawas County Health Department. “We in Tuscarawas County are having a measles outbreak right now that’s happening in the unvaccinated community.”


ICE. WYSO’s Adriana Martinez-Smiley is reporting, “As ICE agents descend on Ohio towns, many local agencies are silent on whether they’re assisting.”
On July 27, the Department of Homeland Security ended Temporary Protected Status for Haiti, Syria and Yemen.
Temporary Protected Status allowed hundreds of thousands of Haitians, Syrians and Yemeni people to live and work legally in the U.S. while their home countries experienced political violence and turmoil.
With the change in legal status, locals in Springfield have noticed a heightened Immigration and Customs Enforcement presence and arrests in the community in recent weeks. Local law enforcement agencies are deciding what level of cooperation they want to have with them.

name: Nevada Current
title: Private gas plants to power data centers would skirt state’s renewable energy law
description: A major data center developer is looking to build two private gas power plants less than 30 miles from Reno as data center growth outpaces NV Energy’s ability to supply electricity for a surge of new developments. Denver-based Fleet Data Centers, a subsidiary of Tract Capital Management, is asking the Public Utility Commission of Nevada […]
text:
Gov. Joe Lombardo, fourth from left, and other state and industry officials at the groundbreaking for a Fleet Data Center in Storey County in May, 2026. (Photo posted by Fleet on LinkedIn)A major data center developer is looking to build two private gas power plants less than 30 miles from Reno as data center growth outpaces NV Energy’s ability to supply electricity for a surge of new developments.
Denver-based Fleet Data Centers, a subsidiary of Tract Capital Management, is asking the Public Utility Commission of Nevada (PUNC) to approve their plans to build two massive gas-burning plants, which would power Fleet’s Peru Ridge and South Valley data center campuses at the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center.
If approved, the Peru Ridge and South Valley gas power plants would generate more than 360 megawatts of electricity using methane gas-fired engines, or enough power to serve about 396,000 homes, according to filings.
Once operational, the facilities would burn about three times as much methane gas as NV Energy’s entire Northern Nevada residential and commercial customer base in 2025, or enough gas to supply about 652,000 homes.
Advocates opposing the approval of the gas-burning plants say the case could effectively defeat the purpose of the state’s renewable portfolio standard, established by the Legislature in 2019, which mandates power providers utilize 50% renewable energy by 2030.
Fleet’s application is now before utility regulators at the PUCN, which will make a final decision on the gas-burning plants on Sept. 8. The proposal could be the first methane gas power supply approved specifically for data center use in Nevada. 
The case is an example of data center builders increasingly turning to private fossil fuel plants in the race to build and power enough data centers to meet the surging demand for artificial intelligence services. 
Since January, gas-fired power generation for data centers in the U.S. has doubled, driving a 50% increase in the amount of gas-powered electricity under development, according to a new report by Global Energy Monitor.
Data center growth in the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center is outpacing NV Energy’s ability to build permanent infrastructure to serve the industrial site, according to Fleet. 
In filings, the data center developer said they expect the gas power plants to operate for about two to three years “until NV Energy can deliver permanent utility service to the site.”
NV Energy says it entered a large load electric service agreement with Fleet Data Centers subsidiary — SV RNO Property Owner 1, LLC – in May for the South Valley data center campus at the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center, and has filed a large load electric supply agreement with PUNC which is pending review and approval.
Methane gas power plants release much more greenhouse gases that drive climate change and contribute to human health issues, like asthma and heart disease. 
NV Energy, the monopoly electric utility provider for the state, is required by state statute to provide a more diverse resource portfolio, including significant renewable energy sources. 
In 2019, the Nevada Legislature passed SB358, requiring the state’s renewable portfolio standard (RPS) to increase each year, rising to 50% renewable power by 2030. NV Energy achieved nearly 48% RPS compliance in 2025, well above the 34% requirement as of that year.
But even in the short-term, advocacy groups say the scale of the gas-burning plants would be damaging for both local air pollution and for the climate. 
In PUCN filings, Nevadans for Clean Affordable Reliable Energy said the size and capacity of the private gas power plants would nearly rival utility scale methane gas plants across the U.S., where about 80% of gas power plants average about 500 megawatts or less.
An analysis by Nevadans for Clean Affordable Reliable Energy, found that the new gas-burning plants, if built to specifications, would produce nearly 980 pounds of carbon dioxide per megawatt hour. 
If the new gas-burning plants were operating in 2025, Nevada’s emissions would have increased by nearly 12%, according to Nevadans for Clean Affordable Reliable Energy’s analysis. 
In filings, advocates urged public utility regulators to deny Fleet’s request to build gas power plants, pointing to the state’s renewable portfolio standard. Nevadans for Clean Affordable Reliable Energy told utility regulators that any move allowing data center developers to be excluded from the state’s renewable portfolio standard could attract more gas-burning plants. 
“It will inevitably lead to thousands upon thousands of megawatts of dirty data center development in Nevada that will likely degrade regional air quality and be an effective abandonment of Nevada’s clean energy goals,” said George Cavros, on behalf of Clean Affordable Reliable Energy, during an August PUCN hearing. 
The developers argued they are not subject to Nevada’s renewable portfolio standard, because they are not energy providers like NV Energy. 
“I will add that there is no self-generation exemption to those statutes,” Cavros said. 
Eric Gimon, a senior fellow with Energy Innovation, a non-partisan energy think tank, said in an interview that in the West private gas-burning plants are also being pushed in Wyoming, Utah, and New Mexico to provide power for data centers. 
Gimon warned that “temporary” generation often remains in use longer than promised and may later support data center expansion.
“The worry is that so many of them at the same time could really put a lot of congestion on the region’s pipeline system,” Gimon said, adding that multiple projects could strain pipeline capacity during heat waves or cold snaps when demand is at its peak. 
More gas-burning plants are likely to be proposed in Nevada as data center demand grows, said Gimon, adding the question is whether backlash will slow it down. A recent Gallup survey found that 70% of Americans oppose building a data center near them.
“People are pretty leery. I mean, people would rather have a nuclear plant in their backyard than a data center,” Gimon said, referring to the Gallup survey, which found about only 53% of respondents opposed building a nuclear energy plant in their area.
Both Gov. Joe Lombardo and Attorney General Aaron Ford did not respond to requests of comment about private gas plants circumventing the state’s renewable energy standards.

name: Nevada Current
title: As Waymo expands fleet, some wheelchair users will be left at curb, says advocate
description: Kelsey Brickl can’t get a ride from the airport to the Las Vegas Strip. Brickl is a non-ambulatory wheelchair user who cannot ride in a conventional passenger vehicle. Her medically prescribed power wheelchair weighs 388 lbs. The concierge team at the hotel where Brickl initially planned to stay this fall attempted to assist her but […]
text:
If Waymo and other autonomous vehicles take over the roadways, the already meager transportation options for disabled passengers will be further diminished, warns a disability rights advocate. (Photo: Waymo)Kelsey Brickl can’t get a ride from the airport to the Las Vegas Strip.
Brickl is a non-ambulatory wheelchair user who cannot ride in a conventional passenger vehicle. Her medically prescribed power wheelchair weighs 388 lbs.
The concierge team at the hotel where Brickl initially planned to stay this fall attempted to assist her but struggled to find suitable options. According to Brickl, one private transportation company quoted the concierge $373 each way, then hung up on Brickl when she questioned the price disparity between a power wheelchair accessible vehicle and a standard SUV. Another company could only accommodate wheelchairs up to 300 lbs, and that still would have been $254 one way.
Brickl and her husband decided to switch from a standard room at one hotel to a suite at another because they could add on a $1,000 “VIP arrival experience” that promises transportation to and from the airport. Now, the resort is tasked with finding an option that works.
“Yes, it’s an uncomfortable workaround, but we are paying for it, not asking for it for free,” she told the Nevada Current.
“It shouldn’t need to be this complicated,” she added, but that’s the reality of traveling as a power wheelchair user.  
While autonomous vehicle companies pitch their fleets as safer, more accessible transportation options, Brickl, a national disability rights advocate, warns that the industry’s largest player appears to have zero interest in accommodating people with the biggest mobility challenges.
The Nevada Transportation Authority (NTA) on Aug. 21 unanimously approved Waymo’s application as an autonomous vehicle network company (AVNC), paving the way for it to begin operating up to 1,000 fully autonomous vehicles for one year.
Brickl wants the NTA to pause the rollout of Waymo’s fleet until the company can demonstrate how they plan to accommodate wheelchair users like her.
“They can’t fit in Waymo,” she says. “You can’t fold them up. You can’t store them in a trunk. And the people who need these wheelchairs can’t slide onto a seat; they cannot use any other wheelchairs.”
Brickl late last month requested the NTA add her to Waymo’s docket and reconsider its recent approval.
A spokesperson for the NTA, in an emailed statement to the Nevada Current, said “there is no mechanism for a person who is not a party of record to challenge the NTA’s decision with the agency directly once it has acted on an application. Any challenge to the agency’s decision would have to be brought through a judicial petition.”
Brickl, who is based in New York City, told the Current the NTA is being disingenuous and has created “deliberate and circular” barriers. She says Nevada law does have intervention by a person with a direct and substantial interest.
“Given my disabilities, I cannot realistically initiate and conduct emergency judicial litigation in Nevada simply to force the NTA to consider disability access within its own approval process,” Brickl said.
And she shouldn’t have to, she argues.
“The NTA’s deliberate procedural obstruction does not extinguish its obligations under federal law or make the underlying approval nondiscriminatory.”
Disabled people “already have civil rights,” Brickl emphasized. “I just want them enforced. I’m not trying to get any special treatment or anything like that.”
[subhead]Autonomous accommodations[/subhed]
Nevada state law requires AVNCs to adopt policies to prohibit discrimination against passengers based on disability, among other protected classes. AVNCs that cannot provide an accessible vehicle “must direct the passenger to an alternative provider or means of transportation that is wheelchair accessible, if available.”
Teri Williams, spokesperson for the NTA, said the agency “does require that this is addressed as a compliance item prior to issuance of the final permit.” But she did not elaborate further.
Waymo, through its public relations firm, did not directly answer the Current’s questions about what their accessibility plan will entail, but said in a statement that “accessibility is a fundamental part of Waymo’s mission.”
The statement continued, “We will comply with applicable Nevada accessibility requirements. We are also actively assessing how we can provide an even more accessible service in Las Vegas above and beyond these requirements.”
Brickl believes Waymo needs to be more transparent about its plan. “Who do they intend on actually deferring these people to? Does that service actually accommodate these complex power wheelchairs?”
Representatives of the company have for years attempted to put the blame to vehicle manufacturers.
“We are a technology company focused on building a driver, not a vehicle,” one rep told New Mobility in 2022.
In July of this year, NOTUS quoted a Waymo spokesperson telling a District of Columbia Council committee that the company has “not been able to identify an electric vehicle platform that is fully wheelchair-accessible while also meeting the very unique specifications that we need to retrofit that vehicle with our technology.”
Brickl says she doesn’t have a problem with the existence of autonomous vehicles, commercial or otherwise, at large. Questions about AV safety and their potential to displace jobs dominate conversations about Waymo, Zoox and similar companies.
“Those are legitimate conversations,” she said, “but I always think of it as those are conversations for people other than me to have because those are other people’s areas of expertise.”
She added, “What I have a problem with is any fleet of vehicles that endangers existing access for people who have medically necessary Group 3 power wheelchairs.”
Brickl argues that Waymo poses an existential threat to existing wheelchair accessible infrastructure that is already “very fragile.” If Waymo and other autonomous vehicles take over the roadways, the already meager transportation options for disabled passengers will be further diminished.
She points to her ongoing experience trying to secure transportation for her upcoming trip, saying it “underscores why bringing Waymo into Las Vegas is risking an already incredibly fragile ecosystem for people in complex wheelchairs.”
[subhead]Not just Waymo[/subhead]
Waymo is not the only AV company that received approval from the NTA last month. Two others — Tesla and Aviari — were also given the greenlight.
Aviari, a subsidiary of Uber, was approved to operate a 1,000 AV fleet. Tesla, which operates a transportation service that utilizes underground tunnels known as the Vegas Loop, was approved to operate a fleet of 5,000.
Brickl believes Aviari also warrants scrutiny in Nevada — “I have found no evidence that Aviari’s autonomous vehicles will accommodate (complex) power wheelchairs.”
She continues, “Uber does, however, already operate an established WAV (wheelchair accessible vehicle) network in several major American cities, with accessible booking infrastructure, vehicle providers, and operational experience for passengers who remain seated in non-folding manual or power wheelchairs.” 
That doesn’t guarantee Aviari will be accessible for all, but Brickl says it does distinguish the company from Waymo.
Tesla, meanwhile, has previously said that it is developing a purpose-built wheelchair-accessible autonomous vehicle, though specifics, including a timeline, remain unknown.
Up until now, the only AV company showing any meaningful sign of putting commitment to Group 3 power wheelchair compatibility on the record is Tesla,” says Brickl. “Waymo hasn’t been taking responsibility for wheelchair access. They’re also the chosen rideshare of numerous institutions in Vegas, like the Raiders, so the stakes are higher.”
Brickl, who has taken on Waymo in other states, added that beyond the material differences she sees between the AVNCs, it also comes down to a personal capacity.
Brickl says her campaign against Waymo really began when she started noticing the company using language like “mobility” and  “accessibility” in its marketing and promotional materials.
“Waymo has kind of co-opted it and said, ‘Oh, our cars are really great for blind people.’ I’m, like, ‘Okay. I’m sure that’s great, but what about who you’re deliberately excluding?’”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Democrat drops out of Utah Senate race, leaving Forward Party incumbent to face GOP challenger
description: Democrat MacKenzie Miller has dropped out of the race for Utah Senate District 11, leaving a two-way race between the Utah Legislature’s only currently elected third-party lawmaker and her GOP challenger.  Now incumbent Sen. Emily Buss — a Forward Party candidate who currently holds the party’s highest-ranking elected position in the country — is left […]
text:
Sen. Emily Buss, a member of the Forward Party of Utah from Eagle Mountain, listens on the Senate floor of the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City. (Courtesy of the Utah Senate)Democrat MacKenzie Miller has dropped out of the race for Utah Senate District 11, leaving a two-way race between the Utah Legislature’s only currently elected third-party lawmaker and her GOP challenger. 
Now incumbent Sen. Emily Buss — a Forward Party candidate who currently holds the party’s highest-ranking elected position in the country — is left to face Republican challenger Brooks Benson in the upcoming Nov. 3 general election. 
Late last year, Buss, of Eagle Mountain, won the Forward Party of Utah’s unprecedented midterm preference poll to replace her predecessor, Sen. Dan Thatcher, of West Valley City, who resigned less than a year after he unaffiliated from the Republican Party to join the Forward Party while citing frustration with the GOP.
Utah Forward Party’s first-of-its-kind preference poll picks a winner to replace Sen. Thatcher

Buss and Benson are competing to represent a sprawling Senate district that spans across parts of the west and south sides of Salt Lake County and across rural Tooele County to the far west side of the state. 
The district is expected to lean heavily Republican. But Buss, acknowledging it will be a “challenging” race given its political makeup, argues there’s more appetite in the district for a “moderate” like her than some may think. 
The last time District 11 was up for election, Buss’ predecessor, Thatcher, ran unopposed as a Republican. 
Miller, of Magna, filed his withdrawal paperwork on Friday — a step he said he decided to take after realizing a three-way race would likely mean the district would fall back under the Legislature’s Republican supermajority control, he told Utah News Dispatch on Monday.
“I’m giving Sen. Buss the best chance to win,” Miller said, adding that if both he and Buss stayed in the race, they likely “would have just destroyed” each other’s chances while handing the win to Benson. 
Miller said the Forward Party and Buss didn’t pressure him to drop out — but rather he arrived at the decision himself after looking at likely outcomes of a three-way race, and it was apparent to him that Buss had no plans to withdraw. 
“I don’t want me and Emily competing and kind of ruining both our chances,” Miller said. “I don’t think a supermajority is good in either direction. … Having fair representation and (ensuring) one party can’t just steamroll everything through is more important than my pride in staying in.”
Mackenzie Miller, a Democrat, dropped out of the race for Utah Senate District 11. (Courtesy of MacKenzie Miller)
Benson, in response to a request for an interview Monday, issued a prepared statement saying he’s “focused on meeting and talking to the people of District 11 about the most important issues our communities are facing.”
“Listening to the voters is my number one priority. From my conversations, it’s clear that we need to cut government waste, lower taxes, stop government mass surveillance, and prioritize road infrastructure throughout District 11,” Benson said. “I’m prepared to serve through listening to the people who live in this district and giving them true representation.”
Buss expressed gratitude to Miller for making a “difficult decision” to step aside “to create a more competitive race.” 
“This is a really, really challenging district, and it was going to be an uphill battle for either of us,” Buss said. “It’s unfortunate that in some districts, a three-way race just splits the vote so much that it is not competitive … and I’m grateful that he was able to see that in this race.” 
She called District 11 a “very gerrymandered district” that’s geographically expansive and mixes highly conservative areas with liberal areas in Salt Lake County. But she also argued that especially as President Donald Trump’s approval rating sinks, “I don’t think it’s as conservative-leaning as a lot of people are banking on.”
“I’ve heard from dozens and dozens of constituents (saying) they’re a lifelong Republican, and they’re so happy to have me as their senator because they’ve never felt listened to or truly represented at the state level,” Buss said. “People are tired of politicians acting like they answer to political insiders over the people. So this is the time for something like this to succeed.”
The Forward Party of Utah issued a statement on Monday announcing that Miller’s withdrawal had major implications for the District 11 race, giving voters a chance to treat it as a “referendum” on a two-party system.
“By re-electing Sen. Emily Buss, voters have a chance to reject partisan Politics-as-usual,” the Forward Party statement said. “The two-party system is broken. The gridlock and hyperpartisanship of our two-party system actively rewards division, enforces strict loyalty, and locks out independent candidates. Something must change.”
Brooks Benson is the Republican candidate for Utah Senate District 11. (Courtesy of Brooks Benson)
The Forward Party pointed to a recent Gallup poll that shows confidence in U.S. Institutions remain near an all-time low, and a Deseret News poll published in April that showed 6 in 10 Utah voters don’t feel well represented by Republican or Democratic parties.  
“The Forward Party has a clear mission. We are building an organized, resourced, and effective coalition of independent candidates; Sen. Buss is one of many,” the Forward Party said. “Our goal in Utah is not to replace one supermajority with another. It is to build a political system where no one party can ever hold a supermajority, ever again.”
What happens next in District 11 “is more than a competition for a single seat,” the party added. “It’s a contest between the status quo and a new vision for how our political system might work.”
The Forward Party also pointed to an analysis Brigham Young University professor Adam Brown posted on X, that showed her voting record aligns as “genuinely moderate” with an ideology score that landed squarely in the middle. 
“In just her first year, Senator Buss has already begun to prove the Forward Party concept. Separated from the pressures of party politics, she was free to be herself, and she did just that,” the Forward Party said. “She showed us that a senator can put her constituents first, then work across the aisle on their behalf. Her voting record is a clear example of independence in practice.”
Now, Buss “stands in the center of something bigger than herself,” the party said, “and she won’t be standing alone. We believe that the voters will see her as a welcome alternative to the two-party system.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Out-of-state doctors need NJ license to treat residents here via telehealth, court says
description: Out-of-state physicians need a New Jersey medical license to treat patients here using telehealth, a federal appeals court panel ruled Monday.
text:
Two doctors sued to block a New Jersey law requiring out-of-state physicians to obtain a New Jersey medical license to practice telehealth with Garden State residents. But that law does not place substantial burdens on doctors, an appeals court said Monday. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor.)Requiring out-of-state medical specialists to obtain a New Jersey license to treat people here via telemedicine is not a violation of the doctors’ or the patients’ Constitutional rights, a federal appeals court ruled Monday.  
A panel of three judges with the U.S. 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals agreed with a lower court decision dismissing a case brought by two doctors and representatives for two of their patients who claimed their First Amendment rights were being violated by a state law that requires all physicians treating New Jersey-based patients to be licensed in state.
The judges decided New Jersey’s law does not violate the free speech rights of the doctors or infringe on the rights of the patients to access care. They also found that the requirement that all doctors providing telemedicine in New Jersey be licensed here does not discriminate against out-of-state doctors but treats all physicians the same.  
New Jersey’s law is a “viewpoint neutral” and “content-based” restriction that reflects a long history of regulating medical practice, the judges said, noting that licensing laws date back to at least 1518 in England. New York and New Jersey were among the first American colonies to adopt physician licensing, regulations that predated the American Revolution, they noted, and the practice became widespread nationwide by the mid-1800s.  
“The upshot is this: for well over a century, the States have uniformly required a license to practice medicine, including when that practice takes the form of speech, and those licensure laws have always been content-based speech Restrictions,” wrote Judge Thomas Hardiman for the panel.
The ruling is a win for the defendant, the president of the State Board of Medical Examiners, which licenses physicians here.
He was sued by Dr. Shannon MacDonald, a Boston-based radiologist who specializes in rare pediatric cancers, and Dr. Paul Gardner, a neurosurgeon in Pittsburgh who is an expert in certain skull surgeries, who argued that New Jersey’s licensing process is overly burdensome.
The plaintiffs also included a minor referred to as J.A., a patient first treated by MacDonald when he was 18 months old and previously lived out of state; his father, New Jersey resident Michael Abell; and Hank Jennings, a New Jersey resident who underwent surgery with Gardner in Pittsburgh when he was 19 years old. Both patients want the option to continue their treatment with the out-of-state specialists.
Monday’s decision notes that the plaintiffs agreed medical licensing is important to protect patient health and safety and didn’t fault New Jersey for its requirements, including that physicians be trained, pass exams, and undergo a background check.  
“They instead argue that the licensure process is an undue burden on specialists who, like Drs. MacDonald and Gardner, have national practices and are already licensed in states with essentially the same substantive conditions for licensure,” Hardiman wrote in the ruling.  
Attorneys for New Jersey said medical licensure here for out-of-state doctors typically costs $550 and takes about three months. New Jersey also participates in the Interstate Medical Licensing Compact, which includes 42 states — including Massachusetts and Pennsylvania — and physicians in participating states can obtain a license here for $700 in a process that takes “weeks,” according to the decision.  
“Plaintiffs have plausibly pleaded only that Dr. MacDonald and Dr. Gardner desire not to assume additional burdens, and that is not enough for us to conclude that the burdens are substantial,” Hardiman wrote.  
Telemedicine has grown in New Jersey and nationwide since the pandemic. Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed legislation in June that extends a requirement that doctors get paid the same for telehealth consults as they would earn for in-person patient visits.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri redistricting referendum fight puts Supreme Court precedent to the test
description: When the Missouri Supreme Court considers Wednesday whether voters can force a referendum on congressional redistricting, the judges will confront a constitutional question the court has never squarely answered. But decades of Missouri Supreme Court decisions offer clues about how the judges may approach it. A recent analysis of 37 state Supreme Court cases[...]
text:
The Missouri Supreme Court on Wednesday will hear three cases on ballot measures, two over efforts force a referendum on redistricting and one on a constitutional amendment proposed by initiative. The court is shown on Sept. 10, 2024. The judges are, from Judges Kelly C. Broniec, Robin Ransom, W. Brent Powell, Mary R. Russell, Zel. M. Fischer, Paul C. Wilson and Ginger K. Gooch (Pool photo by Robert Cohen/St. Louis Post-Dispatch).When the Missouri Supreme Court considers Wednesday whether voters can force a referendum on congressional redistricting, the judges will confront a constitutional question the court has never squarely answered.
But decades of Missouri Supreme Court decisions offer clues about how the judges may approach it.
A recent analysis of 37 state Supreme Court cases since the start of 2000 found the court looked to precedent as the major or controlling factor in 15, the meaning of the text of the constitution in 10 and a mixture of methods in another 12.
If the court maintains that record, it would be reasonable for it to find that the referendum power applies to congressional redistricting, said Michael Smith, associate professor of law at the University of Oklahoma and author of “Missouri’s Law of Constitutional Interpretation.”
“If the Supreme Court reads the referendum provision in context, they will see that there are these other provisions emphasizing the inherent power of the people,” Smith said. “That provides strong textual support to a liberal and broad referendum power by the people.”
Smith analyzed 105 cases from the earliest years of the Missouri Supreme Court to the present in his paper, published last year by the University of Missouri-Kansas City Law Review. Cole County Circuit Judge Daniel Green’s ruling that kept the referendum off the Nov. 3 ballot used a method of constitutional interpretation called structuralism that has not played a dominant role in recent decisions, Smith said.
“There’s an absence of common law reasoning” in Green’s decision, Smith said in an interview Monday with The Independent. “That absence is a little bit glaring, given the Missouri Supreme Court’s pretty consistent treatment of cases that implicate direct democratic power. This case really comes down to the scope of the referendum provision, which implicates how much power the people directly have over the legislature.”
On Wednesday, Chuck Hatfield, attorney for a political action committee called People Not Politicians, will argue that the text of the referendum provision, which says “any act” of the General Assembly is subject to a petition-initiated vote, includes redistricting. It will be one of three cases Hatfield will argue that day that will finalize the statewide November ballot.
Two cases are about the referendum. Along with the question of whether it will be on the ballot, the court will also hear a case over when it is legal to begin collecting signatures to qualify a referendum.
The third case is about whether an unrelated constitutional amendment proposed by initiative will be on the ballot. Like the referendum, Secretary of State Denny Hoskins’ determined the proposal was unconstitutional.
 Questions settled

The two redistricting cases will complete the high court’s reinterpretation of the referendum power and the legislature’s authority to revise congressional maps at any time. So far, Republicans pushing for the gerrymandered map designed to win the 5th District for their party have prevailed in every case.
The Supreme Court has upheld Gov. Mike Kehoe’s power to call the legislature into special session; ruled the Constitution allowed redistricting absent a new census report; and decided that Hoskins was correct to allow the redistricting law to take effect while signatures were being verified.
In those cases, the court relied on the meaning it found in the text of the Constitution. The governor decides when “extraordinary occasions” require the legislature to be convened and because there is no language prohibiting a new redistricting plan, it is allowed, the court ruled earlier this year.
Signature verification is necessary to determine if a referendum petition is “legal, sufficient and timely,” the court found in a May decision allowing the map to take effect.
 Questions remaining

In filings ahead of oral arguments, attorneys seeking to overturn Hoskins’ decision that the two measures were “insufficient” contend he far exceeded his authority and considered issues that are not within the scope of his review.
Hoskins made his decision, Hatfield wrote, because he knows Republicans would lose a vote on the redistricting plan.
“Stripped of paper-thin legal dressing, the secretary and intervenors’ contention is simply that they do not like the consequences of applying the referendum to redistricting bills, so it must be illegal,” Hatfield wrote.
In the state’s filing, Lou Capozzi, state solicitor general, argues that requiring a referendum would invalidate the results of the Aug. 4 primary election. If a referendum is placed on the ballot, the law it puts before voters is not in effect until approved. That would mean the congressional map used in the primary would not be used in November. 
Chuck Hatfield answers questions from members of the media outside the Cole County Courthouse in Jefferson City on Aug. 6, 2021 (Tessa Weinberg/Missouri Independent).
That would create chaos for the political parties and candidates, Capozzi wrote, and force many voters to choose from candidates they did not have a role in selecting. Doing so would violate the U.S. Constitution and federal law, he wrote.  
The case before the court does not challenge the validity of the primary or require the candidates to be disqualified, Hatfield wrote. If implementing the text of the referendum provision creates problems, he said, it is because Hoskins waited until the last possible date to deny the referendum a spot on the ballot.
“But those hypothetical problems are not a reason to ignore the law and are extremely overblown,” Hatfield wrote.
 The arguments

Hatfield will lean heavily on the text of the Missouri Constitution, pre-argument filings show. There is nothing prohibiting a referendum on redistricting, the filings state, so it is allowed.
Missouri held a referendum on redistricting in 1922, 14 years after the referendum power was added to the Constitution. That shows the intent of the drafters to allow such votes, Hatfield wrote, because no prohibition was added when the Constitution was revised in 1945.
“Because the referendum had been successfully used on a congressional redistricting bill in 1922, the framers were aware it might happen again — yet they did not address that possibility,” Hatfield wrote. “It is not for the courts to second-guess that choice.”
Capozzi wrote that because the map was used for the primary election, it is too late to change now. 
And, he wrote, the federal constitution’s provisions directing state legislatures to set the boundaries of congressional districts puts the plan beyond the reach of a referendum.
Lou Capozzi, right, solicitor general of Missouri, and Michael Patton of the attorney general’s office leave the Cole County Courthouse on Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, after the trial over whether Missourians will have a referendum on redistricting on the November ballot (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
The most important question this week, constitutional law attorneys told The Independent, is whether the people are a branch of government or whether they are the government.
In Green’s decision, Smith said, the judge adopted the argument pressed by Republican Party attorneys that the federal Constitution, by directing legislatures to set district lines, shields those plans from review by other branches of the government.
“There’s a fair amount of analysis that really applies the logic of separation of powers, treating the people as though they were another branch of government, which I think is just generally not how separation of powers doctrine works,” Smith said.
Allen Rostron, associate dean of law at UMKC, said Republican arguments echo the case where the U.S. Supreme Court rejected what is called the “independent legislature theory” that redistricting plans are not subject to court review.
“And the Supreme Court’s like, ‘no, that’s not true. Courts can rule. Legislators can legislate. Voters can vote. Judges can judge,’” Rostron said. “Everybody will do their part.”
In his filing to the court, Capozzi wrote that Missouri could only have a referendum if the Constitution included language explicitly allowing it. 
“Just as all other parts of American government are protected by clear statement rules before courts find their power stripped, state legislatures are treated no differently under the elections
clause,” Capozzi wrote.
In addition to the 1922 redistricting referendum, voters nearly got the chance to vote on a congressional map referendum in 1952. In 1962, the Missouri Supreme Court upheld a redistricting plan but noted that “the people of this state have a remedy for even valid redistricting, which they do not like, through our initiative and referendum provisions.”
The resistance to a referendum on the map drawn in 2025 is the first time anyone has denied that a referendum is possible, Hatfield wrote.
“That understanding remained undisturbed until now,” he wrote.
One argument Capozzi has emphasized is that a redistricting plan is essentially a political choice that should not be second-guessed or placed on a ballot.
“If a referendum were permitted, virtually any group could use the initiative process to propose congressional maps,” he wrote.
In one sense, Rostron said, Capozzi is right. The case in front of the court because of partisan politics.
“And in this instance, I think the same thing is really true of the legal issues,” Rostron said. “In other words, these are not things that have a clear right or wrong legal answer. They are very debatable.”
 Final appeal

The Missouri Supreme Court must rule by next Tuesday if the referendum is going to be on the ballot. That is the last day in state law for the courts to add items to the ballot.
The way Republican arguments are structured, Smith and Rostron said, leaves a narrow path for a final appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court if Green is overturned. Whether the nation’s highest court would intervene is doubtful, they both agreed.
The path is through the arguments that the U.S. Constitution’s elections clause bars a referendum. The court already rejected the theory that courts cannot second-guess redistricting plans in a 2023 case out of North Carolina. 
Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians speaks to reporters Wednesday, Aug. 19  after the Cole County trial over whether Missourians will have a referendum on redistricting on the November ballot (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
And if the Missouri Supreme Court rules only on questions of state law and constitution, intervention is unlikely, Smith said.
“If something is a matter of state constitutional law, there’s a doctrine called adequate and independent state grounds,” he said. “If the decision below is based on the state constitution, the United States Supreme Court does not weigh in.”
If the Missouri Supreme Court includes an extensive discussion of the federal constitutional questions in its opinion, that would open the door for the last-chance appeal, Smith said.
“An appeal would be possible, but, I would hope, be unlikely to succeed,” Smith said.
Rostron agreed that an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court would be unlikely to succeed.
“I would guess,” he said, “that the [U.S.] Supreme Court would probably just stay the heck out of it and let the people of Missouri do what they’re going to do.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: ‘Just pick’: Missouri clerks dispute claim that switching congressional maps is impossible
description: An order directing Secretary of State Denny Hoskins to use congressional district maps drawn in 2022 for the November election would not pose the technical obstacle described by the state and a Cole County judge, two county clerks told the Missouri Supreme Court in a filing last week. Boone County Clerk Brianna Lennon, a Democrat, […]
text:
Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins contends in a filing at the Missouri Supreme Court that it is too late to switch the Nov. 3 election to congressional districts used in 2022 and 2024 (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).An order directing Secretary of State Denny Hoskins to use congressional district maps drawn in 2022 for the November election would not pose the technical obstacle described by the state and a Cole County judge, two county clerks told the Missouri Supreme Court in a filing last week.
Boone County Clerk Brianna Lennon, a Democrat, and Polk County Clerk Rachel Lightfoot, a Republican, filed an amicus brief in the case over a referendum on redistricting. Though they have no position on what the court should do with the case, Lennon said they want to make sure the court knows Cole County Circuit Judge Daniel Green was wrong when he wrote in his ruling that using the maps in effect for the 2022 and 2024 elections was a “remedy that is impossible to implement.”
For election officials, Lennon said, the question is simply which set of congressional district assignments to use.
“You just pick which map you want us to use and we are ready for you,” Lennon said.
The question of which map will be used Nov. 3 — along with whether Missourians will vote in a referendum on the map drawn in 2025 — will be answered after the court on Wednesday hears oral arguments in a case seeking to overturn Green’s decision. 
In the state’s arguments filed in advance of the hearing, Lou Capozzi, Missouri’s solicitor general, echoes Green’s conclusion that the election process is too far advanced to change back to the older maps.
“Missouri courts and federal courts refuse to change election rules in the middle of an ongoing election cycle,” Capozzi wrote.
Anything that changes the lines now “would be catastrophically disruptive and technically ‘impossible’ — as Missouri’s election administration system will be locked and cannot be altered,” Capozzi wrote.
That is not true, Lennon wrote in the brief.
The Missouri Centralized Voter Registration system, maintained by Hoskins’ office, links every address in the state to both the gerrymandered map drawn by lawmakers in 2025 and used for the primary and the map used for 2022 and 2024, Lennon said.
“If the current situation was that local election authorities were being asked to implement an entirely new map today, for example, it would be too late to redefine or edit a new district because MCVR does ‘lock’ that ability,” she wrote. “However, that is not the case here.”
New voters who register in advance of the November election will be assigned to both districts as well, Lennon said.
“The addresses themselves are what are tied to two districts,” Lennon said. “So, if you register to vote at an address within Boone County, it is tied to both the new district and the old district.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri wants AI data centers. Communities want answers
description: Missouri has good reasons to want a share of the artificial intelligence boom. Billions of dollars in proposed data center investments could bring construction jobs, new tax revenue and economic growth. They could also help position Missouri for an economy increasingly shaped by AI and cloud computing. But these projects come with costs and unanswered […]
text:
Interior of a modern data center (Getty Images).Missouri has good reasons to want a share of the artificial intelligence boom. Billions of dollars in proposed data center investments could bring construction jobs, new tax revenue and economic growth. They could also help position Missouri for an economy increasingly shaped by AI and cloud computing.
But these projects come with costs and unanswered questions. Across Missouri, communities are raising concerns about electricity use, water, infrastructure, noise and local control. There are also broader questions about data privacy, cybersecurity, who will operate these facilities, and how their enormous computing capacity will ultimately be used.
They are all part of a basic question Missouri needs to answer: Who benefits from these projects, who pays for them, and what protections should communities expect in return?
Communities are already responding differently. St. Charles has effectively banned large-scale data centers, while St. Charles County adopted a six-month ban on new developments to give officials time to study their potential impacts. St. Louis is taking a different approach: allowing data centers, but setting conditions intended to protect the community.
St. Louis Mayor Cara Spencer summed it up by saying the city wants to be “open for business, but business on our terms.” On Aug. 28, the Board of Aldermen advanced a new regulatory framework addressing where and how data centers can operate, including energy use, noise, light and impacts on surrounding communities. Yet the conflict is far from settled. Opponents have filed a lawsuit seeking to halt the proposed $3 billion data center near the Armory.
These different responses point to three choices for Missouri: ban large data centers, pause their development, or allow them under stronger rules intended to protect communities. But frameworks and promises alone will not settle the debate. What matters is whether developers are held to their commitments and whether communities are actually protected from the costs and risks these projects create.
Missouri has several advantages in the race for data center investment, including available land, relatively affordable electricity and a central location. Large projects can bring billions of dollars in investment and additional tax revenue. But a multibillion-dollar investment does not automatically mean a multibillion-dollar benefit to the community.
Consider the scale of some recent projects. Meta’s Kansas City data center represents more than $1 billion in investment and employed about 1,500 skilled-trade workers at peak construction, but supports just over 100 permanent operational jobs. A recently announced $1.4 billion data center in Liberty is expected to create at least 30 permanent jobs.
At the same time, the infrastructure demands can be enormous. Data centers require large amounts of electricity, and some also use significant amounts of water for cooling. For example, Google’s planned $15 billion investment in its New Florence, Missouri, data center comes with enormous energy needs. Google says it has committed to supporting more than 1 gigawatt of new power generation in Missouri, including more than 500 megawatts of additional capacity through its agreement with Ameren.
These numbers alone do not tell us whether a particular data center will ultimately be a good or bad deal for Missouri. But they help explain why communities are looking beyond the headline investment figures and asking harder questions about long-term benefits, infrastructure demands and who ultimately bears the costs.
As public opposition has grown and communities have pushed back against proposed projects, state and local officials are facing increasing pressure to provide stronger protections.
Against this backdrop, the bipartisan Missouri House Future Caucus released the AI Infrastructure Community Evaluation Framework (AICEF) in August, a guide designed to help cities and counties evaluate proposed data center projects.
The framework reflects a shift in the conversation, from simply attracting investment to asking harder questions about who benefits, who pays and who bears the risk. Whether it leads to a real shift in practice will depend on what state and local officials actually require from developers.
Money and resources are only part of the issue. Communities are also raising questions about who is behind these major projects and how they will ultimately be used.
St. Charles provides a warning. A proposed hyperscale data center generated strong opposition after city staff signed nondisclosure agreements and the identity of the end user was not publicly disclosed. Documents later obtained by St. Louis Public Radio connected the project to Google. The secrecy surrounding the proposal helped fuel community opposition.
Companies may have legitimate reasons to protect confidential business information. But when projects require enormous amounts of electricity and water, affect surrounding communities, or receive public incentives, questions about who is behind them are likely to become part of the public debate.
AICEF requires developers to disclose ownership, affiliates, and key project parties. But the questions being raised go beyond ownership. As these facilities become more powerful and more important to the AI economy, concerns are also emerging about cybersecurity, data privacy, who will operate them, and how their computing capacity will ultimately be used.
The experience in St. Charles suggests that when communities feel they do not have enough information about what they are being asked to host, distrust can grow quickly.
Missouri clearly wants a share of the AI investment boom. But growing opposition across the state shows that being open for business is becoming more complicated than simply attracting the next big project.
New frameworks and proposed safeguards may change the conversation, but the real test will come when the next major data center project is proposed: how much information is made public, who bears the costs and risks, what benefits are actually delivered, and whether the protections now being discussed are actually enforced.
The debate is no longer simply about “How do we bring these projects to Missouri?” Increasingly, communities are asking a different question: “Will these projects actually be good for Missouri?”

title: Expanded Epic program gives students, including Afghan refugees, ‘second chance’ at high school
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Parwana Nazari once lived as a “very open and free girl back home” in the Jowzjan province of Afghanistan. She was studying Uzbek literature at a university when the Taliban took control of the country in August 2021. Nazari, who used to go to work and school by herself, suddenly was prohibited […]
text:
Misty Kline, language and culture services coordinator at Epic Charter School, right, and Behroz Bashari, the school's Pashto and Persian language liaison, left, are pictured at Epic's headquarters in 50 Penn Place in Oklahoma City on Aug. 3. Kline and Bashari helped launch Epic's Pathways program, which helps Oklahoma students age 21 to 30 complete a high school diploma. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Parwana Nazari once lived as a “very open and free girl back home” in the Jowzjan province of Afghanistan.
She was studying Uzbek literature at a university when the Taliban took control of the country in August 2021.
Nazari, who used to go to work and school by herself, suddenly was prohibited from leaving her house unaccompanied by male relatives. She became one of millions of girls and women in Afghanistan barred from attending secondary school and higher education.
Her life changed again in 2024 when she won a “golden chance” to move to America through a visa lottery.
She arrived last year in Oklahoma City alone with no documents proving her level of education. 
A program Epic Charter School created, called Pathways, has given Nazari and other Oklahoma students age 21 to 30 the chance to earn a U.S. high school diploma — an opportunity she said she never knew would be possible. Recent changes the Oklahoma Legislature enacted in state law have helped the program grow significantly.
Although she started with zero high school credit, Nazari said Epic is providing “enough support and help for me that I could finish.”
“I want to be as independent as I can because I live here on my own,” Nazari said in Dari through an interpreter. “I want to reach a level of speaking English that I would be able to run my life on my own without needing help of translation or someone else to help me.”
Since leaving Afghanistan and resettling in Oklahoma City, Nazari and other Afghan women have set their sights on earning a high school diploma, something largely impossible in their home country under ultraconservative Taliban rule. Each woman is completing free online courses — like English, U.S. history and algebra — through Epic’s Pathways program. 
The program serves Oklahomans of all nationalities and genders, but administrators at Epic said it wouldn’t exist had local Afghan refugees not pushed for an opportunity to earn an American diploma.
“These few people that were calling me daily, they changed the trajectory for thousands of Oklahomans that didn’t get the chance to finish their education in the first place,” said Misty Kline, Epic’s language and cultural services coordinator who helped found the program.
Misty Kline, language and culture services coordinator at Epic Charter School, said Afghan refugees called her daily for an opportunity to earn American high school credits. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
The initiative has helped almost 500 students graduate high school since it was established in 2023 and now enrolls 1,020 students so far this school year, Epic officials said. The school spends $3.1 million annually on Pathways for the cost of curriculum, devices and staff compensation.
A high school equivalency test, like the GED, for years has been the traditional option available to adults 21 or older wanting to earn a diploma. 
Kline said Pathways is a better fit for students who have gaps in their education. Each student is assigned an individualized learning plan and a one-on-one teacher, who is “their guide, their cheerleader,” she said, and there’s no make-or-break exam at the end of the process.
Pathways started with 20 students, all from Afghanistan, and a budget of $100,000 from payment card refunds. The unusual funding source was necessary because Oklahoma law at the time forbade state dollars from supporting most high school students over the age of 20.
But, recent legislative changes created a dedicated funding stream and enabled more students to enroll.
Oklahoma lawmakers in 2024 permitted state funds to support free public high school courses for students age 21 to 25. A year later, the state Legislature raised the age limit to 30 and required these courses to be delivered online.
When Asia Stanikzai arrived in Oklahoma from Afghanistan, she was older than the maximum age of 20 to enroll in a traditional high school program. She said it left her feeling “hopeless” and “frustrated.”
Stanikzai already had finished high school in Kabul, but her family left the country without most of her education records. Pathways offered an opportunity to prove her level of learning and to study English.
“I (found) out that Epic school is offering such a program for us, and I got really excited and happy,” she said in Dari through an interpreter. “Since the day I started, I’m getting better every day. The way I’m speaking, my communication, and I’m so happy.”
She’s been taking classes for two years and expects to graduate in May. Stanikzai and her sister, Saria, also a Pathways student, said they hope to study cosmetology and own their own makeup styling businesses once they finish their high school credits.
Epic Charter School is headquartered at the 50 Penn Place complex in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Many of the original 20 Pathways students similarly lost their education documents in the rush to evacuate from Afghanistan. Tens of thousands of people, including many who cooperated with the American military, were quickly airlifted out of Kabul when U.S. troops withdrew and the Taliban took control in 2021.
Nearly 2,000 Afghan refugees have since settled in Oklahoma. Although initially welcomed, these refugees have faced recent calls for removal by some politicians in the state.
Tabasum Hussaini, one of the original Pathways students, said she and other Afghan refugees never wanted to have to leave their homes, but her life under the Taliban would be “scary” if she had stayed.
“We had no choice except coming here, and we want to build a better life for our kids, for their future,” she said in an English interview with Oklahoma Voice. “We don’t want them to go through the same thing that we went (through).”
Hussaini was in her fifth semester of law school and was working as a teacher when her family fled from Kabul five years ago. She hasn’t given up on her dream of earning a law degree. 
Earning her high school diploma through Epic has enabled Hussaini to enroll in pre-law courses at Oklahoma City Community College. Hussaini, who was working as a Walmart stocker when she first learned of Pathways, now has a job supporting other refugees at The Spero Project, which aids in resettlements.
Multiple Afghan women who spoke with Oklahoma Voice recounted similar stories of interrupted schooling and lost academic transcripts.
Others said they already had dropped out of school in Afghanistan because of marriage. 
Malaika Ander never finished her schooling after getting married at the start of 12th grade, but she said “the flame of my passion for learning and my dream of graduating never died in my heart.” 
She enrolled in Epic’s Pathways program this year to finish her education.
“This great initiative gave us a second chance to reclaim our academic identity,” she said in English.

title: Colorado River drought lawsuits may dampen Wyoming dam plans
description:
Two legal actions raise questions about Wyoming’s water supplies and plans to construct another dam in southern Wyoming.
The post Colorado River drought lawsuits may dampen Wyoming dam plans appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
As drought and over-allocation of Colorado River water shock the West, two lawsuits raise serious questions about irrigation in Wyoming and state plans to build a new dam and reservoir in Carbon County.
As soon as the federal government announced that it would cut Colorado River supplies to California, Nevada and Arizona, Nevada went to court claiming that the headwater states of Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah could more easily handle the reductions.
At the same time, Colorado conservationists argued in court that Denver’s plans to pour Colorado River water into an enlarged reservoir for the city’s use amounts to building an $819 million bathtub that might never be filled.
Together, the lawsuits raise legal arguments regarding Wyoming’s reliance on irrigation water from the Green and Little Snake rivers, whether ranchers would still have access to traditional diversions and whether a proposed dam and reservoir above the Little Snake River valley is feasible and worthwhile.
The Nevada lawsuit is a direct challenge to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s plan to cut allocations to three of the seven states that rely on Colorado River flows — Nevada, California and Arizona. Burgum’s Aug. 21 approval of the new allocations left the headwater states of Wyoming, Colorado, Utah and New Mexico largely untouched.
But Burgum made “no analysis of the very real and dire economic effects to millions of municipal water users if the taps are turned off or water use must be significantly curtailed,” the Silver State’s lawsuit asserts. Instead, Nevada says, Wyoming and its headwater-state cohorts, “where water conservation has been less of a priority … have additional lower-cost options to respond [to] reduced … water deliveries.”
Three weeks before Burgum’s decree, conservation groups were in the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals in Santa Fe arguing that the city of Denver shouldn’t be allowed to complete an expansion of the Gross Dam that would bolster the city’s supplies with water from the Colorado River Basin. Among other reasons, conservation lawyers argued the city was squandering taxpayer money on a boondoggle.
“They’re building a giant bathtub, even though there’s likely no water to ever fill it,” attorney William Eubanks said on behalf of the river-protection group Save the Colorado.
Collectively the cases raise questions regarding whether Wyoming irrigators will continue to receive their traditional shares of Colorado River Basin water and whether Wyoming’s plan to build the West Fork Dam and reservoir above the Little Snake River Valley makes sense and will be challenged.
Should Wyoming share the pain?
River flows have declined from some 14.6 million acre-feet to about 12.3 million acre-feet, the Nevada lawsuit states, underscoring the shortage. Nevada’s challenge could upend what so far has been an easy ride for Upper Basin states, including Wyoming.
Wyoming was pleased with Burgum’s plan for the Colorado River because the plan would impose no administrative cuts to the state’s 7% share of river flows. Wyoming believes it has not yet used what it’s entitled to and has plans to construct the West Fork Dam on Carbon County’s Battle Creek to impound 10,000 acre-feet and irrigate every year with 6,000 acre-feet from the proposed reservoir.
An aerial view of the general site of the proposed West Fork Dam at the head of the Little Snake River Valley in Carbon County. The proposed dam would be 264 feet high, 700 feet long and made out of concrete. (Major King for WyoFile)
But while Wyoming might skate under Burgum’s plan, the suit states Burgum didn’t consider whether “to equitably reduce water distributions … between the Upper Basin States and Lower Basin States.” In other words, Nevada wants Burgum to consider mandatory cuts to Wyoming’s water use, not just voluntary ones that Burgum endorsed.
Nevada makes its case by arguing it has “a relatively meager 3.3%” of the water apportioned to the Lower Basin States and Mexico,” but that amount accounts for 90% of what’s used in the Las Vegas Valley. That region has taken significant efforts to conserve water, the suit states.
Burgum’s plan was forged without detailed consideration of impacts to Nevada residents and in violation of environmental and procedural laws, the suit states. That misstep comes with real-world consequences, Nevada claims.
As a result of flawed analyses, Burgum “obscure[s] the full extent of economic and social costs to cities like Las Vegas, North Las Vegas, Boulder City, and Henderson,” a region with an $180 billion annual economy, the suit states.
The solution may lie upstream in headwater states, the suit contends, where water conservation has been less of a priority and lower-cost options abound.
Nevada wants the Burgum plan, a 10-year program, blocked and struck down.
Water for Wyoming’s new reservoir?
The Denver water lawsuit and challenge to the city’s Gross Dam enlargement has been ongoing for years and has produced more detailed arguments and criticism that could have implications across the West. The lawyer representing conservationists said the city and federal government didn’t look deep enough into drought and climate change.
Those planners “never analyzed whether there will be any average-to-wet years in which Denver can divert the water under its existing water rights, let alone whether there will be enough of those years to ever fill this expanded reservoir of 72,000 acre-feet,” Eubanks told the court.
Denver and federal officials did not “demonstrate that there would actually be enough water during these average-to-wet years to fill this reservoir,” he said. Too, there would be “massive environmental destruction on both sides of the Continental Divide.”
Planners also failed to consider many other options to satisfy Denver’s water needs, critics say. The city’s lawyer, and one representing the federal government, argued the opposite — that relevant factors were taken into account and that there would be enough water — diverted across the Continental Divide — to fill the new storage space.
A group of natural resource law professors filed a brief supporting the conservation groups and slamming the government for not taking climate change and drought into account. In its evaluation of the Goss Dam expansion, the federal government “entirely neglected to consider the potential environmental consequences of diverting water out of a Basin experiencing its worst period of drought in over a thousand years,” the 11 experts stated.
“The proposed project on Little Snake River drainage is probably the most threatened by what’s going on in the Colorado River.”Gary Wockner
Gary Wockner, executive director of the 17-year-old Save the Colorado nonprofit, said drought could lead to mandatory cuts to Wyoming’s water use, potentially rendering the proposed West Fork Dam useless.
“Ranchers and farmers are likely going to be subject to being forced to send water downstream,” he told WyoFile. “The proposed project on Little Snake River drainage is probably the most threatened by what’s going on in the Colorado River because it’s solely for a handful of ranchers.
“If you follow just the politics of how this is playing out,” he said, “the bullseye is on agricultural water. There are more members in the U.S. House of Representatives in Southern California, in the areas that get Colorado River water, than there are in the rest of the Colorado River Basin combined.”

title: From clashes to care: Fort Washakie mom finds way out of troubled path
description:
