name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama high schools earn national recognition — but some rural schools miss out
description: I’ve heard the same thing, over and over, for as many years as I’ve lived here. At some point during a discussion about K-12 education in Alabama, someone will say something complimentary about a school’s performance, and someone else will feel moved to chime in: “Yeah, they’re doing well. For Alabama.” I heard it again […]
text:
A student working on a "reflections" worksheet in their ninth grade math class at Crossville High School in Crossville, Alabama, on Aug. 28, 2025. Eight Alabama high schools are in the top 5% of high schools in the country, according to U.S. News and World Report.  (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)I’ve heard the same thing, over and over, for as many years as I’ve lived here. At some point during a discussion about K-12 education in Alabama, someone will say something complimentary about a school’s performance, and someone else will feel moved to chime in: “Yeah, they’re doing well. For Alabama.”
I heard it again two weeks ago, at a Fairhope High School community forum. When principal Jon Cardwell held up a summary of the highest-ranked schools in the state and pointed to Fairhope’s spot near the top, someone in the crowd invoked that reflexive caveat: “Sure, we’re near the top,” they said. I could feel the next part coming.
“For Alabama.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
It’s not breaking news that nationally, Alabama has been stuck at the bottom of the educational pile since the early ’90s, when the federal government started tracking state-by-state test scores via the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP). Our reading and math results aren’t usually dead last — there’s a reason people say “Thank God for Mississippi” — but we’re always in the mix.
So it felt like sweet validation when on the same day as that community forum, word got around that U.S. News and World Report had just released its fresh list of public high school rankings. Eight Alabama schools had made the top 5% nationally. Including Fairhope.
Here I’ll add a caveat of my own: There should have been nine schools on that list, but the state’s top-ranked high school, Loveless Academic Magnet Program (LAMP) High School in Montgomery, appears to have been left out because the Alabama State Department of Education (ALSDE) didn’t send U.S. News the school’s ACT scores.
LAMP’s snub notwithstanding, Alabama Daily News tallied up the totals and found that nine more high schools in the state landed between the top 5% and 10% nationally.
Overall, in a horse-race comparison against the other states, Alabama’s stats put us in a respectable position in the middle of the pack — a welcome change for a state accustomed to eating everyone else’s dust.
But never satisfied with simply accepting good news and moving on with my day, I decided to compare the U.S. News rankings to the ALSDE 2025 state report card to see how closely they align — or don’t.
When ALSDE released the 2025 state report card last November, they highlighted all the findings that showcased progress: higher graduation rates, improved math and science outcomes, greater academic growth, fewer schools getting Ds and Fs. State officials’ upbeat remarks from that time made it sound like all systems were pointing in the right direction. 
But I found myself wondering how those cheerful projections measured up against U.S. News’ analysis. 
The state report card and the U.S. News rankings are never going to align perfectly, because they measure different things. The state measures six variables, including academic achievement, graduation rate, college and career readiness, and attendance.
U.S. News measures college readiness, state assessment performance, and graduation rate. I’m simplifying it a little bit, but those are the broad strokes. The point is that it’s a bit of apples and oranges. 
Filtering the state report card to show only academic achievement — the metric most directly tied to students’ knowledge — the eight high schools that made U.S. News’ elite top 5% list are indeed all clustered near the top. 
But several other high schools that scored the highest marks in academic achievement on the state report card are missing from U.S. News’ best-of list. I counted 15 other high schools with top-tier report card scores that U.S. News assigned a low ranking or no ranking at all.
For example: Kinston School in Coffee County falls right below Huntsville’s New Century Technology High School on the state report card. But while New Century Technology took Alabama’s number-one spot in the U.S. News rankings, Kinston was relegated to the bottom half of Alabama schools. 
The common denominators among the schools that didn’t get any love from U.S. News? They’re generally small and rural, with higher percentages of economically disadvantaged students. Many serve not just high school, but lower grades as well. 
But that alone doesn’t explain the disconnect, because some schools fit that profile and received high rankings.
So what gives? 
I can’t speak to any one school’s results, but looking at the bigger picture, a pattern emerges: The schools that offer AP classes shoot to the top of the rankings, and those that don’t sink to the bottom. 
This aligns with how U.S. News measures college readiness: not through SAT and ACT tests, but through AP and IB tests. The tests account for a full 40% of a school’s overall ranking, and if a school doesn’t offer AP or IB, it gets a score of 0 on those metrics. U.S. News says it adjusted schools’ scores so that schools without AP or IB offerings wouldn’t plummet to the bottom of their list, but it clearly weighed heavily on them.



Quotation







The schools that offer AP classes shoot to the top of the rankings, and those that don’t sink to the bottom. 


You can hardly blame small-town schools for not offering AP or IB; they must staff essential units first, and if they have low enrollment, they might not have enough resources left over for extras.
Lack of access is a known problem nationwide. A report published last year by the Center for American Progress found that “only 50% of rural school districts offer AP courses, compared with 76% of urban districts and 85% of suburban districts.”
So, on the one hand: Don’t sweat the mismatched rankings. U.S. News pinned almost half its scoring to a single metric that half of rural schools across the country can’t provide. No one data set is ever going to paint the full picture of a school anyway, so it’s not worth losing any sleep over. 
On the other hand: It is illuminating, even if it isn’t the end-all, be-all. AP and IB offerings help bright students meet their potential, and it’s a shame not everyone has access to them. 
But what if they did? In a world of seemingly infinite technological possibility, it doesn’t feel like a huge stretch to imagine an equitable solution.
At least we don’t have to solve that riddle on our own. It’s a challenge for communities across the country to tackle — not just “for Alabama.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Trousdale Turner prison guards to turn on body cams
description: Prison guards at privately-run Trousdale Turner Correctional Center will start wearing body cameras Tuesday as required by a new state law designed to improve safety at the embattled facility. The CoreCivic prison was supposed to initiate the body cams in July, but delays with the purchase of equipment postponed operations for two months, according to […]
text:
Guards at CoreCivic-operated Trousdale Turner Correction Facility will begin wearing body cameras on Sept. 1, 2026. (Photo: Tennessee Department of Corrections)Prison guards at privately-run Trousdale Turner Correctional Center will start wearing body cameras Tuesday as required by a new state law designed to improve safety at the embattled facility.
The CoreCivic prison was supposed to initiate the body cams in July, but delays with the purchase of equipment postponed operations for two months, according to Republican Sen. Tom Hatcher of Maryville, who sponsored the bill to start the pilot program.
CoreCivic, a Brentwood-based private company that runs four prisons in Tennessee, agreed to pay more than $300,000 for the cameras and train guards to use them. They are to be turned on at all times, Hatcher said, and the Tennessee Department of Correction will review any incidents captured on video and send them to the local district attorney to determine whether cases should be prosecuted.
“We hope with these body cams we’re going to be able to catch a lot more of any events that occur because of (cameras) being right there when it happens instead of trying to use the stationary cameras in the facilities,” Hatcher said.
Security and safety of guards and staff are the primary purposes for running body cameras, Hatcher said. And once inmates see they’re being monitored by officers’ video, incidents of assaults, false allegations against guards and contraband smuggling could be reduced, he said.
Tennessee senators push for body cameras at CoreCivic prison

CoreCivic and the Department of Correction will be required to file monthly reports with the Senate corrections subcommittee on the cameras’ effectiveness. The panel also can request to see video at any time, according to Hatcher, who chairs the subcommittee and will review the incidents. 
Yet under the measure lawmakers passed this year, video recorded by prison guards at Trousdale Turner will be exempt from the Tennessee Public Records Act because of “safety concerns,” he said.
“We don’t want to give somebody outside all of the arrangements inside … and how they go and the procedures,” Hatcher said. “That’s for safety reasons.”
The pilot program is supposed to run for one year. But because of the delay in starting, the senator said he will introduce a bill next year to keep it going through December 2027.
CoreCivic spokesperson Ryan Gustin said Monday the company supports efforts to improve safety, security and accountability at the prison.
“Body-worn cameras are one of many tools that can help provide greater transparency and documentation of staff interactions and incidents within a correctional setting,” Gustin said in a statement. 
Stopping contraband from being smuggled into the prison and other prohibited activities also requires staff training, established security procedures, the use of technology and “close coordination” with the Department of Correction, Gustin said, which the company is constantly trying to improve.
Department of Correction Correction Commissioner Frank Strada supports the legislation for the body camera pilot program, according to spokesperson Dorinda Carter.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Strada, though, disagreed early this year with the idea of putting body cameras on every prison officer in the state, which he said would cost $6 million for equipment and $2 million to handle public records requests for video that isn’t exempt from the Public Records Act. 
Strada said in January the department, instead, was putting together a central intelligence center in Nashville to monitor prisoners. Carter did not answer questions about that proposal Monday.
The U.S. Department of Justice started investigating Trousdale Turner and CoreCivic in August 2024 over alleged civil rights violations, citing a record of assaults, murders and understaffing at the facility since it opened in 2016. Strada said this spring he understood the investigation was ongoing.
In June 2025, three inmates suffered minor injuries and a staff member was stabbed when inmates commandeered an inner yard at Trousdale Turner, destroyed property and refused to take orders, according to CoreCivic. 
Strada blamed the incident on prison officers instead of the company. After the incident, CoreCivic installed a new warden, increased officer pay and adopted new procedures. The state removed some 600 inmates and limited the population to inmates 50 years and older with four years or less on their sentences.
The state has levied at least $45 million in civil penalties against CoreCivic since 2022 for failing to meet contractual requirements, mainly for staffing shortfalls.

title: Providers ‘stuck holding the bag’ for unpaid disability care amid agency delays
description: After more than two years of erroneous Medicaid disenrollments, communication challenges and slow responses from state agencies, the nonprofits and companies providing developmental disability services say they are near a financial breaking point.
text:
The developmental disabilities community along with care service providers and support staff rally outside the State House in February against proposed cuts in the state budget. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)After more than two years of erroneous Medicaid disenrollments, communication challenges and slow responses from state agencies, the nonprofits and companies providing developmental disability services say they are nearing a financial breaking point.
Developmental disability service providers say they won’t be able to absorb the costs of months of unpaid care much longer while their clients wait for Medicaid coverage to be restored by the state. Some organizations believe they’re owed hundreds of thousands to more than a million dollars for unpaid services due to lengthy lapses in Medicaid coverage.
With ongoing budget challenges at the state’s Developmental Disabilities Administration, providers feel they’re “stuck holding the bag” as they continue what is often complex behavioral and health care for a vulnerable population.
“What I worry is that the state is shifting costs from themselves to the provider system,” Katie Collins-Ihrke, executive director of the Arc of Howard County said. “We’re not just seeing cuts. Costs are being shifted to us on top of that.
“It’s a very scary time,” she said. “I feel like we don’t have state support … There’s all these changes coming federally too – it’s just a perfect storm.”
Meanwhile, providers fear the instability will start to impact the people with developmental disabilities who rely on those services.
“These are issues that are really going to have to be addressed sooner than later, because the bottom line is people with developmental disabilities cannot suffer because of these issues,” said Laura Howell, executive director of CEO for the Maryland Association of Community Services.
Disability community left with heads ‘spinning’ from sudden delay of proposed wage cuts

At issue are a series of financial and administrative challenges at the DDA, the state agency overseeing Medicaid waivers that covers people with developmental disabilities for a wide variety of services, from live-in caregiver support to transportation, respite care, employment services and more.
Each year, waiver recipients must prove that they are still financially eligible and still need coverage for their disability, in a process known as “redetermination.”
Annual redeterminations were suspended in March 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, when states were prohibited from canceling Medicaid coverage for most recipients. But since it restarted redetermination requirements in May 2023, advocates and providers say the department has struggled to keep pace with applications.
State officials say they are aware of the challenges and are trying to fix administrative operations to ensure that there is a longer grace period for waiver recipients to prove financial eligibility before being completely cut off from Medicaid coverage.
“Maryland is committed to the sustainability and integrity of the waiver program while supporting the health, safety, and independence of participants and promoting community living through both self-directed and community provider-managed delivery models,” the Department of Health said in a statement Friday.
It’s hard to get a firm number, but several provider organizations attest to dozens of waiver recipients who lost their Medicaid enrollment slot.
Over the years, these individuals fell out of the waiver slot at some point for a variety of reasons. A frequent challenge is the appearance that someone’s income is “over asset,” meaning they appear to earn too much to qualify for the Medicaid waiver.
That happened to a woman under the care of the Arc of Howard County, Collins-Ihrke said.
“The Social Security check hit before the first of the month, which can happen. What regulations state is that if it hits before the first of the month, you don’t count it in the current month, you count it in the next month because it’s next month’s income,” she said.



Quotation







There are hundreds of people that this has happened to that are still in limbo. There are millions of dollars in unpaid claims for services provided by providers that had no other choice but to provide these services to protect the health and safety of people with developmental disabilities, unless they become homeless or end up in hospitals or perish.


– Ande Kolp, executive director of The Arc Maryland


“They [state officials] didn’t do that … she lost her Medicaid, they kicked her out of the waiver,” said Collins-Ihrke, who noticed the error swiftly enough to correct it with state officials and restore the woman’s coverage quickly.
She said since 2023, about 42 individuals at the Arc of Howard County have fallen out of the Medicaid waiver at some point.
While many of them were able to get their Medicaid coverage restored and the state paid some outstanding claims back, Collins-Ihrke believes she is still owed almost $400,000 in unpaid claims for developmental disability services over the years.
Another error occurred with a man who was erroneously disenrolled because it appeared he had too much income from a work program he was enrolled in. He was left out of the waiver for longer.
“We were told he was denied because … he was in another Medicaid program – which was incorrect,” Collins-Ihrke said.
“Because they denied him, he ended up falling off of the waiver because he came into some money,” she said. “We found out in the fall …  and then he didn’t get back on the waiver until April of 2026. So, he was off the waiver for a year, maybe a little more.”
Because Maryland law prohibits a waiver program from discharging someone until they are taken in by another provider, the Arc of Howard County continued to provide services for him.
“We didn’t have an option to discharge him … he would be homeless. DDA probably wouldn’t allow us to discharge him, so we’re stuck holding the bag,” she said. “We still have $130,000 – $140,000 out there that we have to, I guess, now absorb.
Medicaid recipients sue state over ‘dysfunctional’ eligibility system

“My concern is that had I not caught that and not understood or had our staff not understood how it works – they might still not have their Medicaid,” she said. “People who don’t have providers who have the infrastructure to deal with these kinds of things are even more so lost.”
Greg Miller, president and CEO of Penn-Mar Human Services, says his organization has also provided services to people with developmental disabilities that should be covered by the Medicaid waiver.
“We have tried to work with our governmental partners to resolve this issue,” he said. “We’re basically told that they are not going to pay for services that we provided.
“My biggest concern is that although there are promises to fix this in the future, they have set a very, very dangerous precedent and one that cannot be repeated for people who are of vulnerable populations,” Miller said. “They’re making a very, very dangerous choice and that’s not something that is going to be acceptable to me or any other provider who have given their lives basically to help men and women with disabilities participate in our communities.”
A lawsuit filed last year by The Arc Montgomery County alleges it had, at the time of the court filing, provided $9 million in care to clients since January 2024 for DDA services that have not been reimbursed by the state.
Miller, Howell and advocates say other providers are considering their options, which could include legal action.
The department said in its statement Friday that it has “been working with participants and families, providers, stakeholders and advocates throughout the Moore-Miller Administration on ways to improve processes to support service delivery. This has included steps, such as creating a waiver help team, increasing the use of automation in application processing, and reviewing policies and practices that govern eligibility and enrollment processes.”
But ongoing fiscal challenges at the department, including two years of massive budget cuts to the DDA, may limit the department’s ability to restore those funds.
At a recent meeting of Developmental Disabilities Administration Waiver Advisory Council, Deputy Health  Secretary Marlana Hutchinson said that, starting this month, waiver recipients would have three months to fix any financial discrepancy that may risk a loss of coverage. If recipients or their providers prove financial eligibility during that time, the coverage would continue.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“We do know we have had challenges where folks have gone over asset, going into a financial ineligibility time period, and that it’s taken longer for them to get back on the waiver program,” Hutchinson told the advisory council. “We are seeking to get this policy in place ASAP so that … beginning Sept. 1, individuals don’t have to go through that lengthy disenrollment process if it is done within the 90 days.”
Some of the other advisory council members argued that policy was already in place, but the state’s application of that policy changed in recent years. Providers and families were told in recent years that waiver recipients needed to go through the reenrollment process again to get their Medicaid restored, which is where the delays tend to occur.
Regardless, the new policy does not ensure that providers who have been giving months of care without payment will ever see those dollars returned, said Ande Kolp, executive director of The Arc Maryland, during the meeting.
“Something must be done for people who have endured this over the last 18 months,” she said. “It’s not going to be OK for us to just move forward.
“There are hundreds of people that this has happened to that are still in limbo,” Kolp said. “There are millions of dollars in unpaid claims for services provided by providers that had no other choice but to provide these services to protect the health and safety of people with developmental disabilities, unless they become homeless or end up in hospitals or perish.”

title: Dementia care navigators help Latino Coloradans get the support they need
description: This commentary was originally published by The Conversation. Latino Americans are 1.5 times more likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease than white Americans, according to the Alzheimer’s Association. In Colorado, nearly a quarter of the overall population identifies as Hispanic or Latino. As Coloradans age, more individuals and families in these communities[...]
text:
(Getty Images)This commentary was originally published by The Conversation.
Latino Americans are 1.5 times more likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease than white Americans, according to the Alzheimer’s Association.
In Colorado, nearly a quarter of the overall population identifies as Hispanic or Latino. As Coloradans age, more individuals and families in these communities will be affected by dementia.
Today approximately 11,000 of the 91,000 Coloradans ages 65 years and older who live with Alzheimer’s disease are Latino. Many face barriers to timely diagnoses, medical treatments and coordination of care.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Nearly 9 in 10 Latinos say it is important for dementia care providers to understand their cultural backgrounds, according to an Alzheimer’s Association 2021 report. Two years later, another study found that dementia care often misses or overlooks unique perspectives and needs of Latinos. The study described the importance of reducing stigma about cognitive decline, helping people care for their brains to decrease dementia risk and acknowledging the impacts dementia has on families and households.


Doctors encourage family members to pay attention to the warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease on a “Good Morning America” report.
As a geriatrician, palliative care physician and researcher in dementia care and caregiving, my work focuses on improving dementia care across cultural backgrounds, including in Latino communities.
I am also the founding medical director of the University of Colorado Medicine GUIDE Program. GUIDE stands for Guiding an Improved Dementia Experience and is a new Medicare program that provides a trained dementia care navigator to individuals affected by dementia.
‘Nothing about us without us’
In 2024, my research team convened eight Latino caregivers as research advisers to help improve studies in dementia palliative care.
This is an example of community-engaged research, the practice of including in the research process the perspectives of the individuals and communities that research aims to help. Individuals who are part of such studies often describe it this way: “nothing about us without us.”
Palliative care for dementia is designed to help patients understand how the illness progresses and what decisions they need to make. It also focuses on how to improve the patients’ quality of life and support caregivers at each stage of the disease.
We asked the caregivers who joined meetings to provide input on how we might conduct a hospital-based palliative care study so that it would better address the cultural needs of older Latinos with advanced dementia.
The advisers described to us the challenges they faced navigating the healthcare system, especially related to a lack of interpreters or services in their preferred language or dialect.
Their insights emphasized the need for tailored, culturally responsive dementia care. Findings from this study are helping our team implement the GUIDE program in Colorado.
The GUIDE model
Launched in 2024 by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, the GUIDE model provides care and support for Medicare beneficiaries living with dementia as well as their caregivers.
There are currently 292 GUIDE programs across the U.S., including four based in Colorado. The Colorado programs serve areas that include the cities of Grand Junction, Durango, Pueblo and Denver.
The program aims to address the overwhelming stress and concern people living with dementia and their caregivers have due to progression of the disease.
Dementia limits a person’s ability to live and function independently. It affects people’s ability to make decisions on issues such as money and safe driving. Dementia can also cause behavioral symptoms such as confusion, apathy, personality changes, anxiety and depression.
The GUIDE model connects eligible Medicare parts A and B beneficiaries who have dementia, and a caregiver if one is involved, with a trained dementia care navigator at no additional cost.
That navigator works to understand their needs and challenges, and then provides tailored recommendations. These recommendations often include resources for dementia education, advice on how to coordinate care across healthcare systems and information about community resources.
The GUIDE program also provides a comprehensive assessment and care plan from a dementia specialist, including a medication review. If eligible, patients and caregivers can also receive respite care, such as in-home care, adult daycare or facility-based care.
In the first two years of our team’s GUIDE program at the University of Colorado, we have enrolled 200 patients who have a dementia diagnosis and their caregivers. We are tracking how the program is working, including their perspectives on quality of care and levels of caregiver strain.
Moving forward
Public health agencies, community organizations and GUIDE programs are working together to help the tens of thousands of Coloradans with dementia and their families find services and support.
One outcome is the Colorado dementia GUIDE model map, which helps families and caregivers find a GUIDE program.
GUIDE programs in Colorado are also working to incorporate the specific needs of Latino communities. Insights from Latino caregivers encouraged us to hire bilingual dementia care navigators and include Spanish-language dementia resources. In 2024, the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment launched the Talk About Dementia campaign, which included education and resources for caregiver support in English and Spanish.
Colorado’s GUIDE programs are contributing to the national effort to study how dementia care navigation can best help patients and families living with dementia.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Valvoline Global didn’t leave Lexington. We let them go.
description: Valvoline Global Operations announced Monday that they are moving its global headquarters from Lexington to downtown Cincinnati. Cincinnati’s mayor called it “a huge win… for our local economy, and for the momentum our city and partners have been working to build.” Their gain is Lexington’s – and Kentucky’s –direct loss.  Valvoline Global is not an […]
text:
Lexington and other Kentucky cities are losing big businesses, which affects jobs, a columnist says.Valvoline Global Operations announced Monday that they are moving its global headquarters from Lexington to downtown Cincinnati. Cincinnati’s mayor called it “a huge win… for our local economy, and for the momentum our city and partners have been working to build.”
Their gain is Lexington’s – and Kentucky’s –direct loss. 
Valvoline Global is not an isolated loss. Tempur Sealy absorbed Mattress Firm, became Somnigroup, and is putting its corporate headquarters in Dallas–Fort Worth. Lexmark, the business IBM left behind, was bought by Xerox and has been shedding Lexington workers ever since. Fazoli’s, ceremonial headquarters on Palumbo Drive shut down all but one Lexington locations. And for manufacturing, Trane took 600 jobs off Mercer Road and moved them to South Carolina. 
One may have been a warning shot that our local and state leaders are not serving the major employers; all of them abandoning Lexington show that our leaders no longer prioritize or respect them as the major economic engines they are and could have been. 
Though Louisville has lost Papa John’s to co-headquarter in Atlanta and KFC headquarters in Texas The General Assembly invested over a billion dollars in Louisville for “infrastructure, public safety, economic development, the arts, and other community priorities.” Lexington was only allocated $57 million by the state, for every seventeen dollars Louisville got, Lexington got $1. 
Lexington’s Affordable Housing and Homelessness Fund carries $9.4 million, set by ordinance at one percent of the prior year’s recurring revenue. The Lexington Economic Development Fund known as the JOBS Fund, is $720,154. Two years ago it was $2.87 million. Lexington cut it by three-quarters and then flat-lined it. The budget reveals we are not prioritizing the attraction and retention of economic engines, even though the most sustainable way to make housing feel more affordable to everyone is through community investment in stronger jobs for everyone. 
Previously, working with economic development departments in Texas, I see why household names chose Texas communities, and no, it was not just the taxes. The local leaders showed how serious they are about their future by not waiting on a site selector’s Request for Proposals but rather proactively sending their staff, elected officials and consultants all across the country and globe to meet and court executives; hosting major brands and developers in their communities to show off the best of what they have; working regionally to put their money where their mouth is and it worked. 
For years, I would eagerly share strategies from back home to lackluster interest, or recently bring great potential quality employers to officials in Lexington and not get responses for months after repeated calls and messages,
Those losses turned into gains for other counties in Kentucky. The mega-corporate losses we are witnessing are not a surprise based on first-hand experience. 
Many have shared the same relationship advice with me that if you never stop pursuing your spouse after marriage, they will never look anywhere else but you. I see a lot of parallels of that dating advice in attracting corporate relocations and catching the eye of site selectors to choose Lexington but no intentionality to continuing the pursuit decades after the ribbon cutting on headquarters. 
Our community leaders need to step up to the pursuit or move on, like these major companies moved on. Lexington families and neighborhoods will begin to face the fact that we are no longer a city and must retreat to town status and give up the advantages that come with cities.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana Democratic Party comes out against amendment to limit governors’ time in office
description: The Louisiana Democratic Party voted over the weekend to oppose a constitutional amendment to prohibit governors from running for office again after they have served more than one and a half terms, equal to six years.
text:
Louisiana Democratic Party chairman Randal Gaines said he believes proposed constitutional amendment #4 on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot unfairly targets former Gov. John Bel Edwards. (Photo by Jonathan Peterson/Louisiana Illuminator)The Louisiana Democratic Party voted over the weekend to oppose a constitutional amendment to prohibit governors from running for office again after they have served more than one and a half terms, equal to six years. 

Proposed Amendment 4 will appear on the Nov. 3 election ballot that also features the U.S. Senate and congressional races. The Democratic State Central Committee approved a campaign against the measure at its meeting Saturday, chairman Randal Gaines said. 
“I think it limits the democratic rights and choices of voters,” Gaines said in an interview Monday. 
The amendment would only prevent former Govs. Bobby Jindal and John Bel Edwards from running for office again because all other former Louisiana governors are deceased. It could also impact Gov. Jeff Landy if he wins a second term next year, in addition to any future governor elected to two terms. 
Several Democrats have said they believe the amendment is aimed at Edwards, the two-term Democrat who left office in 2024. He is often mentioned as a potential candidate who could take on Landry, though Edwards has not said he is seriously considering running again. 

“It’s evident that it is targeting John Bel Edwards. I think it is a self-serving proposal by this administration,” Gaines said in an interview Monday. 
Unlike most legislation, Landry did not get to formally weigh in on this proposal. Constitutional amendments don’t go to the governor’s desk for a signature or veto before they end up on the voters’ ballot. 
Only one governor has served more than two terms since Louisiana’s present constitution was approved in 1974. Edwin Edwards, not related to John Bel Edwards, served four terms: 1972-76, 1976-80, 1984-88 and 1992-96. He died in 2021. 

The amendment’s sponsor in the legislature, state Rep. Mike Bayham, R-Chalmette, said it isn’t meant to target John Bel Edwards.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE 

“This is about the future. This is not about the past,” Bayham said in an interview Monday. ”I view this as a nonpartisan issue.” 
Through a spokesperson, Edwards declined to comment Monday. Shortly after the legislature approved Bayham’s bill in May, he shared his thoughts about it on social media. 

“I think this is what the kids call ‘living in somebody’s head rent free,’” Edwards wrote on X about the proposal. 
Bayham said he offered to create an exemption for governors who had already served in office within the amendment, such that it wouldn’t affect Edwards, Jindal or Landry. People close to Edwards declined to take him up on the offer, Bayham said. 
The Chalmette legislator said he hopes the amendment will allow “new blood” to enter the upper echelons of Louisiana politics. When the same people run for governor over and over again, it can be hard for new candidates to raise the money to get elected, he said. 

“When a former governor gets in a race, what does that do to new candidates who don’t have a machine behind them? Who don’t have $10 million or $20 million behind them? That keeps them from being able to run,” Bayham said during a legislation committee hearing on amendment in May. 
If the amendment passes and is used to prevent Jindal, Edwards or Landry from running for a third term, it could face some legal challenges. During discussions over the bill in the legislative session, Democrats suggested it could not apply retroactively for constitutional reasons. 
“It would only apply to the future,” state Sen. Jay Luneau, D-Alexandria, said about the amendment on the Senate floor right before a vote on the legislation. 

The Louisiana House voted 73-25 for the proposal, with a handful of Democrats in support and state Rep. Mandie Landry, D-New Orleans, as its House cosponsor. The Senate voted 28-10, with all Democrats in opposition. 

The amendment needed two-thirds of members in each legislative chamber to get on the ballot. A simple majority of voters have to approve it Nov. 3 for the law to take effect.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia education board updates graduation requirements, expands course options for students
description: The Virginia Board of Education has approved updates to its list of approved courses, clarifying expanded graduation requirements for schools. The measure spells out graduation rules that schools must understand and follow, building on legislative efforts to expand how students can earn a standard or advanced studies diploma by meeting graduation requirement[...]
text:
A group of high school graduates. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)The Virginia Board of Education has approved updates to its list of approved courses, clarifying expanded graduation requirements for schools.
The measure spells out graduation rules that schools must understand and follow, building on legislative efforts to expand how students can earn a standard or advanced studies diploma by meeting graduation requirements in math, science, history and social studies,  economics and personal finance.
These new standards give certain students more ways to satisfy requirements, such as in history and social sciences. This is especially useful for students taking Advanced Placement and International Baccalaureate courses, or transferring to Virginia schools later in high school.
For example, students may use African American History or AP African American Studies, if available, to meet their World History I or World Geography requirement. However, they must pass an approved alternative assessment to receive the history and social studies credit needed to meet the graduation requirement.
The list of changes also allows more approved Economics and Personal Finance (EPF) courses, such as IB Economics or IB Business Management, to count toward the EPF requirement if they include the required EPF material. The course must be approved by the state education department and meet EPF standards.
Students who transfer into a Virginia public high school after 10th grade can also use International Baccalaureate courses to meet some graduation requirements, substituting for Virginia and U.S. history, government and economics, and personal finance classes.
The revamped standards also provide an exception for the required first aid, CPR, and AED training if the student’s IEP or 504 Plan states they cannot complete the training, or if they transferred after 10th grade from a school or program that did not require or provide credit for the training. 
The changes went into effect for the current school year.
The board did not make any direct comment on the graduation requirements at its most recent meeting on Aug. 27.
However, Board Member Amber Northern, appointed by former Gov. Glenn Youngkin, asked department staff to return at a future meeting with guidance showing how schools can use existing seat-time flexibility.
Seat-time flexibility allows students who have mastered the required material or skills to earn course credit through alternative learning experiences rather than spending a fixed number of hours in a traditional classroom. Virginia authorized the option in 2024.
Northern said students have “no time” in their schedules to participate in alternative learning pathways because so many of the credits required for graduation are already committed to mandatory courses.
“Our kids have no time to take a CTE (career and technical education) apprenticeship, to do work-based learning, do all the stuff that we’re doing when our course requirements consume 22 of our 24 credits,” Northern said last Thursday.
She later called for clearer guidance for school divisions, saying, “I think we’d do a real service to our divisions if we could supplement our graduation requirements with here’s how you can use the flexibility that you’ve been given.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: The day Virginia took down Confederate statues, a Black church remembered a lynching victim
description: On Aug. 28, 1899, hundreds of Black residents of Alexandria, Virginia, gathered at Shiloh Baptist Church after a white mob lynched 16-year-old Benjamin Thomas. On Friday night, August 28, 2026, exactly 127 years later, I sat inside the same church as Alexandria gathered there again. The same day, about 100 miles south, workers in Richmond […]
text:
A statue of Confederate General Thomas "Stonewall" Jackson in Virginia's Capitol Square on Jan. 29, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)On Aug. 28, 1899, hundreds of Black residents of Alexandria, Virginia, gathered at Shiloh Baptist Church after a white mob lynched 16-year-old Benjamin Thomas. On Friday night, August 28, 2026, exactly 127 years later, I sat inside the same church as Alexandria gathered there again.
The same day, about 100 miles south, workers in Richmond were removing three Confederate memorials from Capitol Square, statues honoring Thomas J. “Stonewall” Jackson, former Virginia governor and Confederate general William “Extra Billy” Smith, and Confederate physician Hunter Holmes McGuire.
The coincidence was difficult to ignore. In Richmond, Virginia was reconsidering whom it had placed on pedestals. In Alexandria, a community was remembering someone history nearly forgot.
Together, the two events posed a larger question: Once we decide whom we should no longer venerate, whom do we choose to remember instead?
Benjamin Thomas offers one answer. Thomas had joined Shiloh as a young teenager and was baptized there. On Aug. 7, 1899, he was arrested after being accused of assaulting a 7-year-old white girl.
Black community leaders warned police and the mayor that Thomas had been threatened with a lynching. When authorities ignored them, Black Alexandrians attempted to protect Thomas themselves.
New information in 138-year-old Virginia Beach lynching shatters state’s genteel veneer

The police arrested them. The next morning, according to the remembrance program, the men who had tried to protect Thomas were tried, fined and sent to the chain gang.
That night, the mob came. It seized Thomas from the city jail, dragged him roughly half a mile through Alexandria and lynched him at King and Fairfax streets.
Black Alexandria responded. African American domestic workers in Alexandria and Washington, D.C. stopped working. The Black press documented what had happened. The community raised money. Churches organized.
And on Aug. 28, Black Alexandrians gathered at Shiloh to remember Thomas, proclaim his innocence and protest lynching. The Evening Star newspaper described what was taking place that night as a “mass meeting.”
They had come to mourn. But they had also come to mobilize.
Alexandria Mayor Alyia Gaskins captured that tradition during last Friday night’s remembrance when she imagined what Thomas’s grieving mother needed after losing her child.
There were “other mommas who showed up to mourn and to mobilize,” Gaskins said, not only for Thomas but to make sure other children might have a better future.
Mourn and mobilize. Those words may be as useful an action plan for civil rights defense in uncertain times as any.
That history became especially relevant Friday when Myesha Braden, deputy general counsel of the NAACP, addressed the congregation. Braden knows something about what happens when hatred moves beyond rhetoric. 
Before joining the NAACP, she served as an associate deputy attorney general at the Justice Department, where her responsibilities included oversight of the Civil Rights Division and Community Relations Service. 
Earlier in her career, she prosecuted civil-rights cases and helped lead the federal prosecution arising from the hate-crime killing of Luis Ramirez, a 25-year-old Mexican immigrant in Shenandoah, Pennsylvania.
“The mob is a tool,” Braden told us. “The mob is a method.”
She traced that method across American history, from racial violence in Wilmington and Tulsa to the attacks in Charleston and Buffalo.
“Different faces, different decades, same tool,” she said.
But Braden also offered the counterweight.
“The struggle for civil rights is a discipline,” she said. “It’s a discipline that has to be practiced generation after generation.”
A program honoring Benjamin Thomas, a 16-year-old Black boy lynched by a white mob in Alexandria, Va. in 1899, presented by Shiloh Baptist Church 127 years after his death. (Photo courtesy Jeff Bennett)A program honoring Benjamin Thomas, a 16-year-old Black boy lynched by a white mob in Alexandria, Va. in 1899, presented by Shiloh Baptist Church 127 years after his death. (Photo courtesy Jeff Bennett)
Alexandria itself demonstrates how much has changed. A Black woman now serves as mayor of a city where a white mob once murdered a Black teenager. The city publicly commemorates Thomas. Historians, churches and community members have worked to restore stories once neglected or suppressed.
And inside the program I held Friday was another measure of that progress. Each year, the Alexandria Community Remembrance Project awards two Alexandria City High School seniors $3,000 scholarships in the names of Thomas and Joseph McCoy, another Black teenager lynched in Alexandria.
The program describes the scholarships as part of Alexandria’s commitment to acknowledge past injustices while “investing in our youth and the future.”
There is something profound in that transformation. A Confederate general once received a pedestal. A lynching victim now gives a student a scholarship.
Thomas was denied his future at 16. Today, his name helps another Alexandria teenager build one.
Virginia cannot undo what happened to Thomas. It cannot restore the years he never lived, the family he might have raised, the work he might have done or the person he might have become.
But remembrance can do more than preserve the circumstances of his death. It can give his name work to do among the living.
That, too, is mobilization.

title: Inside Virginia’s city halls, concerns, confusion rise with Flock surveillance protests
description: By Kunle Falayi/Virginia Center for Investigative Journalism at WHRO A Williamsburg resident in March asked the police department at the College of William & Mary how data collected by the school’s Flock Safety surveillance system is shared. Police Chief Don Butler asked Flock for the answer, according to records obtained by the Virginia Center for […]
text:
A protester outside Richmond City Hall during a demonstration against Flock cameras before a City Council meeting on July 27, 2026. (Photo by Jaysun Silver/VCIJ at WHRO)By Kunle Falayi/Virginia Center for Investigative Journalism at WHRO
A Williamsburg resident in March asked the police department at the College of William & Mary how data collected by the school’s Flock Safety surveillance system is shared.
Police Chief Don Butler asked Flock for the answer, according to records obtained by the Virginia Center for Investigative Journalism at WHRO. “I’m trying to be transparent with some folks who would rather we didn’t have Flock cameras,” Butler wrote to the company, “and want to make sure I tell them correctly.”
Flock Safety vice president Chris Colwell replied several days later with a list of talking points, each one with a supposed question and scripted answer: “Has Flock been ‘breached’ and why do I keep hearing that it has? No. The recent concerns agencies are hearing are not the result of a successful hack or compromise of Flock’s platform or cloud environment.”
Colwell wrote that “having simple, ready-to-share language is often just as important as the underlying controls.”
The response did not directly address Butler’s question.
Colwell instructed Butler to “forward this email as-is” or “copy and paste” into a memo to send to residents, according to records obtained by the Virginia Center for Investigative Journalism at WHRO.






A page from Flock Safety’s letter to William & Mary police chief, Don Butler

William & Mary spokesperson Nathan Warters said the exchange was standard. “Sometimes we lean on the specialized knowledge of Flock’s experts to accurately answer questions pertaining specifically to the company’s technology,” he said. The information is then shared with the public.
The email exchange was revealed in the thousands of public documents obtained by the Virginia Center for Investigative Journalism at WHRO from Norfolk, Alexandria, Mecklenburg and Fairfax counties. VCIJ’s requests sought correspondence and materials related to the operation of Flock cameras, sent by residents to public officials or police departments, or exchanged between officials and residents.
A VCIJ review of the documents shows city and county leaders in communities with Flock cameras frantically sought basic information about data security, sharing and privacy concerns as residents grew alarmed by Flock surveillance in their hometowns.
The correspondence reveals increasing pressure from citizens on city and county leaders to amend or cancel contracts with Flock.
Despite the widespread use of Flock cameras, local officials often had little knowledge of how data was collected, shared and stored. Sometimes, police departments did not fully understand the AI-powered system operated before the cameras were installed.
“The pattern we’ve seen in many places with new technology is that police go out and sign the contract with no city council vote on it or oversight by the mayor,” said attorney Michael Soyfer of the Institute for Justice, a privacy advocate. “Oftentimes, the department vetting is very minimal. It usually consists of reading the marketing materials that are delivered by Flock or any other vendor and talking to another police department that uses license plate readers.”

Michael Soyfer, attorney at the Institute of Justice (Photo courtesy Institute of Justice)

 A Flock training manual for local officials to blunt public criticism 

Residents across Virginia pressing for answers about Flock cameras tend to circle the same core concerns: who can access the data, how it may be misused, whether the system enables mass surveillance, and what it means for personal privacy. Privacy advocates argue the cameras collect enough information to track people’s movements in detail, creating a system vulnerable to abuse.
Those concerns have already played out in court. The Institute for Justice sued Norfolk in 2024, arguing that Flock’s continuous collection of vehicle movements amounts to a warrantless search and violates the Fourth Amendment. A federal judge rejected that claim in January.
Meanwhile, VCIJ’s 2025 reporting showed how data from small towns like Bridgewater were accessed by hundreds of agencies nationwide before Virginia banned out‑of‑state sharing. Vague or insufficient reasons cited by officers for searching the system also complicate oversight.
Misuse has also fueled scrutiny. Officers in multiple states, including Texas, Georgia, the Carolinas, Wisconsin and Florida, have been accused of abusing Flock data. One Florida officer used it to track an ex‑girlfriend, according to 404 Media. As these questions mount, Flock Safety has worked to shape public perception, providing Virginia law enforcement agencies with detailed scripts for responding to citizen and media concerns about privacy and potential misuse.
One of Flock’s training documents obtained by VCIJ and first reported on by 404 Media, “How to Speak to City Councils About Public Safety Technology,” teaches law enforcement to “spend less time defending the technology’s capabilities” when the public asks if it constitutes mass surveillance.
“Don’t avoid the concept of mass surveillance because you are not going to convince opponents that it’s not.”
The company suggests a different approach. It asks law enforcement agencies to focus on relating the surveillance to “your local need, your local community, the effect it’s going to have on quality of life and crime reduction.”
It said “public safety technology is no longer evaluated on performance alone” and that “councils and communities increasingly expect transparency, oversight and accountability alongside public safety outcomes.”
The Flock manual warned law enforcement agencies: “Opponents have a very carefully scripted narrative. They come prepared. You should also have a carefully scripted presentation that addresses the concerns ahead of time.”
In the document, Flock Safety’s Director of Public Trust and Technology, Max Weinstein, tells agencies to “compare technology investments against the costs of unresolved crime,” if they are asked whether the surveillance system is worth the investment. “A single recovered vehicle can often exceed the annual cost of a camera.”
A Flock Safety spokesperson, Holly Beilin, said the company had no comment.
Brad Lehmann, assistant professor of criminal justice at Virginia Commonwealth University, said Flock and other ALPR vendors are private businesses and may not be held to the same level of scrutiny as city leaders, even though they should.

Brad Lehmann, Assistant Professor of Criminal Justice, Virginia Commonwealth University (Photo courtesyVCU/VCU Faculty Bio)

Lehmann, a former police officer, said many departments do not have the capacity to vet and learn a new technology before they start using it.
“I think that’s very fair to say that police did not expect this much controversy over the technology,” he said. “They weren’t thinking about the big-time mass surveillance-type human usage of a technology that is this powerful. I don’t think any of us really completely thought about how big this was going to be.”
 

Elected leaders, police struggle to ease community doubts
[/subhed]In Bridgewater and Alexandria, community questions are forcing council members and law enforcement agencies to seek answers to unanticipated questions.
Alexandria Mayor Alyia Gaskin sought information about the city’s surveillance system and grew impatient when she was not getting answers fast enough from the Alexandria Police Department, according to records obtained by VCIJ. The system had been in place for two years when Gaskin, a new mayor, wanted to know more about data sharing and the number of cameras the city had.
In a June 2025 email to the city manager, Jim Parajon, Gaskin asked how many cameras the city had, if anyone outside of APD could retrieve the data from the cameras, or if agencies outside of Alexandria, including federal partners, could access the data from the city’s 67 Flock cameras.
“It is my understanding that my colleagues have also reached out requesting this information and not received an answer,” she said, asking for a response before the council’s recess five days later.
Months later, Gaskins was still dealing with how to respond to continued inquiries and concerns.
In January 2026, her office received multiple emails from residents calling on the city to cancel its Flock contract.
“In documented cases, some devices have been compromised through physical access alone, while others have been found broadcasting live video feeds on the open internet without authentication,” one resident said, and called for suspension of the operation of current cameras and termination of Alexandria’s contract with Flock.
Ten minutes after Gaskins read the resident’s complaint, Gaskins sent an email to a sergeant in the city’s Homeland Security Section, John Jones, requesting that he “provide the council with a response that can be shared with the public that outlines what we do and do not do.”
In Bridgewater, records show how town officials ignored inquiries from VCIJ when this news organization asked why the town’s Flock data was searched millions of times by outside agencies nationwide and by federal agencies for immigration enforcement.
After a series of emails and calls from this reporter went unanswered, Bridgewater’s Mayor Ted Flory messaged town manager Jay Litten, reiterating that he knew that the town’s Flock cameras were available to other agencies from across the nation.
“I’m not at all eager to talk to the reporter about this,” Flory wrote. “I’m just going to sit tight for now and not respond.”
Litten agreed, saying that the town needed to step cautiously and not become “the poster child for one side or another in the immigration debate.”
Days after VCIJ published its story showing that data from Bridgewater’s five Flock cameras had been accessed more than 7 million times nationwide, the town manager began seeking answers to the questions VCIJ had posed. He directed his questions to the Virginia State Police.
“We were hoping that the State Police might consider weighing in very brieﬂy on these four questions,” Litten wrote in an email to the VSP’s Public Relations Officer, Robin Lawson. “What happens to Flock photos after 21 days? In what ways might the Flock photos become associated with a particular person? Is Virginia aware of any safeguards which work to prevent Flock photos from being leaked or misused? If you’re able, we would be greatly obliged. The answers would be most helpful this week before Council gathers again.”
Lawson replied to Litten that he should direct his questions to Bridgewater’s police chief, who signed the contract with Flock Safety.
 



Who’s responsible for policing ALPRs?


Despite these controversies, the Flock surveillance network is expanding nationally. In Virginia, at least 159 law enforcement agencies use ALPRs, including 139 with Flock Safety, according to Virginia State Police’s 2025 ALPR report. Businesses like Lowe’s also use them on their premises.

The drumbeat from the public for accountability hasn’t stopped.
The issue comes down to evidence, not talking points, said Newport News-based anti-surveillance advocate Clayton Tye. “If you claim that this has been solving crime, then prove it,” he said. “I want to see the proof that this actually has solved crime.”
Tye filed multiple record requests in January to over a dozen localities asking for the number of cases, including homicides, in which Flock data was used as evidence. Norfolk, Newport News, and Virginia Beach all said they do not track how Flock data is used in criminal cases.
Flock cameras have assisted in investigating two shootings since March, a Norfolk police spokesman told VCIJ.
The lack of evidence “beyond anecdotes” showing Flock’s extraordinary effectiveness is statewide, Tye said. “How can you make claims that these are effective when you don’t even track the data that would prove that it?” Tye said.
Soyfer, the privacy advocate, said city officials need to take responsibility for understanding the technology and protecting people’s constitutional rights.
“Flock’s responsibility and duty is to maximize profits for its shareholders,” he said. “It is up to police chiefs and public officials to figure out if the use of Flock cameras in their jurisdiction is consistent with the Fourth Amendment and not just blindly deferring to a corporation that has different interests and responsibilities.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: International student enrollment grows at Maine’s public universities amid national decline
description: Maine’s universities are enrolling more international students for the fifth year in a row, defying the national trend of higher education enrollment declines.  The biggest reason for the growth is the 250% increase in international students enrolled online, according to preliminary data from Fall 2026. An overwhelming majority of those students will never a[...]
text:
The University of Maine at Orono campus. (Photo by University of Maine)Maine’s universities are enrolling more international students for the fifth year in a row, defying the national trend of higher education enrollment declines. 
The biggest reason for the growth is the 250% increase in international students enrolled online, according to preliminary data from Fall 2026. An overwhelming majority of those students will never attend Maine’s public universities in person and thus are not impacted by President Donald Trump administration’s crackdown on foreign students and immigration. 
From imposing fees for post-degree practical training to reducing the duration of international students’ visas and, in some cases, to students with valid visas facing arrest and detention by federal agents, the administration’s policies have resulted in fewer foreign students enrolling in U.S. colleges and universities, according to national data.
But in Maine, the popularity of online programs and the steady stream of students from Canada have allowed the state’s public universities to start the semester with 1,169 international students — the highest in five years — while overall enrollment also grows across all seven campuses. Canadian students, who can attend Maine’s public universities at the in-state tuition rate, account for 393 of the total. Roughly 500 foreign students are pursuing fully online degrees. 
“I think this has been a confusing couple of years for international students,” University of Maine System Chancellor Dannel Malloy said. “And we’ve put a lot of time and effort into explaining how you can be one of our students and what type of program you can be in and what you’re looking for.”
The YourPace program — an 8-week flexible degree program run by the University of Maine at Presque Isle — which allows students to learn entirely online, is how international students are completing undergraduate degrees through Maine’s public universities.
President Ray Rice said the program has grown exponentially since it started in [what year] and is helping meet thousands of students’ needs for specific certifications and in-demand degrees. While a majority of YourPace students are U.S. citizens, it has proven to be a useful tool for international students as the Trump administration tightens restrictions on foreign degree seekers.
Rather than navigating the immigration system, international students enrolled in YourPace have to demonstrate English proficiency and have the required GPA for their program, Rice said. 
“I think that simplicity without the complexity of the current vicissitudes probably make us attractive to a number of students,” he said.
Some popular programs international students are enrolling in through YourPace include business, psychology and organizational leadership.  
However, the growth in international student enrollment does not mean an increase in revenue. The state’s Orono-based flagship, the University of Maine, saw a slight decline from 515 students at this same point in Fall 2024 to 455 now, according to data obtained by Maine Morning Star.
Because of that drop, “there is going to be a reduction in net tuition revenue from international students in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, and that obviously has budget implications,” said system spokesperson Samantha Warren.  
That’s because students enrolled in YourPace pay a flat fee as opposed to the higher revenue the university system charges for in-person international tuition.
The latest policy introduced by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security made student visas time-limited instead of issuing them for the duration of the degree programs. Students will have to apply for extensions if they need more time to complete their degrees or want to gain hands-on training after. 
Warren said the impact of those changes on the University of Maine System is yet to be seen, especially on graduate programs. 
“I don’t think we’re seeing it fully yet, though certainly the overall climate is affecting the number of students who are coming in person,” she added.

title: State Personnel Department seeks raises for hundreds of employees in next budget session
description: The Indiana State Personnel Department is seeking $151 million in raises for state attorneys, laboratory technicians and other employees whose wages have not kept pace with the market. Secretary of Management and Budget Lisa Hershman presented the State Budget Committee last week with findings from a new compensation study, which identified 37 state jobs tha[...]
text:
Secretary of Management and Budget Lisa Hershman before the Senate Appropriations Committee on March 13, 2025. (Whitney Downard/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Indiana State Personnel Department is seeking $151 million in raises for state attorneys, laboratory technicians and other employees whose wages have not kept pace with the market.
Secretary of Management and Budget Lisa Hershman presented the State Budget Committee last week with findings from a new compensation study, which identified 37 state jobs that pay more than 20% below the market.
Those jobs include state attorneys, specialized maintenance technicians, grant coordinators, laboratory technicians and business administrators.
“Salaries need to go up to compete with the rising costs of day-to-day life that our employees are experiencing,” said Matthew Brown, State Personnel Department director.
(Review Item) Compensation Study - State Personnel Department
 
The study identified another 62 jobs whose wages are 10% to 20% below market, such as construction engineers, maintenance foreman and arson investigators.
Fifty-six jobs align with the market or lag by less than 10%.
Meanwhile, Indiana leads the market in 42 jobs: correctional officers, data scientists, laborers, veterinarians, highway engineers.
Brown said Indiana’s compensation philosophy prioritizes market competitiveness, internal equity, performance and fiscal conditions, but the Personnel Department’s analysis found wage compression is prevalent.
The state updated pay scales in 2022 following a market analysis, which sought to bring salaries to mid-range for similar government and non-profit jobs.
State employees got a 3% cost-of-living raise the following year, but the Personnel Department did not implement the second phase of its plan to alleviate wage compression for mid-level employees.
State employees are now without a pay raise for two consecutive years, though many received one-time bonuses of up to $2,500 this summer.
It’s official — no pay raise for state employees

The result, Brown said, is that more than 80% of state employees are now paid below the midpoint of the state’s established pay scales despite an average of 10 years’ experience.
More than half of state employees remain in the bottom quartile of the pay scale, he said.
“Someone who’s been at the state and in a role for five years is going to make very similar to someone who’s been in the job for one year,” Brown told the State Budget Committee, “and at that point, you lose the ability to distinguish performance-wise or salary-wise based on that experience.”
In one example, Brown said 108 of the 114 state attorneys remain below midpoint of the state’s pay range for attorneys — 60 of those attorneys haven’t made it out of the bottom quartile.
The minimum starting salary for a state attorney is $67,000 and rises to $85,000 after five years, but “that is still significantly below what we would expect” in the private sector, he said.
The raises would not affect minimum and maximum salaries, Brown said, but would instead move employees through pay ranges to better reflect experience. It would amount to a 5% general salary adjustment for a majority of affected state employees.
“If we’re able to start moving folks through those pay ranges, we think we’ll be able to compete better in the marketplace right now, which we’re seeing a lot of struggles with,” he said.
Indiana employs around 30,500 employees statewide, according to the transparency portal.
