title: In Alaska’s U.S. House race, a Libertarian and a federal inmate advance to the November election
description: This article has been updated as of 6 p.m. to include the withdrawal of another candidate. Weeks after suspending his campaign, the leading Democrat in Alaska’s U.S. House race officially withdrew ahead of Monday’s 5 p.m. deadline. That withdrawal triggered a sequence of events that put the eighth-place finisher, Libertarian candidate Jim McDermott, on the [[...]
text:
Independent candidate Bill Hill, a former teacher and school superintendent from Bristol Bay, speaks at a U.S. House candidate forum held Aug. 27, 2026, by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)This article has been updated as of 6 p.m. to include the withdrawal of another candidate.
Weeks after suspending his campaign, the leading Democrat in Alaska’s U.S. House race officially withdrew ahead of Monday’s 5 p.m. deadline.
That withdrawal triggered a sequence of events that put the eighth-place finisher, Libertarian candidate Jim McDermott, on the ballot in November.
Democrat Matt Schultz received 8.1% of the vote in the August primary, good enough for third, behind incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III and independent challenger Bill Hill.
Begich had 44.6% of the vote, and Hill had 32.5%, according to official results published Monday. 
Hill, a fisherman and former superintendent from Bristol Bay, is a first-time candidate for federal office. 
Under Alaska’s unique elections system, all candidates for an office run against each other in the primary election. The top four candidates, regardless of political party, advance to the general election in November. There, voters rank the candidates in order of preference.
The candidate with the fewest top rankings is eliminated, and any votes for them are redistributed to their voters’ second choices.
The process continues until only two candidates are left, and the person with the most votes wins.
If a top-four finisher withdraws, their spot is taken by the fifth-place finisher. If two top-four candidates withdraw, the sixth-place finisher also advances. 
Schultz suspended his campaign on July 17 in order to consolidate opposition fundraising and voter support. His withdrawal was followed by that of other trailing candidates.
With Schultz’s withdrawal, fourth-place finisher Eric Hafner — a registered Democrat in federal prison who received 3.8% of the vote — moves to the third spot on November’s election ballot. 
Two years ago, a state judge ruled that Hafner could remain a candidate even if he would be unable to serve his term due to his federal imprisonment.
Fifth-place finisher John Williams, a Democrat from Fairbanks who received 2.7% of the vote, withdrew from the race on Monday morning, he said by phone. 
The sixth-place finisher, Republican candidate Clay Strickland, withdrew from the race before Monday, the Division of Elections said.
That left seventh-place finisher Yaquelin Reynoso, who received 1.8% of the vote in August’s primary. 
Reynoso, who ran as a Democrat, does not appear on Alaska’s list of registered voters, didn’t answer a candidate survey and didn’t supply a phone number to the Alaska Division of Elections. 
They also didn’t immediately respond to their listed email on Monday afternoon.
But sometime before 5 p.m. Alaska time on Monday, Reynoso also withdrew from the race, the Division of Elections said Monday evening.
That left the eighth-place primary finisher, Libertarian candidate Jim McDermott of Fairbanks, to advance to the November election as the fourth of four candidates despite earning just 1.2% of the primary vote among 15 candidates overall. A call to McDermott’s listed phone went directly to voicemail at 5:50 p.m. Monday.
Ranked choice voting reduces the chances that candidates from the same party will split available voters and improve the odds for a candidate from a different party, but the system does not eliminate that chance entirely.
Since 2022, when Alaska began using the current system, a significant number of voters have continued to rank just one candidate.
As a result, political parties have pressured lower-finishing primary candidates to withdraw ahead of the general election in order to consolidate support. 
Williams, by phone from Fairbanks, said he talked with “a lot” of people from the Alaska Democratic Party and with Hill before making his decision.
“I’m going to step away because that’s the best thing for Alaska,” he said, not because of any particular request that he quit. 
Williams said he supports Alaska’s ranked choice election system, and he said he was discouraged by the number of Democratic Party officials who appeared to be acting against democratic values — the idea that voters, not political parties, decide candidates.
“I almost put my heels in the sand but ultimately decided not to,” he said. 
“If (Hill) wins, he wins. If he loses, it’s not going to be because of me,” Williams said.
Editor’s note: This story has been updated with the withdrawal of Yaquelin Reynoso, which advances Jim McDermott to the final four candidates.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky writer, farmer and advocate Wendell Berry dies at 92
description: Kentucky writer and conservationist Wendell Berry once wrote: “Beware the machinery of longevity. When a man’s life is over the decent thing is for him to die. The forest does not withhold itself from death.”  A lover of forests, the farmer, author and former English professor died on Monday at his home in Port Royal, […]
text:
Wendell Berry with two horses on his Henry County farm in 2010. Photo by Guy Mendes.Kentucky writer and conservationist Wendell Berry once wrote: “Beware the machinery of longevity. When a man’s life is over the decent thing is for him to die. The forest does not withhold itself from death.” 
A lover of forests, the farmer, author and former English professor died on Monday at his home in Port Royal, according to the New York Times and other media reports. He was 92.
Born in 1934 to Virginia Erdman and attorney John Marshall Berry, Wendell Berry was a prolific writer of nonfiction, poetry and fiction from Henry County, Kentucky. 
In dozens of books he wrote of the need to protect — and ethically use — land, of God as a part of nature and of modernity as a force to be rebelled against. 
Berry was a member of a group of Kentucky writers called the “Fab Five,” which included Bobbie Ann Mason and the late Gurney Norman, James Baker Hall and Ed McClanahan. 
He leaves behind a sprawling legacy of advocacy, conservationism, literary pursuit and protest that inspired people from the hills of Kentucky to Hollywood and beyond. 
His death leaves a vacancy of voice that was not always without controversy throughout his life but was decisive and steady throughout a long career. 
Tobacco and love of land 
Berry came from a long line of tobacco producers. John M. Berry, Wendell Berry’s father, co-founded the Burley Tobacco Growers Co-Op in the 1920s, which stabilized the price of tobacco and helped farmers who’d been subject to the pricing impulses of the monopoly American Tobacco Company, according to a Bitter Southerner article.
“The brilliance of the program was that it successfully matched supply and demand, preventing farmers from falling victim to overproduction,” the Bitter Southerner article says. “Within this equilibrium, farmers in the co-op were guaranteed parity prices, which meant a price that compensated them for all of their inputs.” 
That article also quoted Mary Berry, daughter of Wendell Berry, as saying the co-op “was the only farm program that I know of that served the people it was supposed to serve, and that was small farmers. It was never a subsidy, it was a price support. It cost the government nothing.”
His family farmed in Henry County for generations. In a 1987 interview with the Kentucky Historical Society, Berry’s father said his great-grandfather bought 500 acres of land in the county after serving in the Army in the War of 1812. 
When Berry left New York City and returned home to Kentucky for good in the 1960s, he did so with “some fear and trembling, but also a sense of doing the right thing,” he told The New Yorker in 2019. 
When he started the trek home, with all his belongings in a Volkswagen Beetle, he told the New Yorker: “I felt a great, deep relief — as if I was following, at last, my true path.” 
‘Cheerful in dissent.’  
Berry was a man of many lanes. 
He protested the Vietnam War, saying in 1968 that “peace is more important than victory,” according to a Messenger Inquirer article from Feb. 11 of that year. 
Berry was arrested in 1979 for trespassing as he protested the Marble Hill Nuclear Power Plant in Madison, Indiana. In a 2010 CounterPunch conversation, he said of that day: “People asked if I wanted to be arrested and I said, ‘Hell No’ but I was willing to be.” 
In 2009, Berry joined thousands of people who marched in protest of the Capitol Power Plant in Washington, D.C., Inside Climate News reported at the time, in an effort to fight for cleaner emissions. 
He echoed the same trepidation and resolve about the prospect of arrest: “Somebody asked me if I wanted to get arrested. The answer is very brief: No. But I’m willing to get arrested. Nothing else is working.”
The farmer fought to preserve a controversial piece of University of Kentucky art condemned as racist for many years and pushed back against mountaintop removal by joining a sit-in at former Gov. Steve Beshear’s office in 2011. 
The National Endowment for the Humanities described him in 2012 as “cheerful in dissent” and a person who “writes to document and defend what is being lost to the forces of modernization, and to explain how he lives and what he thinks.” 
The Berry Center was established in 2011 to put “Wendell Berry’s writings to work by advocating for farmers, land-conserving communities and healthy regional economies.” 
The nonprofit works to bring “focus, knowledge and cohesion to the work of changing our ruinous industrial agricultural system into a system and culture that uses nature as the standard, accepts no permanent damage to the ecosphere, and takes into consideration human health in local communities.” 
Honoree Wendell Berry attends the 2013 Roosevelt Institute Four Freedoms Awards & Benefit reception at St. James’ Episcopal Church on October 16, 2013 in New York City. (Photo by Taylor Hill/Getty Images)
The center educates farmers “in agrarian thought and practice,” runs a bookstore, has a cooperative to help farmers sell to markets and more.  
The work is in line with Berry’s legacy of advocacy for land preservation and agrarian life.  
Berry and the  University of Kentucky
Berry had a complicated relationship with his alma mater, the University of Kentucky.
He earned his bachelor and master’s degrees in English from UK, according to the Kentucky Historical Society. He then taught at the University of Kentucky from 1964-1977 and again from 1987-1993. (His teaching roster also includes Stanford University, Georgetown College, New York University, the University of Cincinnati and Bucknell University). 
In late 2009, Berry withdrew papers he’d loaned UK, a quiet protest against the university’s acceptance of $7 million from coal producer and philanthropist Joe Craft to rename a residence hall the “Wildcat Coal Lodge.” 
The Kentucky Kernel, the independent student newspaper at UK, reported that Berry could not abide what he considered an indignity as an advocate for the land and water polluted by mining. 
“I was taught that taking care of land was one of the primary human responsibilities,” the Kernel quoted Berry as saying. “In the long run, the top soil, the forests and the woodland of this state will be more valuable than the coal deposits.”
Berry felt the university’s move was a split from his values and those held by other farmers. 
“When the university accepted the gift from (the) coal industry in return for naming the basketball dormitory ‘Wildcat Coal Lodge,’ the university had sold an advertisement,” Berry said, according to the Kernel. 
That wasn’t the only time Berry and UK clashed. 
In July 2020, Berry joined a lawsuit against the University of Kentucky seeking to preserve a controversial 1934 fresco mural many criticised for its depictions of slavery in America and of Indigenous people. 
Ann Rice O’Hanlon painted the fresco as part of the Public Works of Art Project and President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal. 
It was a site for  protests on campus and requests to have it removed for years. According to court documents, complaints began in the 1970s. 
University of Kentucky President Eli Capilouto agreed to cover the mural in 2019 following a sit-in protest on campus that included the Black Student Advisory Council and others. In June 2020, seemingly moved by the racial justice movement sweeping through the country, he announced the university would remove it. 
The next month, Berry stepped in and asked a court to halt the removal. In court documents from the time, Berry argued the art needed to be conserved because of its historical significance, difficulty to create and rarity, being one of around 42 frescos from the time. 
“The O’Hanlon Mural is a figurative representation of the history of Lexington and Central Kentucky,” Berry’s petition read. 
He wrote of her “artistic choices that abstract the essential truths of the art as opposed to mere representation,” which he said “is part of what makes the O’Hanlon Mural unique and a valuable piece of the cultural assets of Kentucky held in trust by the University.”  
The Lexington Herald-Leader reported in January 2026 that the mural remains in its place on campus. 
‘Radical and eclectic’  
The late bell hooks, a renowned Kentucky author known for her many writings on feminist theory, racism and love, among other topics, wrote fondly of Berry in “belonging: a culture of place,” one of some 40 books she published throughout her career. 
She praised him for the “wide range of issues in his essays that were fundamentally radical and eclectic.” She taught at Berea College from his book about race, “The Hidden Wound.” 
Berry also inspired actor and writer Nick Offerman of Parks and Recreation fame. Offerman, himself an outdoorsman, has narrated several of Berry’s books for audiobook format, including his magnum opus, “The Unsettling of America.” 
In a 2020 interview with Literary Hub, Offerman said in Berry he “unexpectedly found a chronicler of the nobility found in good, honest work, and thrift, and affection for one’s family and neighbors and animals and the land that supports and nourishes all of the above.” 
“I have often asserted that if my job were simply to broadcast the works of Wendell Berry to the world, I’d die a happy man,” Offerman said in that interview.
Honors 
Former President Barack Obama awarded Berry with the 2010 National Humanities Medal for his work as a poet, novelist, farmer and conservationist. 
He also earned other notable honors, including the T.S. Eliot Prize, the Aiken Taylor Award for poetry, the John Hay Award of the Orion Society and the Richard C. Holbrooke Distinguished Achievement Award of the Dayton Literary Peace Prize, according to the Poetry Foundation. 
In 1961, he traveled in France and Italy as part of a Guggenheim Fellowship, a prestigious honor for “exceptional individuals in pursuit of scholarship in any field of knowledge and creation in any art form under the freest possible conditions.” The Fellowship has gone to other notable writers including Ada Limón, Roxane Gay, Carmen Maria Machado and Sigrid Nunez. 
His slew of other honors include the Kentucky Libraries Award’ for Intellectual Excellence, the Thomas Merton Award, The Cleanth Brooks Medal for Lifetime Achievement from the Fellowship of Southern Writers,  the Martin E. Marty Award for the Public Understanding of Religion from The American Academy of Religion, the Poets’ Prize and others. 
For a list of Berry’s books, visit this site. 
Funeral arrangements are incomplete at this time.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Here’s how we verified Senatobia Police Chief Vanderford’s racist text messages
authors: Mukta Joshi and Joseph Cranney, Verite News
description: Harold Vanderford, left, took over as chief of the Senatobia Police Department in October 2025.
text:
Mukta Joshi is a reporter at Mississippi Today. She is spending a year as a New York Times Local Investigations fellow. Joseph Cranney is a reporter at Verite News. Both report for the Deep South Today Investigative Reporting Center in collaboration with The Times.
Ten days ago, as our team at Mississippi Today, Verite News and The New York Times reported on the Senatobia Police Department’s fatal shooting of Kohen Wiley, a 1-year-old boy, a source came forward to share texts they said had been sent by Police Chief Harold Vanderford.
An example of one text conversation our team reported on. We scrolled through messages on our source’s phone and photographed them. That’s why there’s a glare on some of our images. We’ve hidden our source’s response in this exchange to protect their privacy.  Credit: Mukta Joshi
The source, a colleague of the chief’s, said they suspected the chief would know who had given us the texts. But they agreed to let us publish the messages if we agreed not to publicly identify them.
The source showed us 10 text conversations from July 2025 to April 2026. In them, Vanderford uses a racist slur more than a dozen times, spelled various ways. As we previously reported, Vanderford wrote multiple times that he had been loudly and repeatedly saying the slur, sometimes so loud that his neighbors might have heard it. In one text, he wrote that he “almost beat a nigger and white woman’s ass a few minutes ago.”
Our source said these text conversations were between them and the chief. We took a number of additional steps to verify their authenticity. Here’s why we stand behind our reporting that Vanderford sent those texts:
1. The numbers lined up.
Under the contact labeled “Hal Vanderford” on our source’s phone, the number listed was 662-897-6708. We are publishing the full number in the interest of transparency.

No one answered at that number, and there was no personalized voicemail greeting. So we contacted three separate acquaintances of Vanderford’s, each of whom confirmed that the number we had matched the number they had saved for Vanderford. In the days since, that phone number has been disconnected.
We captured a photo of the phone number the text messages had come from, and noted it down.  Credit: Mukta Joshi
2. We looked for context clues.
In one of the text messages, Vanderford says he’s with a woman, whose name we’re withholding to protect her privacy. Two acquaintances of the chief identified her as the chief’s girlfriend. The woman is pictured with Vanderford on her Facebook profile, too.
Another text message includes a photo of a person who the chief calls “GAY!!!” We identified that person as a employee at the department. 
Vanderford appears to have sent a number of text messages while watching college sports games, and we separately learned that the chief is a Mississippi State fan.Mississippi State’s schedules show that Vanderford was texting contemporaneously on dates when the Bulldogs were playing. On Oct. 18, Vanderford texted about a football game against Florida. Mississippi State played the Gators that day — we checked. 
3. We reviewed the attached video and photos.
A message the chief sent on Thanksgiving Day includes a video attachment. The man recording the video can be heard addressing our source by name, saying, “You’re missing out.” The metadata of the video shows it was recorded two minutes before it was sent, on the same day. 

We had already obtained the chief’s home address through his voter registration records and spoken to his neighbors, who confirmed he lived there.
So we compared the video he’d shared to a Google Street View image taken in February 2025 from the angle of the chief’s home. The images lined up perfectly.
At left: A screenshot from a video sent by Senatobia Police Chief Harold Vanderford on Thanksgiving Day in 2025. At right: A Google Street View image dated February 2025, captured from the angle of Vanderford’s home address. 
4. We asked Chief Vanderford himself. Many times. 
We first contacted Vanderford on Friday, Aug. 21, and have since made more than a dozen attempts to reach him by phone, email and notes left at his home or office, sharing the specifics of our findings, and explicitly asking for his side of the story.As recently as Monday, we asked Vanderford and Lt. Shane Howell, a Senatobia police spokesperson, if Vanderford denies the texts came from him.Neither have responded to our inquiries.
Below, we are publishing Vanderford’s uncensored text messages. 












Editor’s note: Mississippi Today does not normally publish racist slurs, but we chose to do so in this case because the slurs themselves are central to why our team reported this story.

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA state workers stage walkout amid clash over pay demands
description: With contract negotiations nearing a critical deadline, hundreds of Washington state workers walked off the job for an hour Monday to highlight demands for wage hikes in their next two-year deal. Roughly 100 employees from an array of agencies lined Capitol Way in Olympia, most facing the domed Legislative Building where Gov. Bob Ferguson’s office […]
text:
Roughly 100 state employees lined Capitol Way in Olympia, Wash. to demand higher wages in their next two-year contract. (Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard)With contract negotiations nearing a critical deadline, hundreds of Washington state workers walked off the job for an hour Monday to highlight demands for wage hikes in their next two-year deal.
Roughly 100 employees from an array of agencies lined Capitol Way in Olympia, most facing the domed Legislative Building where Gov. Bob Ferguson’s office is located. They waved signs, shook cowbells and chanted throughout the noon hour, periodically interrupted by honks from passing vehicles.
The negotiations have led to rising friction between union workers and Ferguson, a Democrat heading toward the third year of his first term, and the third consecutive session where he and legislators will have to navigate a budget shortfall.
Ferguson proposed state worker furloughs in 2025 but lawmakers shelved the idea after union backlash.
“We’re not going to agree to furloughs. We’re not going to agree to cuts,” said Ashley Fueston, vice president of the Washington Federation of State Employees. “We’re not going to agree to takeaways. That’s not acceptable.”
Statewide, employees from more than 100 worksites delivered similar messages as talks on a new collective bargaining agreement enter their final month. Another rally is planned for Saturday at the state Capitol.
State law sets an Oct. 1 deadline for unions to ratify agreements to be considered for funding in the next two-year budget. Failure to meet the deadline can result in an extension of an existing contract without a wage hike, as one public employee union experienced last year. Those workers eventually got paid retroactively.
The Washington Federation of State Employees, which represents 52,000 state government, higher education and public service workers, organized Monday’s walkouts to demonstrate frustration with the progress of talks and the state’s failure to propose adequate pay hikes.
“I think they are just testing our unity. That’s what it seems like to me,” said Sam Brown, who has worked more than a decade with the state Department of Agriculture. He and several colleagues carpooled from their Tumwater office to attend the Olympia event.
“We understand the state has limitations. But there are ways to try to deal with it,” he said. 
For example, he said, a base wage hike could be agreed on, and contract language added to boost it should state tax collections come in higher than estimates relied on by state negotiators.
“If it’s better, we do better,” Brown added. 
Monday’s statewide action followed a mini-protest on Friday where a handful of union members showered the governor with chants as he attended an event at Western State Hospital.
“We’re negotiating. I don’t have anything else to add,” Ferguson said when asked about the workers’ demands.
On Monday, Brionna Aho, Ferguson’s communications director, cited the challenging budget environment clouding this year’s negotiations. 
“In the past 18 months, we implemented billions of dollars in budget reductions,” she wrote. Aho added that the state is also dealing with “draconian cuts” from the Trump administration, including ones that eliminate health care coverage for thousands of Washingtonians.
Wage hikes can amount to a chunky increase for the state budget. The last round of labor agreements yielded general wage increases of 5% — 3% in July 2025 and 2% last month. The total cost of the contracts was about $1.7 billion.
“As he develops his budget, the governor is focused on preserving core services for the most vulnerable people in our state,” Aho said. “In working to accomplish that goal, the governor will face many difficult choices, and understands not everyone will be happy with his decisions.”
Washington state employees walked out of their worksites Monday to protest for higher wages in their next two-year contract. (Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard)
Fueston said it sounded like the governor “is trying to make the case for no wage increase.” Friday is the final scheduled face-to-face negotiation session for the unit representing general government workers, she said. 
One major issue, health care costs, is apparently resolved.
Fueston said a deal reached last week ensures the state will continue to pay 85% of monthly premiums with employees paying the remaining 15%. The state wanted employees to pay a larger share. Maintaining the status quo for all state workers will cost $348.5 million in the next biennium, she said.
“That was huge. That covers every public employee,” Fueston said. 
But the health care agreement wasn’t top of mind for workers at Monday’s rally.
They said they feel disrespected by the governor and his administration’s negotiators from the Office of Financial Management, so much so they wrote a chant.
“OFM you cannot hide, we can see your greedy side.”
One sign waved at passing drivers referenced grounds maintenance work and impolitely targeted Ferguson.
“We cut the grass, Bob can kiss our a**,” it said.  
“I have really supported Bob in the past, so it feels disappointing to be out here having to hold a sign like this,” said Sierra Keough, an accountant at the Department of Social and Health Services. “I didn’t make it, but I hold it with pride.”
Workers at both the Friday and Monday events suggested Ferguson was not living up to commitments he made while campaigning.
“What we’re fighting for is the opposite of what he ran for and promised us,” Keough said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Feds suspend permit for road construction through Alaska wildlife refuge, amid legal questions
description: Federal regulators have suspended a wetlands-fill permit allowing construction of a controversial road through an Alaska national wildlife refuge, but the on-the-ground result of that action is a subject of legal contention. State officials say they still intend to start the work in coming weeks on the first part of the road that is planned […]
text:
Green eelgrass appears at low tide in the vast wetlands of Izembek Lagoon, at the edge of Izembek Refuge on April 17, 2021. The refuge has one of hte world's biggest eelgrass beds, making the area a globally site for migratory birds. (Photo by Kristine Sowl/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)Federal regulators have suspended a wetlands-fill permit allowing construction of a controversial road through an Alaska national wildlife refuge, but the on-the-ground result of that action is a subject of legal contention.
State officials say they still intend to start the work in coming weeks on the first part of the road that is planned to cross through the Izembek National Wildlife Refuge. But environmental groups and Native tribal governments who oppose the road argue that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers’ Aug. 26 suspension of the wetlands-fill permit for the road project precludes work on any part of it.
At issue is an 18.9-mile road that would link the isolated Alaska Peninsula community of King Cove to the military legacy, all-weather airport at Cold Bay. The road, as planned, would cut through an area of designated wilderness within the wildlife refuge.
The Corps in July issued a wetlands-fill permit to the state, a key permit needed for road construction. But on Aug. 18, U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason overturned a land trade that was necessary to allow construction of the road project. The state said it plans to appeal the decision. 
“You are directed to stop any activities that were previously authorized by the suspended permit. . . . Any further work in these areas shall be considered a knowing, repeat, and flagrant violation of Federal law,” the Corps said in its letter following the ruling to the Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities.
The permit suspension will give the Corps time to evaluate the full implications of Gleason’s decision on the land trade, the letter said.
There is disagreement about what the now-suspended permit covers, however.
The Department of Transportation and Public Facilities holds the position that the suspension should not interfere with this fall’s plans, and that it still has the right to build the first 2.8-mile section of the road, according to a department spokesperson
That portion of road is not subject to the wetlands-fill permit because it would not require disposal of fill into waters, state officials argue. And the area involved is outside of the disputed land trade, on land already owned by the King Cove Corporation, the community’s village Native corporation, state officials said.
“The State still plans to begin construction in September. The 2026 construction does not rely upon this permit, as it will not discharge fill into Waters of the U.S., including wetlands,” Justin Shelby, the Department of Transportation and Public Facility’s Central Region administrative operations manager, said by email. 
Areas considered “Waters of the United States,” a legal term, are subject to certain Clean Water Act requirements.
Shelby pointed out that the state itself asked for the permit suspension. In the department’s request letter, the state argued suspension of the permit would reduce possible confusion in the ongoing litigation and allow the federal court “to consider all arguments raised by the plaintiffs without the perception of pressure from the State of Alaska’s need to rely on the permit authorizations.” 
The environmental and Yukon-Kuskokwim tribal plaintiffs who have challenged both the land trade and the wetlands-fill permit, in contrast, argue that the entire road is covered by both authorizations, and that any construction now would be illegal.
 

Emperor geese forage at Izembek National Wildlife Refuge on Oct. 5, 2016. More than half of the world’s emperor geese use the refuge, according to federal biologists. (Photo by Kristine Sowl/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)
 

	Suspension of the permit was good news for road opponents, one of the plaintiff attorneys said.
“What a huge relief to see this permit pulled, because it was clear that Trump officials were ignoring the law with these destructive plans. A road would completely ravage Izembek’s globally important wetlands,” said Rebecca Noblin, Alaska legal director at the Center for Biological Diversity. “The refuge is vital for ​migratory birds that Y-K Delta Tribes like Hooper Bay, Paimiut, and Chevak depend on for food. No administration should be allowed to ignore federal public land protections to push construction projects through crucial wildlife habitat.”
Tribes in those three villages have sued to block the land trade and overturn the Corps permit.
The Corps on Monday declined to comment on the opposing legal interpretations, citing policies on pending litigation. The Corps’ public affairs officer referred questions about the subject to the U.S. Department of Justice.
The Department of Transportation and Public Facilities has mobilized equipment and materials to start building the initial 2.8-mile section. That portion of the road includes a bridge that is “the most complex and expensive feature of the entire road construction project,” according to a state Department of Law status report filed in federal court on Aug. 20.
The state expects an allocation of $18 million for the project during the current fiscal year, with nearly $16.4 million of that coming from federal funds and the remainder from a state match, according to the statewide transportation plan.
The Izembek road proposal has been debated for decades.
State officials argue that it is needed as a lifesaving access for the approximately 750 residents of King Cove. Environmentalists argue that it would harm globally important wetlands and would set a bad precedent for protected lands elsewhere in the nation.
The debate has also divided Native groups.
King Cove residents, largely Aleut and shareholders in the Aleut-owned corporation involved in the disputed land trade, have advocated for it. They say that flying in and out of the  King Cove airport is dangerous in bad weather, while the nearby Cold Bay airport, with a runway extending over 10,000 feet, can accommodate jets providing safe air travel in most conditions.
Members of some Yup’ik tribal organizations on Western Alaska’s Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta, however, argue that the road would do substantial damage to wetlands habitat for migratory birds that are important to traditional subsistence hunting.
The refuge’s lagoons support hundreds of thousands of migratory birds each year, including nearly the entire global population of Pacific black brant and more than half the world’s population of emperor geese.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: No recommendations on autism care  as task force completes second meeting
description: A Florida task force that could recommend a wholesale revamping of services used by some of the state’s needy children spent hours Monday looking at applied behavioral services (ABA) and how and when they are delivered. The blue-ribbon panel is in the information-gathering mode and has not yet recommended how it plans to bring in […]
text:
Applied Behavior Analysis encourages positive behavior and discourages negative behavior for autism and other special-needs patients. 
(Photo by Jack Forrest/ Indiana Capital Chronicle)A Florida task force that could recommend a wholesale revamping of services used by some of the state’s needy children spent hours Monday looking at applied behavioral services (ABA) and how and when they are delivered.
The blue-ribbon panel is in the information-gathering mode and has not yet recommended how it plans to bring in spending on the services.
Information Shena Grantham, Florida’s deputy secretary for Medicaid policy, shared with the panel Monday a breakout of Medicaid ABA funding and where the services are being provided.
Relying on fiscal year 2025-26 claims data Grantham said:

$1.61 billion was spent on ABA services in the home.
$620.7 million on ABA services in schools.
$351.6 million on ABA services in office settings.
$150.8 million for ABA services in the community.

She told the task force that in Florida the average length of time a recipient receives ABA services is 32.5 months. A breakout of the data shows about 10,000 people have received ABA services for five years or more and about 8,000 people receive ABA services for less than six months.
Applied behavior analysis uses structured interventions to decrease maladaptive behaviors and reinforce appropriate ones. ABA is common in the treatment of children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. ABA also is used for people with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, traumatic brain injuries, intellectual and developmental disabilities.
The Legislature established the 10-member task force as part of fiscal year 2026-27 budget negotiations. The task force is reviewing revisions of the state’s healthcare delivery model to “improve care experience and service continuity for enrollees and families receiving ABA services, while safeguarding long term program sustainability.”
The group is supposed to have its recommendations finalized for the Florida Legislature by Dec. 31. Agency for Health Care Administration Secretary Shevaun Harris, chair of the panel as well as a non-voting member, suggested the group complete the bulk of its recommendations by the end of October but acknowledged that wasn’t “set in stone.”
The panel is expected to meet again Sept. 16.
In addition to hearing from Grantham, the panel heard from Center for Medicaid and CHIP Services Principal Deputy Director Caprice Knapp; Director of the FSU College of Medicine Autism Institute Amy Wetherby; and Peggy Aune, vice chancellor for strategic improvement for the Division of Public Schools in the Department of Education.
CHIP is the Children’s Health Insurance Program, and income-based health insurance for kids.
Knapp, who spent 10 years of her career at the University of Florida doing Medicaid research for the agency, discussed the recent State Medicaid and CHIP Applied Behavior Analysis Toolkit, published by the Trump administration.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) released the 173-page document meant to “support state Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) agencies in making decisions regarding ABA service provision for Medicaid and CHIP.”
The toolkit doesn’t carry the official weight of law or regulation, Knapp said.
“And again, these aren’t these are not binding. States always have the ability to take the information from the toolkit and go forward,” she said.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Costs, benefits of data centers take center stage at legislative meeting
description: North Dakota lawmakers studying data centers heard concerns Monday about transparency and nondisclosure agreements while others touted the potential economic benefits.  Many of the people who spoke during public comment raised issues about data centers, with some advocating for a moratorium on data center development, despite legislators’ decision not to tak[...]
text:
Sam Wagner, president of the Casselton City Council, speaks during an Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee meeting on Aug. 31, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota lawmakers studying data centers heard concerns Monday about transparency and nondisclosure agreements while others touted the potential economic benefits. 
Many of the people who spoke during public comment raised issues about data centers, with some advocating for a moratorium on data center development, despite legislators’ decision not to take up the issue during this week’s special session.
“The people have been overwhelmingly in favor of a moratorium,” said Sam Wagner, president of the Casselton City Council. 
Wagner, also an organizer with the Dakota Resource Council, suggested creating state-level regulations to serve as a floor of requirements, allowing local communities to tailor for specific policies if they wish. 
Signe Snortland, a Democratic candidate for the Legislature in District 33, said there has been a notable lack of transparency and public engagement by data center developers in communities like Oliver County. 
“It’s time to slow the roll,” Snortland said. “Let’s do this the right way.” 
Yet others, including Kevin Pranis, representing Laborers’ International Union of North America, said data centers can be built in a way that can benefit everyone. 
“The data centers are actually a critical tool that we can offer to bring new people into construction, into these trades, to do work that we’re going to need for decades and generations to come,” Pranis said. 
Wes Klein, a Mercer County rancher, speaks during an Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee meeting on Aug. 31, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Robert Mayo, a research specialist at North Dakota State University’s Challey Institute of Global Innovation and Growth, warned against banning them completely. 
“Banning data centers guarantees there will be no problems. It also guarantees there will be no benefits,” Mayo said. 
Nondisclosure agreements
Aaron Birst, executive director of the North Dakota Association of Counties, cautioned lawmakers on banning nondisclosure agreements for data centers and other industrial projects, which is a proposal for this week’s special session. 
He said that while some officials were taken off guard and may have signed NDAs with data center developers early on, county commissions have come around to the idea that they are generally a bad idea. But there are some cases where certain information should be protected. 
“Land values will jump up as soon as everybody starts speculating, so there is some basis to have some privacy,” Birst said. “But the citizens need to know if somebody’s coming to town to build.”
North Dakota Legislature prepares for 2nd special session this year, with public testimony Tuesday

Sen. Janne Myrdal, R-Edinburg, said she’s heard citizens say they are not being listened to or informed of projects on the local level. 
“It’s a little troubling to hear,” Myrdal. 
Birst pointed to the fact that a citizen can check the front page of a newspaper and see meetings attended by hundreds of people as evidence the projects are being handled with transparency, but acknowledged open meetings laws can be violated. 
“The status quo, while sometimes uncomfortable, is generally working,” Birst said.
Decommissioning
Multiple people expressed concern there are no provisions for decommissioning a data center down the road.
Public Service Commission Chair Randy Christmann said his agency could develop a program that would plan for taking down a data center after it is no longer in use. The agency manages a coal mine reclamation program and has rules for wind farms to set money aside to pay for dismantling them. 
“If you want to have a reclamation program for AI centers, we can create that, but you need to give us some guidance on how extensive you want it to be,” Christmann told the committee.
Nick Phillips is the executive vice president of external affairs for Applied Digital, which operates the data center at Ellendale. He said data centers don’t need a reclamation program because the buildings have potential for other uses, such as a manufacturing facility. 
Nick Phillips, executive vice president of external affairs for Applied Digital, speaks during an Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee meeting on Aug. 31, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
“I don’t think it makes sense for a taxing body to want its single largest taxpayer in its county, city, whatever, to erase that value when somebody else could use it,” Phillips said.
But he did provide an estimate for what it would cost to tear down an Applied Digital data center building of more than 900,000 square feet — $90 million.
‘Fearmongering’
Mayo said North Dakota has experienced examples of good and bad development practices for data centers in recent years. The difference has been community engagement. 
He said Atlas Power in Williston ran into problems because it built a data center with shorter setbacks that exposed residents to constant noise, and the company chose to build in an area without an excess of electricity available. 
Mayo pointed to Applied Digital’s development of a data center near Ellendale as an example of good community engagement and listening to residents’ concerns. 
“That kind of transparency breeds good will,” Mayo said. 
The Ellendale project has not been without controversy. Local landowners have complained about traffic congestion, damage to roads from construction vehicles, inflated rental rates and other concerns. 
Rep. Todd Porter, R-Mandan, said he views opposition to data centers differently. 
“It seems like the fearmongering has really gotten out of control,” Porter said. 
Rep. Mary Schneider, D-Fargo, speaks during an Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee meeting on Aug. 31, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Rep. Mary Schneider, D-Fargo, pushed back on that. 
“Rep. Porter called it fearmongering. Other people call it concerns for life, health and safety,” Schneider said. 
Wagner and other members of the public cautioned lawmakers against overlooking critics of data center development in the state. 
“Dismiss your critics at your own risk,” Wagner said. 
Mayo said some fear is understandable and the solution is more transparency to shed light on the unknown. 
“Everyone on some level understands that this is going to change the world,” Mayo said. “That kind of change is scary.”
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge can be reached at jorledge@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC father at center of US Senate ad says he was ‘swindled’ by GOP political operatives
description: Ronald Hayes was cautious when he talked to a reporter this week about the political TV advertisement he appears in, talking about the death of his son Shemar, a college football player who was murdered in Charlotte in March 2024 at age 23. “I have already been swindled into an ad that was about politics, […]
text:
Ronald Hayes, left, and his son Shemar Hayes. (Photos: Ronald Hayes)Ronald Hayes was cautious when he talked to a reporter this week about the political TV advertisement he appears in, talking about the death of his son Shemar, a college football player who was murdered in Charlotte in March 2024 at age 23.
Ronald Hayes (Courtesy Photo)
“I have already been swindled into an ad that was about politics, which I don’t want to be about,” Hayes told NC Newsline on Monday.
Despite his intentions, the ad has landed him squarely in the middle of one of the nation’s most watched races.
Hayes says he was tricked by the Senate Leadership Fund, a well-heeled Republican political action committee.
Hayes says he agreed to talk to the video crew about his son’s murder because he thought he would be featured in an  ad against gun violence. But the ad is actually aimed at smearing the political record of former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate.
The TV ad Hayes appeared in has been viewed more than 25 million times on Youtube. It’s part of a $17 million advertising campaign targeting Cooper, who faces Republican Michael Whatley in November. 
Shemar Hayes (Courtesy Photo)
The ad falsely implies that Cooper released Shemar’s killer from prison early as part of a legal settlement during the COVID-19 pandemic. However, Tyzavian Smith, the man convicted of killing Shemar, was 18 at the time Shemar was murdered in 2024, was not in prison, and had no prior adult record. 
NC Newsline could not reach the Senate Leadership Fund for comment. The group has also been accused of using a murder committed by a South Carolina man to attack Cooper as soft on crime. 
“The commercial looks as if I’m trying to sway North Carolinians from voting the way that they want to vote, and that wasn’t my agenda,” Hayes said. “I wanted to let the community know about gun violence and about my son being murdered.”
“Once I saw the commercial, I called [the ad makers] back and I asked them again, and they stated again that they are independent,” Hayes said. “I told them that I felt that this was deceiving, it was conniving and it was sneaky how they used me and my family to get out their word.”
Hayes said he’s now being stopped on the street by people wanting to know if he’s the “guy in the commercial” and whether he’s Democrat or Republican.
“What difference does that make?” said Hayes, a Democrat. “The agenda was not political. It was to get my son’s name said and to speak on gun violence.”
North Carolina’s Senate race no longer a toss-up, top forecasters say, with Cooper in the lead

Hayes said he plans to speak with Cooper to let him know that his intent was not to harm his campaign. He said he doesn’t have anything against Cooper and has “voted for him in the past.”
“I want to turn this tragedy into something beautiful that can possibly make a change,” Hayes said. “I want my son’s name to be able to be used to make this change.” 
Hayes has published a book, titled “Living Through Loss: A Journey of Healing and Hope,” to share the story of Shemar’s death, but also how he lived his 23 years of life. He said the ad’s producers recorded him and took pictures of him talking about that book and others he’s written, but did not include them in the ad.
“That was not their agenda,” Hayes said. “They could care less than a damn about me and my books.”
The still-grieving father said he blames his son’s death on what he says are weak gun laws that are ineffective in keeping guns out of the hands of people who would use them to harm others.
Becky Ceartas, NCGV. (File photo)
A statewide anti-gun violence group agrees with Hayes, and is condemning the political ad and the Republican PAC that paid for it. North Carolinians Against Gun Violence says it is outraged at the commercial, which it says twisted a grieving father’s pain for political gain.
“Losing a child is every parent’s worst nightmare,” said Becky Ceartas, executive director of NCGV. “Every survivor of gun violence deserves to be treated with respect and care if they decide to relive the most horrible day of their lives by telling you their story.” 
NCGV called on television stations across the state to pull the political ad from the airwaves.
“Our organization works with survivors of gun violence throughout the state, and we have witnessed how hard and traumatic it is for them to tell their stories,” said Ceartas. “It requires an immense amount of trust and faith that the person you are sharing this deeply personal experience with will treat it with dignity and respect.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont veterans, Guard families seek support for Defend the Guard Act
description:
"The Constitution is clear that Congress — not the President acting alone — possesses the authority to decide whether the nation enters war," the letter from 27 Vermont veterans and Guard family members states.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont veterans, Guard families seek support for Defend the Guard Act.
text:
Vermont National Guard soldiers salute during a deployment ceremony at the Ethan Allen Firing Range in Jericho in May 2026. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Chris Mays was first published in the Brattleboro Reformer on Aug. 30, 2026.
A letter from 27 Vermont veterans and Guard family members urges Gov. Phil Scott and legislators to support the Defend the Guard Act and expresses “deep concern about the deployment of Vermont National Guard members into foreign combat without Congress first debating and authorizing those military actions.”
“The Constitution is clear that Congress — not the President acting alone — possesses the authority to decide whether the nation enters war,” the letter states. “When Congress debates and votes on military action, it does so as the representative body of the American people after public deliberation and consideration of the risks, costs and objectives involved. Those constitutional safeguards exist for a reason. They help ensure that the decision to place Americans in harm’s way receives the scrutiny such a grave decision deserves.”
The Vermont Defend the Guard Act, the letter states, “prohibits deployment of the Vermont National Guard to overseas combat absent congressional authorization for the conflict. It does not prevent the Vermont National Guard from responding to floods, natural disasters, emergencies, civil support missions under Title 32 or training exercises under Title 10, among other lawful duties. Nor does it interfere with the Guard’s ability to defend our nation when Congress has properly authorized war.”
The legislation was introduced in a majority of states and passed legislative chambers in Arizona, Idaho, New Hampshire and Virginia, according to the letter.
“The effort has attracted support from veterans, military families, civil liberties advocates, constitutional conservatives, libertarians and progressives who share a belief that Congress should fulfill its constitutional responsibility before Americans are sent into combat,” the letter states. 
The letter calls for a public legislative hearing. With turnover in the Legislature and changes in committees, Rep. Ian Goodnow, D-Windham-9, said at a Select Board meeting earlier this month, “I would anticipate this legislation being introduced again, even by maybe more than one rep or senator, and it will get its day in court.”
A bill introduced last year would require the governor to review orders placing Vermont National Guard units into federal active duty for military conflicts for compliance with the U.S. Constitution, according to the letter. 
“The letter comes as approximately 200 members of the Vermont Air National Guard remain deployed to the U.S. Central Command region after being sent on consecutive missions, first to the Caribbean in connection with the U.S. military operation in Venezuela and then to the Middle East amid the war with Iran,” a news release states. 
Referencing the deployments of the Vermont Guard for combat in Venezuela and Iran, the letter states, “Regardless of our views on those conflicts themselves, many Vermonters were troubled that Congress did not publicly debate or vote on these military operations before Guard members were placed in harm’s way.”
“As a combat-wounded veteran of the Vietnam War, I’d like to paraphrase my fellow Vietnam veteran, John Kerry: How do you ask a man or a woman to be the first, or the last to die for a mistake?” Sgt. E-5 Charles F. Monette, 1st Cavalry Division (retired), of Brattleboro, who signed the letter, said in the news release. “Let’s allow the men and women of Congress to deliberate, to debate, and to decide when and why and how to wage war. I would think the rationale for sending our men and women to war would be lessened. Suffering on all sides would be diminished.”
Isaac Evans-Frantz, a member of the Brattleboro Select Board and the director of Action Corps, said the town recently received news that Brattleboro Fire Chief Jay Symonds, a member of the Army National Guard in New York, will be on leave for a year of military service “amid the undeclared war against Iran.”
“Deployments like this have a real impact on Vermont’s small communities,” Evans-Frantz told the Reformer. “I am grateful for Chief Symonds’ service and pray for his safe return to his family and our town.”
Guard members, their families and Vermont communities are in “a difficult position,” Evans-Frantz said.
“We need to do everything we can to protect Guard members and reclaim the Guard for the American people,” he said. “Ensuring adherence to the U.S. Constitution can help ensure that any decision for military deployment occurs only after a vote by Congress. It is the least we can do to respect our service members — our fire chiefs, police officers and all the members of the Guard — who put their lives on the line every day for our local communities and our country.”
Deployment “takes a toll on a family,” retired Lt. Col. Jane Sbardella of Dummerston, who signed the letter, said in the news release.
“We don’t want our sacrifice wasted unless total mobilization is warranted,” Sbardella said. “It is critical now to protect our National Guard in Vermont.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont veterans, Guard families seek support for Defend the Guard Act.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Senate Corrections Chairman Juan Barnett resigns from Legislature
description: Sen. Juan Barnett is seen on the Senate floor at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Feb. 12, 2026.
text:
Sen. Juan Barnett, a three-term Democratic legislator from Heidelberg and chairman of the Senate Corrections Committee, resigned from the Legislature on Monday, Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann said in a statement. 
It’s unclear why Barnett resigned, and he did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but he has dealt with health issues that caused him to miss several weeks of this year’s regular legislative session.
“We thank Senator Barnett for his years of service to the state of Mississippi and wish him a happy and well-deserved retirement,” Hosemann said in a statement. 
Barnett took office in 2016 and has served as the chairman of the Senate Corrections Committee since 2020.  He has represented portions of Forrest, Jasper and Jones counties in the Senate. 
Barnett in the past pushed for earlier release and shortened sentences for many incarcerated in Mississippi prisons, despite his father being shot to death in the early 1990s while Barnett was in the Army deployed to Iraq, and the shooter receiving a relatively short sentence. Barnett said he believes in forgiveness and giving people second chances.
Barnett missed several weeks of the 2026 legislative session because of an extended illness. Gov. Tate Reeves will now have 30 days to set the date for a special election.
While he was absent from the Capitol, legislation that attempted to improve medical care in Mississippi prisons died on key deadlines. The vice chairman of the committee at the time said she let the legislation die at Barnett’s direction. 
Before serving in the Legislature, Barnett was the mayor of his hometown of Heidelberg. 
Mississippi Today reporter Michael Goldberg contributed to this report.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: ‘Not the place to commit financial crimes’: Utah aims to better fight complex scams
description: Utah is stepping up its efforts to investigate scams and connect the dots between them with a new hub that’s the second of its kind in the nation.
text:
Utah Attorney General Derek Brown speaks at a news conference announcing the state's new Financial Crimes Intelligence Center on Aug. 31, 2026. (Annie Knox/Utah News Dispatch)Utah is stepping up its efforts to investigate scams and connect the dots between them with a new hub that’s the second of its kind in the nation, state leaders said Monday.
They want the Financial Crimes Intelligence Center in the Utah attorney general’s office to form a new line of defense against increasingly sophisticated operations, including those using artificial intelligence to multiply their reach, said Utah Attorney General Derek Brown.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The problem is growing, he told reporters, with Utahns losing $108 million to financial crimes last year and almost $60 million so far this year. Once someone’s been scammed, Brown noted a bank typically flags the problem, a police department will open a case and a hotline will field a call from the victim seeking help. 
“But ultimately, none of these organizations are talking with each other,” Brown said. “So it’s hard to know if they’re part of a larger, organized crime ring. There’s a gap. And today the FCIC is filling that gap.” 
Utah lawmakers this year gave their support to the center, committing to $1.7 million in yearly funding. Senate Majority Leader Kirk Cullimore, who sponsored the budget request, said it fits with the Legislature’s recent move to protect digital identity and sends a strong message. 
Lawmakers convene in the House Chamber at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on the first day of the legislative session, Tuesday, Jan. 20, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
“I think this will signal that we are not the place to commit financial crimes,” Cullimore, R-Sandy, said during Monday’s news conference at the state Capitol. 
As they pieced together the plan for the center, state officials met with law enforcers in Texas to learn about a state fraud intelligence center there, Brown said after the news conference. The Utah team’s goal is to bring in enough information to recognize patterns, he told Utah News Dispatch. 
“And frankly, AI is going to help us do that as well,” Brown said, adding that component is still taking shape. “You know, we can use the same tools that they use — to benefit us.”
He’ll measure the success of the program in part by how much money is returned to victims after judges order restitution, Brown said. But it will be more difficult to know how many people never fall victim because of prevention and heightened awareness, he added.  
To fight elder fraud, a top Utah law enforcer is meeting with seniors around the state 

The center’s employees include two prosecutors, two investigators, a forensic accountant, an analyst and a paralegal. They report to a division director in the attorney general’s office overseeing mortgage and financial fraud cases, Brown said. 
Surrounded by representatives from banking and credit union associations at the news conference, Brown and Cullimore said Utahns who fall victim to fraud should not feel ashamed. 
Cullimore said within the last week, someone in his household accidentally gave credit card information to a fake website. And Brown recounted how an attorney friend lost millions to a sophisticated real estate scam.
 “I just want you to reach out, I want you to report it, because a $30,000 fraud that takes place in Cache County and a $30,000 fraud taking place in Washington County may actually be connected,” Brown said. “Our job is to identify that connection.”
Howard Headlee, president of the Utah Bankers Association, added it’s important to file a report right away so investigators can get to work. 
“In these cases, time is of the essence. Time is critical,” Headlee said.  
To report fraud to the center, visit its website at fraud.agutah.gov.

title: Bottoms ups the ante in feud over debates in race for Georgia governor
description: Months after the campaigns of Republican Rick Jackson and Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms first issued challenges to the other over when, where and how to debate ahead of the November elections, there’s still little agreement on how voters will hear from each of the two candidates for governor. So far, both campaigns have agreed to […]
text:
Democratic Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson, both candidates for governor, speak at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens, on Aug. 5, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderMonths after the campaigns of Republican Rick Jackson and Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms first issued challenges to the other over when, where and how to debate ahead of the November elections, there’s still little agreement on how voters will hear from each of the two candidates for governor.
So far, both campaigns have agreed to only one town hall-style debate hosted by Atlanta News First and Gray Media on Oct. 6. 
The Bottoms campaign first challenged Jackson to three debates in June, to which the Jackson campaign responded by proposing one debate. Nearly two months later, Bottoms agreed Monday to it and is now pushing for five more.
“Georgians deserve to hear directly from candidates for public office with multiple debates around the state,” Bottoms said in a statement. “I’m ready to debate Rick Jackson in Atlanta, Macon and Savannah.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Aside from the ANF debate both candidates agreed to, Bottoms is also challenging Jackson to the Atlanta Press Club Loudermilk-Young debate on Oct. 12, another on Sept. 17 hosted by Middle Georgia Matters, an 11Alive debate on Sept. 22, a WJCL-TV debate on Oct. 13 and one hosted by CNN at an undetermined date.
The Jackson campaign criticized the move, with campaign spokesman Garrison Douglas saying that “only the flailing campaign of a failed politician would spend more than six weeks ducking a debate, then suddenly demand six of them after Georgians begin to learn the truth about her disastrous record as mayor of Atlanta.”
The Democratic Party of Georgia instead focused on Jackson not yet accepting the Atlanta Press Club debate. Jackson participated in the press club debate during the Republican primary but cited a scheduling conflict with the debate scheduled for the primary runoff with Lt. Gov. Burt Jones.
“Over two months later and Jackson still won’t commit to a debate that gubernatorial candidates in both parties have participated in for more than twenty years,” said DPG spokesperson Jake Strickland.
The Jackson campaign has not yet indicated a reason for not accepting the Atlanta Press Club debate, where a panel of journalists ask the candidates questions.
Debates are unlikely to change voters’ minds, but participating in them provides candidates a massive platform to build name recognition and excitement amongst voters, said University of Georgia political communications professor David Clementson. 
Clementson said  it’s in both candidates’ interest to participate in as many debates as possible in what he called the “the single most watched political events by far.”
“The upside far outweighs the downsides for both of them, as far as any kind of risk versus reward,” Clementson said. “The rewards outweigh the risk for both of them to be in as many debates as possible to get attention to help boost their profile amongst their bases. They need to remind their supporters, their partisan-aligned supporters, who they are and that they’re running for governor and why they need to get out and vote in this election.”
Candidates can miss on the opportunity to mobilize their supporters by skipping or limiting debates, but Jackson, who won the Republican nomination for governor despite skipping the Atlanta Press Club debate during the runoff, could be feeling confident that he can succeed again in November without it, Clementson said.
“That might be his thinking there, but he needs to be reminding the general election Republican voter base,” he said, adding that “the effect of general election debates is crystallizing the support, crystallizing your base, solidifying your support base, because each side is going to need their respective base to turn out and vote for them in this election.”
